# PREFACE

I can only argue in defense of my book that it is the work of a pioneer, and every pioneer knows that his efforts must necessarily be basic and flawed. I anticipate all the harsh criticisms that reviewers will level against my work, and I shall be more than satisfied if what I have written encourages others to conduct further research.

More should have been said about the lives and teachings of **Hōnen** <note>Hōnen (1133–1212) was the founder of the Jōdo-shū, the first independent branch of Japanese Pure Land Buddhism.</note>, **Shinran** <note>Shinran (1173–1263) was a pupil of Hōnen and the founder of the Jōdo Shinshū sect.</note>, and other leaders of the **Jōdo** <term>Jōdo</term> <note>Literally "Pure Land"; a branch of Buddhism focused on achieving rebirth in the Western Paradise through devotion to Amida Buddha.</note> or Pure Land sects. This omission is because I have already discussed these thinkers in a monograph titled *“Shinran and His Work,”* which I published in Tokyo last year. Even with these omissions, I fear this book will seem quite large.

I owe my sincere thanks to the Master of **Peterhouse** <note>The oldest constituent college of the University of Cambridge.</note>, who went to great lengths to assist me.

->A. LLOYD.<-

Tokyo,
    June 24, 1911.

# PREFACE

I can only argue in defense of my book that it is the work of an earnest and very sincere seeker of truth, and more specifically, of instruction. I trust those who follow my work will feel that my labors are more than rewarded if I have written effectively enough to influence others.

More should have been said about the passions and the imagery of **Milton** <note>John Milton (1608–1674), the English poet and intellectual best known for his epic poem *Paradise Lost*.</note>, along with aspects of his local spirit and character. This omission is due to the fact that I have already addressed those matters in a monograph titled *“Milton and His Works,”* which I published in Tokyo last year. Even with these omissions, I fear this book will seem rather large.

My best thanks are due to the Master of **Pembroke** <note>Likely the Master of Pembroke College, Cambridge; during this period, this would have been William Sheldon Hadley.</note>, who has gone to much trouble on my behalf.

->G. Y. O.<-

Tokyo,
June 21, 1917.

# THE CREED OF HALF JAPAN

## CHAPTER I

### MAHĀYĀNA

<margin>L</margin>
Mahāyāna <term>Mahāyāna: Literally "Great Vehicle," a branch of Buddhism that emphasizes the path of the Bodhisattva and the salvation of all beings.</term> is a form of Buddhism. The word means "the Large Vehicle" or "Conveyance." It is used to distinguish this later and expanded form of Buddhism from Hīnayāna <term>Hīnayāna: Literally "Smaller Vehicle," often used to refer to the Theravada tradition which focuses on individual enlightenment.</term>, or the "Small Vehicle," which contains the doctrines of the form of Buddhism that is purely Indian. 

The original language of the Hīnayāna Scriptures is Pali, which was the language spoken in Magadha during the lifetime of Shakyamuni <note>Shakyamuni (S’akyamuni): The historical Buddha, Siddhartha Gautama, who lived in the 5th or 6th century BCE.</note>. In contrast, the Mahāyāna books were written in Sanskrit, the literary language of the Brahmans. This language was adopted by Greeks, Parthians, and Scythians as a means of theological expression when they each, in turn, became masters of Northwest India and the fertile valleys watered by the Indus River and its tributaries in the Punjab <note>original: "Punjaub"</note> and Afghanistan. Sanskrit became the language used in many controversies concerning both human and divine philosophy as Brahmans and Buddhists competed for the spiritual supremacy of India during the early centuries of our era.

It would be a mistake to assume that the Great Vehicle differs from the Lesser only because it contains more subtle logic and daring speculation. That is not the case; the Pali books are in every way as deep and as full of speculation as their Sanskrit...

<summary>This page introduces Mahāyāna Buddhism, explaining its name as the "Large Vehicle" and distinguishing it from the earlier Indian Hīnayāna tradition through their distinct linguistic and geographic origins.</summary>
<keywords>Mahāyāna, Hīnayāna, Buddhism, Sanskrit, Pali, Shakyamuni, Indian history, Punjab, religious philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the comparison between Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna Buddhism, explaining how the expansion of Buddhism outside of India led to its development from a localized Indian faith into a universal religion.</meta>

rivals. The Hīnayāna is called the "Lesser Vehicle" only because it is more geographically limited. It draws its inspiration from India and from India alone. If it had been possible to confine Buddhism within the borders of the Magadhan kingdom, or even within the limits of Ashoka’s <note>original: "As'oka"; Ashoka the Great (r. c. 268–232 BCE) was the Mauryan emperor who famously patronized Buddhism.</note> actual territories, we can reasonably assume it would have remained Hīnayāna only. This has been the case in Sri Lanka <note>original: "Ceylon"</note>, where the religion has not been forced to deal with deeply modifying or disruptive influences. 

But once Buddhism moved beyond the borders of India to seek converts among the Greeks, Parthians, Bactrians, Medes, Turks, Scythians, Chinese, and the chaotic mix of nations that makes the history of Central Asia so complex, its horizon immediately expanded to include many external elements of philosophical thought. It was no longer the comfortable "family carriage" in which India alone might ride to salvation; it became a spacious "omnibus" intended to accommodate people of all races and nations, conveying them safely to the perfection of enlightened truth. 

It is true that it never forgot its origins; it always spoke of itself as a religion intended primarily for the Indian world. With a certain modest hesitation, it tried to explain away the inconsistency of its own missionary zeal. The boundaries of India were imagined to expand as Buddhist missionaries advanced toward the East. The Hindu Kush and the Himalayas ceased to be the final borders of the sacred land of Jambudvīpa <term>Jambudvīpa: An ancient Sanskrit name for the world or the Indian subcontinent, literally meaning "the land of the rose-apple tree."</term>. Over time, Jambudvīpa came to include Central Asia, China, and even Japan.<sup>1</sup>

***

<sup>1</sup> Nichiren <note>Nichiren (1222–1282) was a Japanese Buddhist priest who founded the school of Buddhism that bears his name.</note>, for instance, constantly speaks of *ichi-en-bu-dai* <note>original: "ichi em bu dai"; this is the Japanese phonetic rendering of the Sanskrit "Jambudvīpa."</note> as equaling India, China, and Japan. This was a protest, by way of adaptation, against the idea that a Buddha could not be born outside of India.

<summary>This page explains how Buddhism evolved into the "Great Vehicle" (Mahāyāna) as it spread from India to Central and Eastern Asia, incorporating broader philosophical ideas and expanding its geographical definitions.</summary>

# MAHĀYĀNA

The Mahāyāna <note>Sanskrit for "Great Vehicle."</note> was probably a matter of slow and, at first, unnoticed growth. Among the numerous sects which divided the Hīnayāna <note>Sanskrit for "Lesser Vehicle."</note> at the beginning of the Christian era, some were probably more inclusive and advanced than others. There must have been some which had almost reached the expansive fullness of the Mahāyāna itself. Very little indeed is known of the history of Buddhism between the death of Ashoka <note>original: "As'oka"</note> and the dawn of the Christian era—the period, that is, when the Mahāyāna was in its formative stage <note>original: "state of gestation"</note>. What we do know is that about the end of the first century CE—between five and six hundred years after the death of Buddha—the Mahāyāna came into existence in Kashmir, Northwest India, and the valley of the Indus. It enjoyed the patronage of the Scythian <term>Scythian: An ancient nomadic people from Central Asia who established the Kushan Empire in India and became major patrons of Buddhist art and culture.</term> conquerors of those districts, whose conversion to Buddhism may have been due, in the first place, to a strategic <note>original: "politic"</note> desire to gain favor with their newly acquired Buddhist subjects. It was distinguished by several great saints and scholars <note>original: "doctors"; here meaning learned teachers or theologians.</note>, and it spread from the land of its birth to the most distant regions of Northern and Eastern Asia.

It is not necessary in this work to write a long and detailed biography of Shakyamuni <note>original: "S'akyamuni"; the historical Buddha.</note>. That subject has been thoroughly covered by many great scholars, and Japan has very little new material to contribute toward it. I shall take up the main thread of my story from the time when the Mahāyāna makes its first distinct appearance on the stage of Eastern religious life—that is, during the first century CE. In doing so, I shall also have to touch on the early beginnings of Christianity. This was a contemporary faith which, in those early days, converted the West while failing, by comparison, to win the East for Christ, just as the Mahāyāna seemed to be hindered from

...[is now] making an impression on the West, while it has developed freely and achieved lasting success in the lands of the Far East. Throughout these pages, I will present several points (leaving it to the reader to decide how convincing they are) to show that the two faiths—Buddhism and Christianity—came into actual contact with each other at many points during the first and second centuries CE. I will also argue that each contributed to the other's successes and failures. This is a very difficult subject to handle. Before I begin my work, I can only pray—a good, old-fashioned custom for which I feel almost embarrassed to have to apologize—that nothing I write will offend against the sacred cause of Truth, which should be the only goal for both a scientific and Christian scholar.

However, before starting the main subject, it seems appropriate to devote a few short chapters to examining the life of the Founder <note>The historical Buddha, Shakyamuni.</note> and the extent of Ashoka's <note>original: "As'oka"; a 3rd-century BCE Indian emperor who promoted Buddhism throughout his empire and beyond.</note> influence. This influence is evident in the rock inscriptions <note>Known as the Edicts of Ashoka, these inscriptions were carved into pillars and cave walls throughout the Indian subcontinent.</note> that the monarch left behind. These chapters will allow the reader to more accurately judge the level of knowledge that Europe and India likely had of one another at the time when Christianity and the Mahāyāna <note>original: "Mahāyāna"; Sanskrit for "Great Vehicle," the branch of Buddhism dominant in North and East Asia.</note> emerged simultaneously.

# CHAPTER II

## THE STAGE ON WHICH SHAKYAMUNI MADE HIS APPEARANCE

The Sutras <note>Sacred scriptures of Buddhism, believed to record the spoken teachings of the Buddha.</note>, which are generally accepted as providing an authentic account of the teachings of Shakyamuni <note>The historical Buddha, also known as Siddhartha Gautama.</note>, also provide us with certain geographical and other information. This data is essential if we want to form an accurate picture of India in the sixth century BCE—the India in which Shakyamuni taught and labored.¹

We do not need to look at a very large geographical area. What concerns us is a small part of the Ganges Valley, consisting mostly of the two districts of Awadh <note>original: "Oudh"</note> and Bihar.² This region stretches east as far as Patna and west as far as Allahabad. The Himalayas form the northern border of Shakyamuni’s country, while the Ganges River is practically its southern limit. The only exception is Bodh Gaya <note>original: "Bodhigaya"</note> and the district closely connected with the Enlightenment of the Tathagata <note>A title the Buddha used for himself, often translated as "The one who has thus gone" or "The one who has thus come."</note>, which lie to the south of 

---

¹ Compare, in Japanese, "Treatise on the Life of Buddha" <note>original: *Buddha no Juseiron* by Maeda</note>; in English, *Buddhism in Translations* (by Warren), and *The Gospel of Buddha* (by Paul Carus); and in German, "The Discourses of Gotama Buddha" <note>original: *Die Reden des Gotama Buddhas* by Neumann</note>. The first of these is the most useful for this book because it was compiled from an openly Mahayana <note>The "Great Vehicle" branch of Buddhism popular in East Asia.</note> perspective.

² It is difficult to overestimate the importance of the sixth century BCE, which saw the start of so many religious and philosophical movements.

³ Bihar is said to derive its name from *vihara* <note>A Sanskrit and Pali term for a Buddhist monastery.</note>. It was one of the last strongholds of Buddhism in India, just as it had been one of the first.

### SHAKYAMUNI'S STAGE

...from one another by tribal names as well, such as the Licchavis, Vrijjis, Mallas, and Andhas, some of which remain to the present day. The Shakyan nobles,¹ it is said, welcomed the person of Shakyamuni, their kinsman prophet, whose teachings encouraged them in their resistance to Brahmin <term>usurpations</term> <note>original: "usurpations"; the seizure of social and religious authority by the priestly class</note>. However, they were not always equally willing to adopt his practical teachings. The Brahmins, who were ultimately victorious in the struggle for political and religious supremacy in India, have had their revenge on these Shakyan tribes by refusing to consider them as families of pure descent. It is hard to determine the point. All Buddhists claim that Shakyamuni’s lineage came from *Ikshvaku*,² the descendant of Manu, the descendant of the god Brahma. The Licchavis ruled later, by virtue of their <term>Kshatriya</term> <note>the warrior and ruling caste</note> descent, in Nepal, Bhutan, Ladakh, and (through marriage) in Tibet; the Licchavi dynasty in Nepal was succeeded by a line of Malla kings. At the same time, it must be admitted that we have from the very earliest times traces of contact between Nepal, Tibet, and China, which should be considered.

China—as shown by the late Professor Lacouperie and others, for example <note>original: "e.g."</note> Mr. Morse (in his "Trade and Administration of the Chinese Empire")—was occupied, before the arrival of the Chinese from Western Asia, by many aboriginal groups.

As Mr. Sylvain Lévi has said, it is impossible as of yet to adequately define the extent of the influence exerted on Buddhism in ancient <note>original: "remote"</note> times by China and neighboring countries.

Buddhism has always been the religion of merchants. The Sutras <note>original: "Sūtras"; the recorded discourses and scriptures of the Buddha</note> tell us of many wealthy traders who supported the monastic order <note>original: "the order"</note> by their generous donations. There must have been a great volume of trade. The Shakyan <note>original: "S'akyan"</note> nobles, who constantly address Shakyamuni <note>the historical Buddha</note> as *Gotama* <note>Gautama; his family name</note>, or "herdsman" (apparently a common way of addressing someone), were of the same race as the herdsmen of the Himalayas. There is at least one Sutra which speaks of a wool merchant from across the mountains, and it is indeed to wandering Shakyan herdsmen that the opening up of the valley of Lhasa <note>original: "Lhassa"</note> in Tibet <note>original: "Thibet"</note> is attributed. One of Shakyamuni’s earliest disciples was a merchant’s son from Benares named Yashas <note>original: "Yas'as"</note>. He has been identified (wrongly, I believe) with Shānavāsa <note>original: "S’anavas'as"</note>, the third patriarch <note>a high-ranking leader or founding father of the faith</note> of the Northern succession. It is true he may only have been the captain <note>original: "skipper"</note> of a Ganges barge; but there are two later patriarchs of whom it is explicitly stated that they had traveled as far as Turkestan.

This seems to me to be another instance of very early interaction <note>original: "intercourse"</note> between India and China, or at least with those districts of Central Asia which had early connections with that empire.

Repeatedly, when reading the biographical accounts of Shakyamuni’s activities, we find that his converts were people who had been searching for the truth for many years. In some cases, such as that of Uruvilva Kashyapa, they had been religious teachers themselves and brought their own followers with them to join the ranks of Shakyamuni's disciples. But it seems that before Shakyamuni's time, there was only one known path for a seeker of truth to follow: the way of severe self-discipline <note>original: "austerities"</note> and physical penance. This path brought power and influence to the priestly Brahmans, but it did not always lead the seeker to the much-desired enlightenment and peace.^2

# THE CREED OF HALF JAPAN

Not all these seekers were convinced by Buddha’s methods. Shakyamuni <note>the historical Buddha</note> had many rivals, at least one of whom founded a belief system that has endured to our own time. Mahavira, the founder of the Jain sect, was a contemporary of Shakyamuni. He died in the Kosala country, not many miles from the place where Shakyamuni went to his rest, apparently in the same year as his more celebrated rival. Jainism and Buddhism are related faiths, and the Jains and Buddhists seem to have always looked upon one another as brothers, or at least as spiritual cousins.^1^

It was in such a country and in such an age that Shakyamuni was born. As the son of Suddhodana, King of Kapilavastu, and his wife, Lady Maya, his birth is said to have been accompanied by miracles which really belong to a later chapter of our book. His boyhood was marked by an extraordinary intellectual maturity <note>original: "precocity"</note> and purity of character. The wise men summoned to the palace at the time of his birth,^2^ and especially one of their number, the aged sage Asita, told the happy father that the newborn babe would be either a world-changing emperor or a world-saving Buddha. The father, perhaps feeling that "charity should begin at home" <note>an idiom suggesting the King preferred his son to stay and rule his own kingdom</note>, determined that, if possible, his son should be prepared for the first of the two options. Young Prince Siddhartha was brought up as became a Shakyan prince of high rank; trained in arms, literature, and science, he was surrounded...

# S'AKYAMUNI'S STAGE

Many incidents, however, show that his mind was not at ease in the midst of all his luxury, and this feeling of dissatisfaction was increased by several sights which brought home to him the inherent misery of the world. A ceremonial ploughing festival, which it was his duty to attend as Crown Prince, revealed to him the strife within Nature: the upturned earth showed worms cut in two by the ploughshare, becoming prey for the birds that followed in the wake of the ploughman. Shortly after, at short intervals, he met an aged person, a sick man, a corpse, and a holy monk. He learned about the sorrow and pain in the world, and also learned that there was a way to escape from the "*Welt-schmerz*" <note>world-weariness or existential dread</note>, and he resolved to follow it. He had received his calling, and he obeyed that vocation.

It was not mere selfishness that led him to leave his home to pursue the Truth. When he bent over the sleeping forms of his beloved wife and his newborn son at the moment of his departure, he resolved that once he had found the Way, he would come back and save his loved ones; and he kept his promise. But the Way was not easy to find, and the search was long and difficult. For six long years—through self-imposed fasting, austerities, and penance—his strained soul, dwelling in an emaciated body and constantly exposed to the temptations of Māra, the Evil One, searched patiently for the Truth, but

<center>THE CREED OF HALF JAPAN</center>

...in vain. At last he gave up his fruitless efforts, ate food after a long fast, had one last struggle with the Evil One who tried to appeal to his pride and fear, and then sat down "under the fig tree" at Bodhi-Gaya and awaited enlightenment. If he had been a Christian or a Jew, we might have said that "he listened to what the Lord God would say to him."

What his soul heard was as follows: "(1) There is Pain in the world, and Pain is universal. (2) All pain is the result of Desire (*Trishna*). (3) Destroy Desire and you free yourself from Pain. (4) There is a path by which you can attain the Destruction of Desire, and its end is Liberation." This Liberation is what is known as Nirvana, and the "result of Desire," which leads to action, is Karma.

These propositions are known as the Four Great Truths. They contained nothing new, and yet the light which S'akyamuni shed upon them was fresh. *Karma* and *Nirvana* were words well known in India before S'akyamuni's discovery of them; the things themselves were known in Greece and to the Jewish people.

The great question of the retribution that follows human actions had been brought solemnly before the Asian world by the impressive fall of the Babylonian Empire, and before both Asia and Europe, during almost the same lifetime as S'akyamuni himself, by the defeat of Xerxes at Marathon and Salamis. The Greek theologian-poet Aeschylus treated this theme in his "*Eumenides*," and again in his tragedy the "*Persians*." The prophet of the Captivity, Ezekiel, had been proclaiming a new law of retribution to his countrymen (Ezekiel 18). Each soul, said the prophet, should bear its own burdens; there should be no more reason to say in Israel, "the fathers had eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth had been..."

Desire, <term>Karma</term>, the wheel of Life and Death: the quenching of Desire, the Destruction of <term>Karma</term>, the Peace of <term>Nirvana</term>.<note>If we remember that most Pali writers speak of the Enlightenment as the *Nibbana* and of the Death as *Parinibbana*, we shall have some light on the word *Nirvana*. It works unobtrusively, but surely; yet it can be broken. 

There is what <term>S'akyamuni</term> calls a noble **Eight-fold Path**, of right views, right aims, right actions, etc., which leads in time to the destruction of evil <term>Karma</term> by the quenching of Desire, and it seems to have been <term>S'akyamuni</term>'s life-work to instill into his hearers the way of the Noble Path, which alone can lead to emancipation. Of philosophy he spoke but little;<note>Neumann, "*Buddha*" (Danish edit.).</note> the so-called Philosophy of <term>Buddhism</term> was a later product.

<term>S'akyamuni</term> was no atheist. He did indeed teach that the enlightened <term>Buddha</term> was higher than the gods of the <term>Brahman</term> pantheon—higher than <term>Indra</term>, <term>Varuna</term>, <term>Agni</term>, <term>Emma-San</term>, or <term>Kompira Sama</term>, who now occupy subordinate places in Buddhist temples. These gods were creatures of imagination, subject—like Venus, Juno, and Neptune—to the Law of Change, and liable to the same extinction that has befallen the gods of Assyria and Babylon, of Egypt, Greece, and ancient Rome. To move from the denial of such gods to the denial of all gods is a very long step, and I think it can be shown that <term>S'akyamuni</term> never took it. Rather, I would say—and this I hope to make clear as I proceed—that wherever <term>S'akyamuni</term>'s own influence reached, it served to give people higher and truer ideas of the Divine Nature, and that his teachings were thus intended to prepare the way for the acceptance of the highest of all truths.

<column-break/>

...had united North-West India and the Central Asian lands for a short while under one rule. The history of the <term>Amitābhā</term> doctrine is well explained in the *<term>Shôshinge Kōwa</term>*, to which I have already referred. <term>Amitābhā</term> is the original <term>Buddha</term>, the First Cause, the Father—not exactly the Creator, but the originator of the Law of Cause and Effect through which the universe came into existence. He has revealed himself many times—the long list of previous Buddhas in the *<term>Sukhāvati Vyūha</term>* being recorded to give definiteness to this idea—and <term>S'akyamuni</term> was the latest of these manifestations. The <term>Ophite Gnostics</term> held exactly this idea, making Christ a still later manifestation who superseded all that had gone before, just as <term>Amitābhā</term> supersedes all other previous Buddhas. In connection with the questions raised here, a Japanese scholar with a great interest in religion has pointed out to me that in some early forms of the Apostles' Creed, there is no clause "Creator of heaven and earth." I shall have to refer to the character used for writing "<term>Buddha</term>" later on. Here I would point out that, to the <term>Shinshu</term> believer, <term>Buddha</term> is always <term>Amitābhā</term>, whose "Divine Name" is pronounced in worship as *<term>Namu Amida Butsu</term>*. This formula is interpreted to mean, "Trust in me; I will save you," which is not a literal translation of the formula, but is instead an interpretation of the Name of Christ. The <term>Shinshuists</term> call this formula "the Divine Name of the Six Letters," for which see <term>Irenæus</term>, book ii, chapter 24.

# CHAPTER III
## THE BUDDHA AND HIS GREATEST DISCIPLE

THANKS to the labors of many students of the Buddhist books, both Pali and Sanskrit, we are able to form a vivid mental picture of the ministerial life of the Founder of Buddhism; indeed, the general indications of time are so wonderfully precise that we can trace his labors year by year for fully half of the forty-six years which his ministry occupied. There is a gap of about fifteen years near the end of his career for which we have no precise sequence of events; but even here we are not left entirely in the dark, for there are many indications given of the troubled days through which India in general, and the Buddhist community in particular, was then passing.¹

<note>¹ Northern Buddhists attribute the pronouncement of two or three most important <term>Sūtras</term> to the closing years of this period of silence. # BUDDHA AND HIS GREATEST DISCIPLE

We are shown the successes that followed S'akyamuni’s first preaching. Conversions were numerous and rapid; converts of all ages and both sexes flocked to his community from every class of society and were welcomed without distinction of caste or rank. Thousands caught the enthusiasm of the Buddha and left everything to follow him, while among the crowds who felt no calling to the monastic life were kings and merchants, who competed with each other in the generosity of their gifts.

Among all these varied people, S'akyamuni moves like a king among men. Bimbisara recognizes the inherent kingship within him and offers to make him the Crown Prince of the kingdom of Magadha; S'akyan noblemen proclaim him as the teacher and saint of their clan. The universal respect in which he is held is shown most strikingly by his arbitration of a dispute over water rights, which the involved tribes referred to him. Evidently, the historical <term>Tathāgata</term> was a practical person, far removed from the ecstatic dreamer of the <term>Hokekyō</term>.<note>¹ This is the Japanese name for the “<term>Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra</term>.”</note>

Religious India needed a sound mind with a practical bent, for the times were full of trouble. Wars and rumors of war troubled the minds of the people; there was civil strife in Magadha, and the sounds of more distant thunder came rolling over from Western Asia. All these hindered “the turning of the wheel;” so did <term>Amitābha</term>. Clearly, such concepts as the unity of the Godhead and salvation by faith were known in India at a very early date. The troubles in Magadha, the civil wars that ended in the destruction of Kapilavastu, and some of the conspiracies against S'akyamuni’s life all fall into this “period of silence.” Beyond the borders of India, all of Asia was caught up in the excitement of the great preparations for the expedition of Xerxes against Greece. In the appendix to “Bukkyō Seiten,” Dr. Maeda provides a very convenient chronology of S'akyamuni’s life, which is likely, however, based on the work of Western scholars.

    S’akyamuni was a brave and strong man, but he felt the disagreements among his disciples very deeply. He soon took political steps to inform his subjects of his change of heart; and he has left us a series of edicts, inscribed on rocks and pillars in different parts of India, which provide our best insight into the character of his religious aspirations. By the year 249, his mind was turning definitely towards the acceptance of the teachings of S'akyamuni in preference to those of any other religious teachers who laid claim to the allegiance of religious India. He went on a solemn pilgrimage to the sacred places of India with Upagupta, the patriarch of the Northern School, as his guide. The sight of the Lumbini grove, where S'akyamuni was born; of Bodhigaya, where he attained Enlightenment; of Benares, where the Wheel of the Law was set in motion; and of the Sacred Grove, in which he died, moved him apparently to a further step. In 240, he was ordained as a monk, and in the Bhābhrā Edict, dated soon after that, he proclaimed himself definitely as a Buddhist. Between As'oka's ordination and his death (which Vincent Smith assigns to <term>B.C.</term> 231) his Council must have taken place. The data for this Council are so confusing that writers like Kern have come to the conclusion that it never took place at all, but was a mere figment of chronologists and historians of the Southern School. Northern Buddhism, it is true, knows nothing of As'oka's Council, but there is nothing in this fact to justify a denial of its having taken place. It is probable that the Council did occur, and that it was an effort on As'oka's part to achieve reforms of abuses which had crept in during the 230 years which had elapsed since the death of the Founder. It is also reasonable to suppose that he labored at the Council for the promotion of those views which he had so persistently advocated in the long succession of rock edicts.

# CHAPTER IV

## THE PRE-CHRISTIAN EXPANSION OF BUDDHISM

The great As'oka, king of Maghada, the Constantine of Indian and Ceylonese Buddhism, has no official place, as I have said, in the history of the Mahāyāna, which takes absolutely no notice of the Council that is said to have been held during his reign. The Council naturally concerned only those monks who lived within As'oka's extensive dominions; the Mahāyāna seems to have originated beyond the Indus, among people, possibly of Indian origin, but who were still not subjects of any purely Indian state.

Yet As'oka is important in the study of the Mahāyāna. For, first, he enables us to correct a major error regarding S'akyamuni's date, which is still commonly made by many of the official defenders of Buddhism in Japan. The Mahāyāna books place the date of S'akyamuni's birth in B.C. 1027, and his death, consequently, about B.C. 950—a chronological misstatement that invalidates all their other calculations. For if this were true, then Aśvaghosha, who lived 500 years after the Nirvana, and Nāgārjuna, who lived in the sixth century after the same occurrence, must be assumed to have flourished respectively about the years B.C. 450 and 400, and the whole Mahāyāna system would predate the Christian era by several centuries.

---

<note>It is said that the falsification of the date was made in China, where the Buddhists were anxious to show that their religion was much</note>

# EXPANSION OF BUDDHISM

29

Fortunately As'oka is well known to us, not only from books, but also from the edicts which he has left engraved in stone in various parts of his former dominions; the data thus provided enable us to determine both As'oka's exact year and approximately that of S'akyamuni's entrance into Nirvana. From the materials at hand, Dr. Fleet¹ has been able to fix the dates for the principal events between the death of Buddha and that of As'oka. We may accept them with confidence. As'oka was anointed king on the 25th of April, 264 B.C., 218 years after the death of Buddha, which consequently took place in 483 B.C.—occurring, it is well to remember, in the interval between the battles of Marathon and Salamis.

Again, As'oka's monuments give us data by which to gauge the extent of his influence. Edict No. 2, translated by Dr. V. A. Smith,² concerns the subject of comforts for men and animals, and runs thus: "Everywhere in the dominions of King Priyadars'in, and likewise in the neighboring realms, such as those of the Chola, Pandya, Sattyaputra, and Keralaputra, in Ceylon, in the dominions of the Greek king Antiochus, and in those of the other kings subordinate to that Antiochus—everywhere, on behalf of his Majesty King Priyadars'in, two kinds of remedies have been disseminated—remedies for men, and remedies for beasts. The kings of Pergamum were famous for their collections of books and parchments (the latter being a *pergamene* substitute for the papyrus that the Egyptian government would not allow to be exported); they were also known for the botanical gardens of medicinal herbs, which predated the more famous collections of Alexandria, into which they were later merged. One of Alexander’s successors, Cassander, who thoroughly disapproved of Alexander’s policy of adopting Oriental habits and ways of life, had a philosopher named Euhemerus living at his court. He had certainly demanded personal loyalty to himself from all his followers, because he had only received them into his Order after a threefold expression of belief—in the Law, the Order, and the Buddha. His relics, divided up after his death, had become the center around which the worship of the entire Buddhist community grew. S'akyamuni was undergoing the process of deification when Euhemerus visited India (indeed, that process may already have been popularly accomplished), and the process was already being applied to other Buddhas as well. The Mahāyāna had not yet taken definite form, but its underlying ideas were in the air; when, later, we gain our first definite literary acquaintance with, for example, Amitābha, he appears as a god deified after a long succession of holy lives led in the fulfillment of his tremendous vow for the salvation of mankind. That the same process was taking place in the case of S'akyamuni himself may be seen from the development of the *<term>Saddharma pundarika</term>* and similar Sūtras,¹ and from the more certain testimony of Buddhist art.

Antigonus Gonatas of Macedon had an ambition—which he realized for a while after many years of conflict—of uniting Greece and Macedon under one scepter. He had opponents in the Achaean League and a rival in Alexander, the son of that Pyrrhus of Epirus who had defeated the Romans with the aid of elephants obtained from As'oka's father, Bindusara. Alexander and Gonatas are both mentioned in As'oka's Edict on the "True Conquest." We can imagine that the peace-loving As'oka, who was fully in touch with what was happening in the West, must have been distressed beyond measure by the desolation of Greece during this period of "False Conquests."

I have already mentioned Magas of Cyrene in connection with medicinal herbs. I need only mention, as another link in the chain showing the extent of Indian influence in the West, that among the dialogues of Aristippus—the founder of the Cyrenaic school of philosophy—there was one which bore the name of *Porus*, a name well known among Indian kings.<note>1</note> Aristippus, born <term>435 B.C.</term>, lived before As'oka, but among the later Cyrenaics was Hegesias, surnamed Peisithanatos from the intensity with which he advocated suicide as the highest form of self-immolation. S'akyamuni's well-beloved disciple, Ananda, is said to have ended his life by voluntary self-cremation, and the *Saddharma pundarika* speaks of it as the highest expression of devotion and gratitude from one who has learned the truth.<note>2</note>

Whether it was influenced by Indian thought is an inquiry beyond our present limits.<note>1</note> But it is evident that the relations—commercial or otherwise—between Alexandria and India were close and constant. The influence was not one-sided. inscriptions that he has left us. In them we shall find Buddhism as it existed in As'oka’s mind, and as As'oka believed it had existed in the mind of S'akyamuni. I can do no better than summarize the contents of the inscriptions.

I. In the first, As'oka speaks of his care to provide medicines and medical herbs for the use of the sick, trees for shade, and fountains for men and cattle; he calls attention to the fact that he has done this not only within his own dominions, but also in those of his neighbors, *e.g.*, in the territories of King Antiochus and in Taprobane (Ceylon).

II. In the second, he speaks of the killing of animals, urges his subjects to abstain from such evil practices, and explains his own custom. He was once in the habit of allowing many animals to be killed for the royal feasts; during recent years the number of animals thus killed has been very small. From now on, there shall be no killing of animals in the royal kitchens.

III. He urges provincial and city governors, and all teachers of religion, to be diligent in teaching obedience to parents, kindliness and courtesy, respect for Brahmans and Buddhist monks, and moderation in speech and conduct, to all who come under their authority.

IV. He speaks with gratitude of the good effects upon the general public of the religion which he has been teaching throughout his dominions. He is glad to find that civic and social virtues, filial piety, respectfulness, kindliness, and toleration are everywhere on the increase.

V. In order to spread further the virtues taught by his religion, he appoints superintendents of morals for all creeds throughout his dominions, as well as in the neighboring countries of the Yavanas, Kambojas, Gandhāras, etc. (these were probably subject or tributary

XIII. A survey of his own life. He describes the horrors of the war against the <term>Kalingas</term>, and his own remorse when he realized the cruelties associated with it. He resolves from now on to reject the role of a conqueror.

### XIV. An abridged edict containing the points on which Piyadasi, the Beloved of the Gods, wishes to insist.

His empire is a vast one, but he has done his best, through inscriptions, to ensure that every part of the empire is provided with the necessary moral teachings. He wants all his subjects to be familiar with the religious law.

The fourteen Edicts mentioned above form a continuous series, as it were, and are found in several versions in different parts of India. There are also isolated Edicts, the contents of which are roughly as follows:

1. *a* and *b*. To the officials at Tosali and Samāpā, urging them to be more diligent in the care of the people entrusted to them, so that those who are doing well do not fail, and those who fail may be restored. The most essential thing in religion is perseverance and patience in doing good. Officials should take care to guide men in the right way, so that they may live without fear and follow their religion. These edicts are to be read publicly to the people at the monthly festivals of the full moon, and privately whenever necessary. His Majesty has taken care to hold a solemn assembly in his own territories every five years, and the princes of Ujjain and Taxila will do the same.

Next to Parthia came Bactria,¹ the reputed home of Zoroaster himself. Bactria asserted its independence in the same year as Parthia. It had Greek kings and a small percentage of Greek settlers, the remnants of the Macedonian invasion; but its main population was probably of S'akyan origin. Indian writers speak of the Bactrian people as Vrijji,² the same name that we found among the Nepalese S'akyans of S'akyamuni's time, and recognized them as being Kshatriyas by caste, though their standing was compromised by reason of intermarriages with other nationalities. Their religion was a mixed one—Parthian, Brahmanic, and Buddhist—with probably a slight preference for the last.
</margin>

Bactria borders the Pamirs. East of the Pamirs, and north of what is now Tibet, lived the S'akyas, separated from the S'akyan brethren of India and Nepal by the common pasture lands of Tibet. When they later emerged from their mountain strongholds, they were divided into four tribes: the Asii, Pasiani, Tokhari, and Sakarauli (Strabo, ix. 8). It is recorded (Kern, “<term>Buddhist</term>mus,” ii. 272) of the Northern Patriarch Dhîtika that he made conversions through his labors among the Tokhari, who eventually gave their name to the whole of that tribe of S'akyans. Ashoka's envoys did not reach these tribes, but there were many traders who carried the faith.

# CHAPTER V

## PUSHYAMITRA

PUSHYAMITRA was an important factor in the development of the Mahāyāna, whose claims to distinction have generally been overlooked.

As'oka, it is evident, ruled over a very extensive kingdom and was one of the great monarchs of his day. It has always been a matter of wonder how his empire, so great and apparently so firmly based on righteousness and judgment, should have come to such a speedy ruin after his death that the Mauryan family practically disappeared from the annals of India.

A recent writer in the *Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal*<note>See *Journal and Proceedings of the Asiatic Society of Bengal*, vol. vi., No. 5 (May, 1910), “Causes of the Dismemberment of the Maurya Empire,” by Mahamahopadhyaya Haraprasad S'astri.</note> calls attention to the fact that As'oka's policy was one of unmerciful antagonism to the Brahmans, whose most cherished prejudices he took pride in shocking. As'oka had, by precept and example, discouraged the taking of animal life, and had thereby put an end to much of the worship of the Brahman rites. He had appointed “superintendents of morals,” <term>Dharma Mahāmātās</term>, whose functions necessarily superseded those of the Brahmans as expositors of the law. He had proclaimed the principle of <term>Vyavahāra Samatā</term>, “equality of punishment,” “equality in lawsuits,” which did away with the peculiar privileges

---

<summary>This page introduces Pushyamitra’s significance to Mahāyāna Buddhism and explores theories regarding the rapid collapse of As'oka's Mauryan Empire. It suggests that As'oka's policies, which challenged Brahmanical rituals and legal privileges, created significant religious and social friction.</summary>
<keywords>Pushyamitra, Mahāyāna, As'oka, Mauryan Empire, Brahmans, Dharma Mahāmātās, Vyavahāra Samatā, Haraprasad S'astri, India, Buddhism</keywords>

--- Page 62 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the downfall of the Mauryan Empire, focusing on how King As'oka's egalitarian policies alienated the Brahman caste and how the general Pushyamitra eventually seized power.</meta>

Above all, he had boasted that he had, in a short period of time, reduced "those who were once regarded as gods"—that is, the Brahmans (whose privileges as the "twice-born" seemed to entitle them to a near-divine position in the eyes of India)—to the position of false gods whose claims to respect he had shown to be baseless.

It could not reasonably be expected that the Brahmans would accept such drastic changes without resentment. They were not warriors, however, and their only course of action was to yield to the pressure and wait for a favorable opportunity.

The opportunity came around 185 B.C., during the reign of one of As'oka's weak successors, the last of the Mauryan dynasty. The Greeks were still active, pushing their conquests further and further east and founding principalities, some of which seem to have still existed at the beginning of the first century A.D. As'oka had lived on good terms with his Greek neighbors; his successors found it necessary to fight against them to defend their own shrinking territories, and the commander-in-chief of the Mauryan army was a man named Pushyamitra. It has been suggested, based on the ending of this man's name, that he was of Persian descent. He was certainly a very determined enemy of the Buddhist religion, and he had the trust of the Brahmans, who had been waiting for their moment and quietly growing in numbers and influence.

After a successful campaign against the Greeks, who had advanced into the very heart of the Mauryan country, Pushyamitra returned in triumph to Pataliputra. A military review was held; in the middle of the festivities, the Mauryan emperor suddenly fell dead, killed

Hinduism was once more the dominant faith, though a Hinduism more elaborate and more philosophical than it had been, and one that had come into fertilizing contact with foreign influences. Buddhism was in its turn downtrodden and oppressed.

But beyond the limits of the kingdom ruled over by the new dynasty, there were principalities and kingdoms in which Buddhism found a welcome and a home: the principalities of the Greeks, the Parthians, the Yuetchi, and the S’akas, who come and go around the northwestern borders of India during the two troubled centuries that precede the Christian era.

It is here, rather than in India itself, that the seeds of thought must be sought which ended by making the Mahāyāna so very different from its more southern and more purely Indian sister. Buddhism has always been a faith that has readily absorbed whatever in its immediate surroundings it has found suitable for its purposes. ## CHAPTER VI

### THE NEW TESTAMENT IN TOUCH WITH THE EAST

There are a few passages in the New Testament which seem to relate to the subject we are discussing. I propose to address them in this chapter.

The visit of the Magi will immediately occur to the mind of every Christian reader as having (or being intended to have) some bearing on the relationship between Christianity and the country or countries from which the Wise Men came. The account given in St. Matthew presents many difficulties due to the apparent impossibility of providing a scientific explanation for the star which is said to have guided these Eastern sages to the cradle of the Infant Savior; consequently, many people, even devout Christians, are inclined to treat the visit as unhistorical. At the present time, we do not have the evidence required to prove the historical accuracy of the story, and it would therefore not be wise to place too much emphasis on the account in the Gospel record. However, certain deductions are clearly legitimate. It is quite clear that St. Matthew believed the story when he placed it at the beginning of his narrative. Or, if it is argued that the narrative is not an essential part of the original Gospel, it is evident that the later interpolator recognized the story as having some important connection to the preaching of Christ in the Orient. St. Matthew’s Gospel—thanks, perhaps, to the <term>Jews of the Dispersion</term>, for whom he wrote quite as much

Capernaum served as the center of our Lord’s ministry. “Galilee of the Gentiles” was a country with a mixed population. It lay on, or near, some of the major trade routes between Rome and the unknown Orient; it must have been constantly visited by strange figures from the lands of Asia. The custom-house at Capernaum must have been frequently called upon to appraise and process bales of precious merchandise from Persia, India, and beyond. He who, before his calling to be an evangelist, had served as head of that establishment must have had many opportunities to become acquainted with travelers from distant countries. The silk trade between Asia and Europe was in the full vigor of its early development. Varro is the first Roman writer to mention the subject. <term>As’vaghōsha</term>,<note>“Bukkyō Mondō Shū,” p. 33 ff.</note> the first great teacher and inspirer of the <term>Mahāyāna</term>, is honored in Japan as the patron saint of silkworm cultivation, and it was the Jews<note>I believe it is Dr. Graetz, in his “History of the Jews,” who brings out this point. It is evident that the trade connections of Galilee of the Gentiles lay much more with the East than the West. The personal influence of the evangelist who sat at the tax office at Capernaum must have tended to spread the gospel he was commissioned to preach among the Jews of the Babylonian, Indian, and Central Asian Diasporas, and, through them, to the Gentiles among whom they lived.

It is quite clear to all students of the history of Northwest India and the lands around the Hindu Kush that things were in a state of religious ferment during the period we are discussing. Some change was imminent. The Mahāyāna was approaching the end of its period of gestation; the vague prophecies of a teacher to come had filled men’s minds with anticipation. The Greeks of Asia had felt it; they had also heard, from the stories of caravan travelers, of the great Teacher who had appeared in the neighborhood of the Sea of Galilee, and some of them went to the Passover at Jerusalem, “desiring to see Jesus,” not from any idle curiosity, but because they had been taught to look for some such solution to their difficulties.

And Christ recognized the significance of their appeal. There was nothing yet to differentiate Him from the one whom the East worshiped as the “Lord of this Saba-world,” but He knew the hidden potential. His death, His being lifted up, would give Him the magnetic power He needed. He would then begin to draw all men to Himself.

Two further points of contact between the infant Church of Christ and the East will be found in the Acts of the Apostles.

If the Acts are a genuine record of facts, Parthians, Medes, and Elamites, as well as Jews of Libya and Cyrene, and proselytes from Rome, listened to that great announcement of the gospel of Christ. # CHAPTER VII

## ALEXANDRIA AND ANTIOCH AT THE TIME OF CHRIST

**THERE** are two words that connect the Japanese *Mahā-yāna*, in one of its many aspects, with the Gnosticism of Alexandria and Antioch, and through it with the Christianity of the Apostolic age. These words are *Abraxas* and *Caulaucau*.

I have already, in a previous chapter, spoken of Alexandria and Antioch, of their mixed populations, of the extent of their commercial relations with Central Asia and India, and of the fact that As'oka's emissaries were sent to both these cities during the third century B.C. It is not necessary for me to repeat what I said then. What is of present importance is that these two cities—the two organs, so to speak, through which the commerce between Asia and Europe was conducted in the early days of the Roman Empire—were the native homes of that syncretic mixture of religious ideas known as Gnosticism. Alexandrian Gnosticism is connected with the name of Basilides,<note>¹ Basilides, (circa) 110 A.D.</note> while that of Antioch (or, rather, Syria) is connected with Valentinus.<note>² Valentinus, (circa) 130 A.D.</note>

The Gnostics, like the Mahāyānists, claimed to have the key of wisdom or knowledge and, like them, tried to interpret the various religions of the world with the help of the key that was in their hands. There seems to be no doubt that the fact of Christ was the impulse that spurred them to activity; it is equally certain that the outward form of Gnosticism varied according to the country in which it appeared. This is what makes Gnosticism such an extremely puzzling subject to the student of philosophy and religion.

Gnosticism, like Proteus, claimed to be "thrice excellent"; it "knew not only things to come, but even things past as well as present"; it had great "skill in divination"; "it was (or claimed to be) the messenger and interpreter of all antiquities and hidden mysteries." But it was at liberty, nonetheless, "to turn itself into all manner of forms and wonders of nature."¹ The underlying matter was always the same; the form differed from country to country and from age to age. The Mahāyāna exhibits a precisely similar Protean power of assuming the most varied shapes.

The existence of Buddhism in Alexandria has often been suspected. Scholars have seen Buddhists in the communities of the Essenes in Palestine, in the monastic congregations of the *Therapeutæ* described by Philo, in the Hermetic books of Egypt, and especially in the <term>κορὴ</term> <note>Kore (Maiden/Daughter), likely referring to the "Kore Kosmou" or "Virgin of the World" from the Hermetic fragments.</note>

It has also often been suspected that Gnosticism was derived from Buddhism. Again, the identity has never been clearly established, possibly because Western scholars have devoted their attention almost exclusively to the Hīnayāna Buddhism of Ceylon and the Pali books. It would not readily occur to anyone to look for traces of Egyptian Gnosticism in remote Japan.

<margin>|</margin>Yet there can be little doubt that the system known in Japan as the Shingon, and introduced into that country about A.D. 804 by the celebrated Kōbō Daishi, must be viewed as a system which is not Indian in its origin, but which has been imposed upon Buddhism from some external source, and that it is essentially Egyptian and Gnostic.

The Gnosticism of Basilides was based on the religions that the thinker found available to him in Alexandria, and the task he set for himself was apparently to reconcile the reality of Christ with the preconceived notions of the Alexandrian people. These religions were mainly two: the ancient Egyptian cults and Judaism. The mythologies of Greece and Rome apparently did not count for much in Alexandria; the philosophies in vogue were not those of the schools of Athens, nor were they the sort that Seneca or Pliny would have delighted in. The Judaism of Alexandria was of a much more liberal type (or shall we call it “broad”? to be “broad” is not always to be “liberal”) than that of Jerusalem, and the “broad” school of Jewish thought that eventually resulted in the Cabbalah looked to Alexandria as its nursery. Basilides is spoken of by Clement of Alexandria—who had better opportunities of judging than Irenæus—as a worthy man and an earnest Christian. His efforts to adapt the facts of Christ to the spiritual prejudices of the Egyptian or Egyptianized Alexandrians were probably quite praiseworthy. A missionary religion must adapt itself to the circumstances and thoughts of the people to whom it comes. <note>This thought is constantly expressed in the *Saddharma pundarika*. It was one of Nichiren's favorite topics.</note>

The system of Basilides was dualistic, like the system of ancient Egypt <note>I have taken my material mainly from Irenæus and Epiphanius.</note> and like that of the Japanese Shingon. It represented two Worlds (*Bythos* and *Zoe*), the World of Light and the World of Darkness. The former—like the glaring noon of an Egyptian summer’s day—was still, immovable, and fixed: the world of permanent ideas. The other—like the streets that are filled with life at sunset—is the world of motion, of birth, and of death; in short, the world of Nature.

In the center of the World of Light—the Diamond-World (*Kongo Kai*), as the Shingon well calls it to denote its fixed and permanent nature—the Egyptians placed God, the unknown I AM, whose name the priests of Pharaoh would not pronounce. The Gnostics called him *Pater Innatus*; in the Japanese Shingon it is *Roshana*, the Buddha of Light, Eternal. From that central and eternal Deity emanate, or proceed, four Beings—Æons in Gnosticism, Buddhas in the Shingon—who surround the central God on the Four Quarters. The Gnostics termed

When an Egyptian died, his soul descended to the realms of Tuat, or Hades. Here it passed through thirteen kingdoms, each with its own guardian deity, until it finally obtained liberation at the end. The same thirteen kingdoms are found in the Gnostic book, “Pistis Sophia,” and the soul is represented as passing through them in a similar manner. However, in the Gnostic version, Jesus takes the place of Osiris. In the Shingon sect, there are thirteen Buddhas<gloss>1</gloss> and Bodhisattvas who take charge of the soul at death; the last two, Vairocana and Kokūzō, remain its permanent guardians. The entire conception of the state of the dead in Shingonism is Egyptian. It is certainly not Buddhist.

I might provide many more examples, but I must content myself with one or two. In Egypt, the guardian deity of the first of the mansions in Tuat bears a name which signifies the “Crusher of the forehead of the enemies of *Ra.*” In Japan, it is Fudō Sama, the fierce-looking but essentially kind-hearted Being who stands amidst the flames and bears in his hands a sword with which to slay the enemies of man’s soul. Shingon astronomy speaks of twenty-eight *chiku*, or constellations, seven in each quarter of the heavens; the Egyptian astronomer knew the same and spoke of them as the “gods of the twenty-eight finger-breadths of the Royal cubit.” The Shingon astronomer uses the Egyptian signs of the Zodiac,<gloss>2</gloss> which are the same as ours,

There is also the statement made concerning the Manichaean books by Cyril of Jerusalem,¹ whom, as a bishop, we must credit with trying to speak only what he believed to be the truth, and who, as Bishop of Jerusalem, probably knew a great deal about the earlier history of his own diocese. Cyril tells us of a certain Scythianus who lived in Alexandria and wrote books that claimed to be the gospel, but "did not contain the acts of Christ, but only His name," to which the *Acta Archelaï* adds that he founded his sect during the lifetime of the Apostles and came to Jerusalem in the hope of getting them approved. Scythianus had a disciple named Terebinthus,² who apparently came to Jerusalem for the same purpose but was rejected by the authorities and retired to Persia, where he took the name Buddas. These books were the basis upon which Manes founded his teachings. The resemblances between the *Saddharma Pundarika* and the *Pistis Sophia* give probability to the story. There must have been in circulation in Alexandria, during the latter half of the first century A.D., a Buddhist book or collection of books which was the <term>Ur-evangelium</term> of several heresies.

## CHAPTER VIII

### THE LEGEND OF ST. THOMAS

It is hoped that the last chapter has prepared the reader's mind to accept the idea that the beginnings of Christianity and of the Mahāyāna were closely related in time, place, and concept. Nicolas of Antioch, who became a worshipper of Caulaucau, was certainly a contemporary of the Apostles. The testimony of St. Cyril and others—to say nothing of the Buddhist Sutra, a chapter of which we have found embedded in the "*Pistis Sophia*"—may be taken as evidence of a local connection in Alexandria. Furthermore, the testimony of these same two books may be taken to show that there was a connection (which some might call a confusion) of thought in Gnostic minds between S'akyamuni and Christ.

An early Christian legend, found in the Apocryphal *Acts of St. Thomas* and supported by the testimony of Eusebius and others, connects the Apostle St. Thomas with the Indus Valley. The legend has undoubtedly been much embellished by later additions, but competent scholars have concluded that it is quite possible that it rests on a foundation of fact. Let us examine the story.<note>"Acts of the Holy Apostle Thomas" in "Ante-Nicene Fathers," vol. 8, p. 535.</note>

# THE LEGEND OF ST. THOMAS

<meta>Faint pencil brackets appear in the right margin alongside both paragraphs.</meta>

Indo-Parthian king, ruling in the Indus valley. Thus St. Thomas goes, according to one story, to India; according to another, to Parthia. Both stories may be true, assuming that he went to Indo-Parthia. Gundaphorus had a long reign, from A.D. 21 to A.D. 60, and he ruled over the districts of Arachosia, the lower Indus, Herat, and Peshawur. He was a great ruler, for the Scythian hordes of the Yuetchi had not yet swept down upon his territories, and, like great rulers, he immortalized himself in stone. He was a mighty builder, and his buildings were artistically adorned. We shall see in discussing Gandhāra art, which is the art of North-West India at the beginning of the Christian era, that it is dominated by Greco-Roman conceptions, and a recent discovery at Peshawur has given the world the name of a Greek architect for the stūpa erected by the Scythian King Kanishka in honor of S'akyamuni's relics. It is, therefore, an altogether possible story that St. Thomas should fall into the hands of kidnappers and be taken, as a slave skilled in building and architecture, to the court of a great Indian king, thus fulfilling, in spite of himself, the desires of his Master.

The Indian merchant, Abbanes, having made his purchases, returns to his master in Indo-Parthia. "They began, therefore, to sail. And they had a fair wind, and they sailed fast until they came to Andrapolis, a royal city." The Syrian trade with India went overland as far as the head of the Persian Gulf, and from there by sea to the mouth of the Indus. If St. Thomas was sold as a slave and taken to India, it would be by that route that he would be taken. Andrapolis means the "city of the man," and Purushapura, the modern Peshawur, has the same meaning. Purushapura was, as the legend says, actually the royal city of Gundaphorus.

After serving Gundaphorus for some time at Andrapolis, or Purushapura—where he preached the gospel extensively—St. Thomas travels to a neighboring kingdom. The sovereign of this kingdom is identified as *Misdeus* or *Basdeo*. The second of these names provides us with the Indian form, *Vasudeva*, and it is known that a king of this name was reigning at the same time as Gundaphorus at *Matharā* on the Jumna.

It is based on evidence such as this that scholars like Fleet, Smith, Dahlmann, and others have concluded that it is quite possible that the story of St. Thomas the Apostle preaching the Gospel of Christ in North-West India is well within the bounds of probability. However, the same cannot be said for the other story, which tells us that he preached in South India and was buried at *Mailapûr*, near the coast of Madras. We can, however, say this much about it: there is a constant tradition in South India which for centuries has connected the shrine of *Mailapûr* (or Meliapore) with the death, rather than the preaching, of St. Thomas. Furthermore, the so-called Christians of St. Thomas can be traced back to a period of great antiquity, though not with certainty to Apostolic times. In A.D. 78, a <term>Pallava</term> king was reigning at *Mailapûr* and its neighborhood, and records from Ceylon mention another king named *Shálivahana*,¹ who was a <term>Takshaka-putra</term>, or "son of a carpenter"—meaning a Christian, a follower of Christ, or a follower of Thomas the Carpenter. This phrase is a Gnostic one; at a later time, I shall show traces of a Gnostic connection between the Alexandrian <term>Gnosis</term>, a Tamil poet from *Mailapûr*, and <term>Kōbō Daishi</term>.

# CHAPTER IX

## THE CALL FROM CHINA

We will assume, then, that Christian preachers visited India around A.D. 45, and that the story that St. Thomas was martyred near Mathura, on the Jumna, in Central India, or at Mailapûr, on the Tamil coast, around A.D. 51 (this being the year traditionally assigned for his martyrdom), is not entirely improbable. These men would have brought no Christian books with them; they would have had their own memories of the things they had seen or heard, and they may have had, or created, *logia*, or short, concise sayings of or about Christ, like those recently found in Egypt, and like those St. Matthew is supposed to have noted down before composing his Gospel. They possibly also had some converts.

Now, in the year 64 A.D., the Chinese Emperor Ming-ti had a dream. On several successive nights, a man in golden clothing stood before him, holding a bow and arrows in his hand and pointing him toward the west. The emperor was much moved by his vision and, sensing its purpose, determined to send men to the west to seek for the *mabito* <note>1. Murakami, “Handbook of Buddhism,” p. 290. The story can be found in the S.P.C.K. “Handbook of Chinese Buddhism.”</note> (真人), “the true man” of his vision. The Roman Empire had good roads; the Parthians had inherited good roads from the Persians and the Seleucid Greeks; and China under the Han dynasty was a progressive military power and must have had them. Kaśyapa Matanga and Dharmaraksha reached China in A.D. 67. Three years later, in A.D. 70, they both died. They had only a short stay in China, but it was not altogether a fruitless one. The *Bukkyō Mondō Shū* gives us, in the chapter from which I have already quoted, certain details of their activities. They at once attracted many inquirers (coming as they did in response to an Imperial dream, they could hardly have done otherwise), and the Taoists and Confucianists were immediately provoked to jealousy. Their enemies appealed to the emperor, and Ming-ti, desiring to do what was right, appointed a day for a public discussion. Not much could be achieved in that regard, however, for one side knew no Chinese and the other knew no Sanskrit. But there were other tests which the missionaries and their friends passed triumphantly. Buddhist relics could not be broken by sledgehammers, Buddhist books emitted a gentle light and would not burn in the fire, and the two Buddhist monks commanded the attention of a large audience with speeches in Sanskrit which, strangely enough, everyone understood. The reasons available are as follows:—
1. It is known that there were such *logia* among early Christians. I believe I am right in saying that there are no similar *logia* in the whole range of Buddhist Sūtra literature, except those which were compiled about this period for similar purposes.
2. The fact that we have in the "Pistis Sophia" the introduction of a Buddhist Sūtra—taken by some Gnostic *cordon bleu* and served with suitable garnishes as the introduction to a book concerning Christ—seems to suggest the feasibility of the reverse process: that a Christian book might similarly be taken by some Chinese literary cook and served up to the devout in China as a Buddhist book, with a suitable introduction to give *local color and tone*.
3. The main contents of the book will be found, *on the whole*, not to be in disagreement with Christian doctrines, and far more suitable for Christian purposes than the Epistle of St. James (which has been claimed as a Buddhist writing) would be for the use of disciples of S'akyamuni.

# CHAPTER X

## BUDDHISM JUST BEFORE THE COMING OF CHRISTIANITY

It is my intention in this chapter to estimate, as far as I can, the condition of Buddhism just before the arrival of Christianity in India, and consequently just before the first visible development of the Greater Vehicle. This will clear the ground for the consideration of the *Mahāyāna* itself in later chapters.

Our most trustworthy guides for the dark period between Ashoka and Christ are the remains of ancient Buddhist temples from the earlier or Persian period of Indian art. From these <note>1. For example, those at Amaravati, Ajanta, Sanchi, Bharhut, Gaya, Nalanda, etc. For a convenient summary reviewing all that has been written on the subject, see Grünwedel, “Buddhistische Kunst in Indien” (Museum for Ethnology, Berlin). Also see Rhys Davids’ “Buddhist India.”</note> we may gather that long before the dawn of the Christian era, Buddhism had, for all practical intents and purposes, formulated for itself a demigod in Shakyamuni. It worshiped him with far more fervor than the Greeks worshiped Heracles, whom they identified with Shakyamuni in Asia. Many myths formed around Heracles in Greece; likewise, the person of Shakyamuni was enveloped in a robe of legends and sayings, and it comes to a Christian reader as an unpleasant and unwelcome shock to find Shakyamuni provided with stories very similar to those which have always endeared the Nativity and the infant life of Christ our Savior to us. There is

There is no use for us to try to ignore the fact. It stands there in the clear-cut stone monuments of India that pre-Christian India believed in Buddha as a Being whose birth was supernatural, the result of a spiritual power overshadowing his mother; as one whose birth was rejoiced over by angels and testified to by an aged seer; as one who had been tempted by the Evil One and had overcome; as one whose life had been one of good deeds and holy teachings; as one who had passed into the unseen, leaving behind him a feeling of longing regret for the one who had thus gone away.<gloss>1</gloss>

Buddhism was also by this time provided with books, or at least with a body of doctrines orally embodied in set forms and recited by the monks with that verbal exactness for which the Indians have always been so famous. On one of his rock inscriptions, in the edict at Bairat in Rajputana, Ashoka mentions the names of seven such *Sutras*, of which five have been identified as still existing in the Pali *Sutta Pitakam*,<gloss>2</gloss> while the sixth and seventh have been, with considerable reason, supposed to be, respectively, the germ of the *Vinaya Pitakam*, or books of Discipline, and the First Sermon delivered by Buddha after his Enlightenment. Shortly after Ashoka's death, about 200 B.C. (and therefore before the accession of Pushyamitra), on the rail around the stupa of Bharhut,<gloss>3</gloss> the names of pious Buddhists are inscribed, who are described as "reciters," "versed in the Dialogues," "versed in the Baskets," and "versed in the Five Collections."<gloss>4</gloss>

These inscriptions bear witness to the continuous tradition of these oral records. And, finally, if we may trust the Ceylon Chronicles, these oral records were committed to writing in Ceylon about 40 B.C., and thus the Hīnayāna books assumed their fixed form.

We may assume, further, that pre-Christian Buddhism, possessing the books, also possessed the doctrines of Hīnayāna Buddhism, as they are still to be found in Ceylon and other Buddhist countries of the Southern School. These sects formed themselves into separate communities outside the limits of the Magadhan kingdom. In this way, the seeds were planted from which the two "Vehicles" later grew. The *Mahāsānghikas* (*Daishūbu*, 大衆部) were divided into: (i) *Issetsubu* (一説部), (ii) *Sesshusebu* (說出世部), (iii) *Kei-in-bu* (鷄胤部), (iv) *Tamonbu* (多聞部), (v) *Setsu-ge bu* (說假部), (vi) *Seitasanbu* (制多山部), (vii) *Seisanjubu* (西山住部), (viii) *Hokusanjūbu* (北山住部).

The *Sthaviras* (上座部) were not as extensively subdivided. Their sub-sects were: (ix) *Setsuissaiubu* (說一切有部), (x) *Tokushibu* (犢子部), (xi) *Hōjōbu* (法上部), (xii) *Kenchōbu* (賢胄部), (xiii) *Shōryōbu* (正量部), (xiv) *Mitsurinsanbu* (密林山部), (xv) *Ketabu* (化他部) (xvi) *Hōzōbu* (法藏部), (xvii) *Onkōbu* (飲光部), (xviii) *Kyōryōbu* (經量部).

Murakami counts twenty sects by including a parent Sthavira and a parent Mahāsānghika sect. Some of these sects—for example, those in which the character 山 (*san*, "mountain") appears—were most likely local groups. Number 9, known in Sanskrit as the Sarvāstivādins, was the most powerful. It was for this sect that Kanishka built the great stupa for Buddha’s relics recently discovered near Peshawar. Number 16, the Dharmaguptas, were very strict regarding the *Vinaya* (monastic discipline) and, through it, exercised much influence in China. Nothing is known about the majority of the sects listed. One must not assume that the Hinayāna disappeared before the rising Mahāyāna. It continued alongside its rival, not only in India but also in China and Japan. However, it seems likely that the Mahāyāna eventually absorbed many of the Mahāsānghika followers.

# BUDDHISM JUST BEFORE CHRISTIANITY

One of the most important books for studying the Dark Period is the so-called "Questions of King Milinda," for which there is an English version by Professor Rhys Davids in the "Sacred Books of the East." Menander (for that is the correct reading of Milinda) was one of the Greek princes who ruled in India during the last century before Christ. The book establishes its own date, as it refers to Sakyamuni's prophecy that his religion would not last for more than 500 years after his death, yet it shows no awareness of the fact that the religion had already lasted beyond that period. We may assume, therefore, that the five centuries had not quite passed when the book was written, and we may date its composition to somewhere around the time "of the Flavian Emperors of Rome."<note>1 Edmunds and Anesaki, p. 4. The date coincides with the dawn of the new era in the religious history of the world.</note>

The book has been called the "Irenaeus" of Buddhism. The Pali Pitakas are "immanent" in its pages, just "as the New Testament is immanent in the pages of Irenaeus." It provides strong testimony to the existence and nature of the Hīnayāna books, as well as to the Hīnayāna doctrine. Better than any other book, it allows us to see the state of Buddhist thought at the end of its first period, when the Age of the Upright Law (as it has since been called) was almost over, and the Age of the Image Law was about to be introduced.<note>2 This is the chronological theory adopted by Japanese Buddhism.</note>

Words such as these, written in all probability before the birth of Christ, and applicable to the Nativity of Shakyamuni as it lives in Buddhist legend and belief, do not at all necessarily imply that the Nativity stories of the New Testament are merely faked-up fables, borrowed from an older cycle of fiction. Rather, they show that when He was born, in the way in which His birth is recorded, He was fulfilling more than one prophecy. It is thus that it behooves a Divine Savior *to be born*; that is the testimony of Isaiah, of Virgil, of the Buddhist Sutra, of many another great teacher who has appeared. It was part of the "stock-in-trade" (if I may so call it) of Shakyamuni; it was also a part of the stock-in-trade of Christ.

If Christ's superhuman credentials had gone no further than the Nativity cycle, Christ would in no sense have differed from Shakyamuni. But Christ's claim of supernatural testimony went further than Shakyamuni's. He claims our allegiance not merely because "He was conceived of the Holy Ghost, and born of the Virgin Mary," but more especially because, having been crucified and slain, He rose again the third day from the dead. It is on the Resurrection that St. Paul bases Christ's claim to be the Son of God; it is this that makes Him unique in religious history. This places Christ at the head of all things in the religious world; its absence puts Shakyamuni into his proper place—a place in which he may yet claim the ungrudging respect of Christian people. It constitutes him a great witness and forerunner of Christ, and no Japanese person can be offended at having him placed in such a seemingly humble position, for it is the place

A clear example of the moral decline of <term>Hinayana</term> during this period can be found in the "Katha Vatthu," translated by Rhys Davids in *J.R.A.S.*, 1892. It is also evident in the *Jataka* stories (published in English by Cambridge University Press). Aesop valued these correctly by making them the basis for many of his fables, and they have left their mark on the folklore of many peoples in Asia and Europe. However, the religion that produced them must have first lost much of its moral strength. They do not speak with the voice of people who are deeply serious about a specific religious teaching. One cannot imagine Tertullian or Augustine solemnly telling a <term>Jataka</term> story. The "Katha Vatthu" contains a discussion, from the perspectives of various Hinayana sects, regarding certain questions of Buddhist philosophy, ethics, and discipline. There was almost no consensus on these questions. Here are some of the questions:

> "Is there a soul in the truest and highest sense?" "No." <note>To this question, two sects gave a positive answer. One of these must have been the Sarvastivadins, as the existence of the soul was one of their core beliefs.</note>

> "Is the Noble Path self-existent? Or the Chain of Causation? Or the Four Noble Truths? Or <term>Nirvana</term>?" Again, "No." <note>And yet these four concepts are the foundation of Shakyamuni's personal teachings. The very basis of the Buddhist faith had disappeared!</note>

> "Is <term>Nirvana</term> a virtuous (moral) state?" "No."

There are also some very interesting points raised in what we might call "Buddhology."

He would be neither the first nor the last person whose conversion was due to a bird's song or a beautiful piece of scenery. Once converted, he moved from the Hindu worship of Mahes'vara to the faith of S'akyamuni, only to find that the Hīnayāna, seen from within, was not all that his imagination had painted it from the outside. He would not be the first idealist to find his dreams destroyed by the disappointments of reality. And yet, we may imagine that during this period of his life, he may still have done good service to his new faith by the publication of the *Vajrasuci*,² in which he combats the mistaken Hindu theory of caste.

Again his imagination is kindled; he recognizes in Pārśva a dialectician greater than himself, and in Aryadeva a master of magic more powerful than any he knows. He accepts this new and expanded faith and becomes its first great advocate.²

In truth, there were, in their early stages, three modes of expression in the new Buddhism then taking shape in the Indus Valley. All three must be taken into account if we are to understand the Japanese Mahāyāna of today. They are not limited to Buddhism; they are found in Gnosticism, in Hinduism, and in Christianity. They are, in fact, religious universals. For the sake of brevity, they may be termed the Way, the Truth, and the Life: the appeal to the emotions, the intellect, and the spiritual imagination of Faith.

The new Life introduced into Buddhism—connected, as we have seen, with the Egyptian Gnosis and deeply influenced by the Magianism of Bactria—was quite ready to claim supernatural powers. It was left to As'vaghosha, while reasserting the half-forgotten claims of S'akyamuni, to provide a philosophical basis for the polytheistic concepts of the diverse multitude of the Northwest. In this way, he recommended the spiritual authority of the new Truth, proclaimed by the new keepers of the Buddha's Begging-bowl, to the people of Hindustan.
