> "Therefore" (these are almost the last words of his *Discourse on the Awakening of Faith*), "it is said in the Sūtra that if devoted men and women would be filled with concentration of thought, think of Amitābha Buddha in the world of highest happiness in the Western region, and direct all the merit of their good deeds toward being born there, they will assuredly be born there. Thus always seeing Buddhas there, their faith will be strengthened, and they will never fall back from it. Receiving instruction in the doctrine, and recognizing the Dharmakāya of the Buddha, they will through gradual discipline be able to enter the state of truth." <note>1</note>

## CHAPTER XII

### NĀGĀRJUNA

We may consider that As’vaghosha, apparently a native of Saketa and for many years a resident of Pataliputra or Benares (probably the latter), brought a certain Magadhan or Central Indian element into the newly formed, or reformed, Mahāyāna. We may suppose that a sage of his wisdom, learning, and reputation would do much to strengthen the dying cause of Hīnayāna Buddhism in the very land of its birth by raising it to a higher level of aim and endeavor, and to nobler—because truer—views of life and duty.

But the Kushan or Indo-Scythian rulers, in their newly awakened zeal for the propagation of a religion with which their hopes for the overlordship of the fair peninsula of Jambudvipa seemed to be bound—where they might rule in peaceful possession, regardless of the disturbances raised by Huns and Alani on their far-distant Central Asian frontiers—were by no means content with spiritual influence on the Ganges plains alone. They might reasonably argue that all India ought to be won to the reformed Buddhism of which they were the acknowledged heads as the possessors of Buddha’s Begging-bowl. If India could be won to spiritual allegiance in this way, temporal allegiance would not be far behind. However, to win all India, there had to be a religious platform that all of India could accept.

<summary>This chapter introduces the influence of As’vaghosha on Mahāyāna Buddhism and explores how the Kushan rulers sought to use the religion as a unifying force to secure their political control over India.</summary>

In Nāgārjuna, they found a man perfectly suited for carrying out their plans to recommend their expanded faith to the spiritual conscience of India. A Brahman by birth, he was born in Southern India sometime around the beginning of the second century.<note>There is no definite date for Nāgārjuna; like As'vaghosha, there are many legends about him. However, it is said that he took part in Kanishka's Council, and if so, his birth must have occurred around the time I have suggested.</note> As a Brahman, he was one of the hereditary teachers and guardians of religion and faith, but at first, he seems to have had very little respect for his privileges. He lived the life of a "*gilded youth*," threw himself into a life of indulgence, and thoughtlessly wasted his birthright. But one night, he and three of his companions broke into the Rajah's palace, partly for robbery and partly for affairs with the ladies of the royal harem, and they were discovered. Nāgārjuna managed to escape safely, but his three companions were captured and killed.

This was the turning point in his career. Why had he been saved while his companions, who were no more guilty than himself, were overtaken by the vengeance of men, if not of Heaven? He recognized the hand of some unseen Providence in his escape, and from that moment, he determined to live a life worthy of his priestly birthright.

But the Brahmanism of that time (we must remember that it was not yet the reformed and elevated Brahmanism which at a later date drove Buddhism out of India) failed to satisfy him, and he turned to Buddhism. This too—which was the divided <term>Hīnayāna</term>—failed to give him peace. He read books without end yet did not arrive at the truth, until at last he traveled as a wandering seeker to the country of the <term>Nāgas</term> in the Himalayas, where he finally found peace and guidance.

# NĀGĀRJUNA

<margin>Who?</margin>
A Japanese writer,¹ in whose thorough scholarship I have learned to place great confidence, says that Nāgārjuna's first journey was to a shrine of Ādi-Buddha (一 佛). Japan regards him as Amitābha, the Supreme and Original Buddha, from whom, as if from a source, comes everything called Light in the human mind. Ādi-Buddha is essentially a Himalayan cult, and it would be among those mountains, if anywhere, that Nāgārjuna would encounter such a teaching. At this shrine, he met a Bodhisattva named Mahānāga (Dai-ryū), who taught him the faith in Amida Buddha. Finding him to be an expert in spiritual understanding, Mahānāga led him to the Palace of the Dragons (Nāgas) under the sea. There, he revealed to him treasures of wisdom and doctrine that had been kept hidden for many generations, but which could now be shared with humanity since the destined² teacher of the secret doctrine had finally appeared.

From the Himalayas, Nāgārjuna went again to southern India. Here, he had a similar experience, which we would be justified in treating as the same event mentioned in the previous paragraph, were it not that the study of Japanese Mahāyāna requires us to consider them as separate occurrences. In Southern India, he is said to have found an Iron Tower (some sort of shrine, we may suppose, similar to the shrine of St. Thomas at Mailapûr) in which lived an elderly Bodhisattva named Vajrasattva (Japanese: Kongōsatta). Vajrasattva was the authorized teacher of a doctrine that came from a Buddha named Vairoc’ana, who was greater than Shakya-

Nāgārjuna listened with sympathy: Vajrasattva recognized that his spiritual successor had arrived, committed the secret Teachings to him, and gave him the rite of Abhis'ekha, a rite which is half Baptism and half Ordination.

We shall soon return to these points. For the present, we will merely summarize what we have said and remind the reader that Nāgārjuna had personally "sampled" a great deal of the religious thought of India. He had been a Brahmanist and a Hinayānist. He had then become a Mahāyānist, and since his conversion to that faith, he had come into contact not only with the faith in Amitābha, but with faith in Vairoc'ana, with the Dragon's Palace, with the Iron Tower, with the Nāgas, and with the religionists whose special symbol is the Vajra.

<margin>ORISSA?</margin>
He then retired to South India, where he spent the rest of his days writing books and evangelizing. The Japanese historians whom I have read say nothing about his connection with Kanishka's Council; they say that after long and successful labors, he died at Kosála, in the northern portion of South India.

He was a prolific writer (the reader will find a long list of his works in the pages of Nanjo's "Catalogue of the Tripitaka"), and his influence on Northern Buddhism has been so great that one is not astonished to read that he was revered by many as a second Buddha—a teacher whose authority equaled that of S'akyamuni himself.

He may be said to have settled, for Buddhism, the long-disputed question of the existence of the soul, which had troubled generations of Buddhist thinkers.

# NĀGĀRJUNA

Buddhists had long been divided into *Astikas* and *Nāstikas*. One party maintained, along with the Sarvāstivādins and others, the existence of the soul, the reality of life after death, and the existence of an Oversoul; the other denied all these things, and in some cases even allowed material substances no more than a phenomenal existence. Nāgārjuna’s philosophy mediated between these two views. The Madhyamika system, of which he was the interpreter, taught that the soul might be said to exist or not to exist, depending on how you looked at it. The soul of the individual is like a wave of the sea; it has an apparently separate existence for a moment, then it disappears into the body of the ocean once more. It was never a distinct entity. So it is with the Buddhas: they appear in the world, and we view them as individual beings. But that is all only an appearance. Buddhas and Saviors are but waves that appear on the surface of the ocean of God’s love. They come and they go, and people talk of their deaths or their Nirvanas; but the ocean of God’s love is unchanged. Only the surface waves have changed. It was in this way that Nāgārjuna was able to recognize the essential oneness of Amitābha, Vairoc’ana, and S’akyamuni. It was through this that the Mahāyāna faith, of which he was the great doctor, was able to adapt itself to the Taoism of China and the Shinto of Japan. It was also how the Buddhist gnosis of the second century tried to overthrow the Christian faith of the Catholic Church. Docetism is nothing but the Madhyamika doctrine applied to the problem of removing the offense of the Cross and the uniqueness of Christ.

Nāgārjuna did not reject the teachings of either the *Astikas* or the *Nāstikas*. He divided Truth into two parts: an apparent truth and a true truth, a distinction which is constantly appearing in Japanese Buddhism. The one, *Zokutai*, is

The other, *Shintai*, is "true truth," the fulfillment of truth, which was to make perfect what the Astikas held only in part. The one is the absolute Truth; the other is the Truth adapted to the mental and spiritual circumstances and capacities of the listeners. This distinction is found in every Buddhist sect in Japan; it underlies the distinction between the two classes of listeners in Manichæism. Was it not the entire argument of the Gnostics that ordinary Christianity was only a form of *Zokutai*, a "truth by common consent," and that they themselves were the possessors of the *Shintai*, "the true Truth," the perfect Gnōsis?

Nāgārjuna is further credited in Japan with having taught that there are two ways of life: one a road of difficulty and pain (*nangyōdō*), and the other a road of ease and pleasure. In the first, the seeker of salvation takes the hard road of asceticism, of fasting and penance, etc., and thus labors to work out his own salvation. In the second, he sets aside all his own efforts and puts his faith in One who has achieved salvation for him; and so, like a ship with a strong sail and a favorable wind, he reaches the harbor of his hopes.<note>See my "Shinran and His Work," p. 51. In that book, I have very fully discussed the doctrinal implications of the Faith in Amida.</note> It is for this reason that Nāgārjuna is considered by all the Amitābha sects in Japan as the great Founder of their faith, second only to S’akyamuni. For, indeed, "Faith in Another" is faith in Amida. Amida is the One Original Buddha (*ichi-Butsu*, *hon-Butsu*), besides whom there is no other, and who has had no beginning. He has manifested himself time and again to people; in the *Sukhāvati Vyūha*, for instance, a list is given of eighty-one such manifestations. At the last

Nāgārjuna does not claim to have invented this doctrine. He claims to have found it, and we know that the doctrine must have existed in India before A.D. 147, because we know that in that year the <term>Sukhāvati Vyūha</term> was taken to China by two men, Anshikao and Lokaraksha. We may safely say that Amidaism was a part of the faith of Mahāyāna Buddhism from the middle part of the second century. Before that time, our notices of it are somewhat vague. By his clearly announced doctrine of salvation by Faith, Nāgārjuna may be considered to have laid—at least as far as Indian Buddhism is concerned—the foundation of that Third Vehicle which may be said to be the One and True Mahāyāna.<note>The Japanese very often divide the doctrines of S'akyamuni into three Vehicles. At other times they are also spoken of as the Vehicles of S'ravakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas, and this is the view taken in the *Saddharmapundarika*.</note>

If we turn to Irenæus, whom we may consider a slightly younger contemporary of Nāgārjuna, we find the first mention of the Ophites, a Buddho-gnostic sect known by various names, such as Naassenes, Peratæ, Marcosians, etc., all of whose doctrines are very similar. Perhaps the best account of these sectaries will be found in Hippolytus, “*Refutatio Omnium Haeresium*,” book v. These men, he says, assert that the beginning of all things is “a Man and the Son of Man” (a term which will apply either to Amida, or to Christ, or to S'akyamuni); that he has three bodies—spiritual, psychic, and material (which is true both of Amida and of S'akyamuni); that he has three natures—one that of the blessed man above, of Adamas (Sanskrit <term>Ajita</term>), which is true of Amida; a second, a mortal one, below on earth; and a third, which is above and has no king over it (Hippolytus, *op. cit.*, book v. pp. 150-151, Migne edition). Nāgārjuna is also regarded by Japanese Buddhists as the first person to introduce a set of doctrines known as the Avatasaṃka or Kegon into Buddhism. Although the Kegon no longer exists in Japan as a separate organization, its views still influence many writers, and the Kegon Sūtras have had more influence on Japanese and Chinese religious art than any other set of Mahāyāna Sūtras.

According to the Sanron<note>Nanjo, "Twelve Buddhist Sects," p. 51, etc.</note> traditions (the Sanron is another sect, now extinct as a separate organization, which claimed Nāgārjuna as its founder), there were three collections of the Buddhist Scriptures made immediately after S'akyamuni's death. The orthodox party made one inside the cave of Rājagriha; the Mahāsaṅghikas made another outside the cave, or in another cave-monastery nearby. In the meantime, Manjuśri (or Ananda? <note>See above, Chapter III.</note>) and Maitreya—who never appear in Hīnayāna books as disciples of S'akyamuni, but who are very active debaters in the Mahāyāna Sūtras—formed a third collection which contained the true Mahāyāna books. For some years, the volumes of this collection had been gradually coming down into the plains from their hiding places among the Himalayas and the Anavatapta Lake. In this way, the doctrines of the Mahāyāna, as explained by the Kegon, were sown in people’s hearts little by little, as they were able to receive them. The honor of bringing the entire collection to light was reserved for Nāgārjuna.

The <term>Kegon</term> claims to be the first of <term>S'akyamuni's</term> preachings. It purports to have been delivered, during the first week after his Enlightenment, to seven assemblies in Heaven and Earth, all of which he addressed simultaneously without leaving his seat under the <term>Bo-tree</term>. It was delivered in a supernatural manner, and thus it came to pass that <term>S'ariputra</term>, <term>Maitreya</term>, <term>Manjuśri</term>, and other disciples of a much later date, came to be spiritually present at it. It was followed by teachings adapted to ordinary people, whom he led by five stages to the perfection which he had found in the spiritual hearers of his first teachings. The five stages are (1) “smallness,” the doctrines of <term>Hīnayāna</term>, based on the <term>Four Truths</term> and the <term>Twelvefold Chain of Causation</term>, as explained in the <term>Agamas</term>; (2) “beginning,” *i.e.* of the <term>Mahāyāna</term>, in which the disciple is shown the unreality of things; (3) the “perfection,” *i.e.* of the <term>Mahāyāna</term>, which consists in the realization of the existence of the <term>Bhūtatathātā</term>, or the impersonal God; (4) “suddenness,” *i.e.* the direct attainment of the knowledge of God by straight and direct intuition; and (5) “completion,” or the absolute identity between God and the soul.<sup>1</sup> Thus step by step, according to the <term>Kegon</term> doctrines, were the believers led

## CHAPTER XIII

### THE MISSIONARIES OF THE HAN

If we could construct a comparative chronological table of the religious phenomena of Europe and Asia during the first two centuries, we would see that the next Buddhist mission (147 AD) coincided with a mission sent by the Kushan sovereigns to the Han emperors. This was perhaps partly to carry out negotiations for a matrimonial alliance, and partly, no doubt, to arrange for joint action for defense against the Huns and other barbarians who were threatening both China and India. Political negotiation and religious propaganda seem to have gone hand-in-hand.

The two pioneer missionaries were Anshikao (who, from his rank as Prince of Parthia, may well have had some political commission) and Lokaraksha. The two arrived simultaneously at Lôyang, or, at any rate, with only a relatively short interval between them; the rest came at intervals during the seventy years that still remained for the Han dynasty to rule. Six of them are mentioned by Nanjo, <note>Nanjo, “Catalogue of the Tripitaka,” Appendix II.</note> but none of them can be compared for diligent translation with the first two. There must have been other missionaries as well: there are sixteen translations by unknown hands, and there must surely have been some missionaries whose methods were not literary. In all, ninety-six Sutras were translated during the later years of the Han dynasty, of which Anshikao

The first notable point regarding these pioneer missionaries is that none came from India proper, and, in particular, none from Magadha and the plains of the Ganges. Two were Parthians; three are described as coming from Tibet; one from the country of the Yuetchi; the others vaguely as from the Western region. They were all subjects of the Kushan kingdom and had therefore all been more or less influenced by the Gandhāra Buddhism which had come in with the new era.

The leader of this successful mission to China was a Parthian prince known to us as Anshikao. His real personal name is not given (Anshikao merely means "Prince of the Ansi," *that is*, Parthians), but it is said that he resigned his throne to his uncle in order to become a monk, and that he was the son of a famous king who had been the enemy of Trajan and the friend of Hadrian. All this enables us to identify him with Axidares, the son of Pachorus, whom his father had nominated to the Armenian throne shortly after 100 AD, thereby giving much offense to the Emperor Trajan. Pachorus's successor on the Parthian throne, his brother Chosroes, at once apologized to Rome for the error in judgment that Pachorus had made, deposed Axidares in haste, nominated his younger nephew Parthamasiris in his place, and wrote to Rome begging for investiture on his behalf. But since Trajan refused to listen, Parthamasiris surrendered himself and was at first treated with clemency, but was later murdered around 115 AD. There seems to be little doubt that the prince Axidares—deposed about 108 AD by his uncle and ousted from his Armenian kingdom after his brother's death by a distant relative—retired to a cloister, as others have done who have experienced...

> “Even before the time of As’oka, the logical void involved in the acceptance of Nirvana had led to the development of a Maitreya Buddha, the 'Future Buddha' of Kindness, who was to mitigate the hardships of an inflexible Karma. Pratyeka Buddhas—those who had attained an individual Buddhahood without regard for others—and Bodhisattvas—those whose progressing Karma was gradually leading them along the 'path' to Buddhahood—were the natural result of the movement. Of these, two—Manjuśri, the Gracious One, and Avalokiteśvara, the Pitiful One—gradually rose to prominence. Thus, when Amida came to take the Buddha's place in the heavenly hierarchy, seats were found beside him for the two great Bodhisattvas, Avalokiteśvara and Manjuśri.”

# THE MISSIONARIES OF THE HAN

Many of the provinces outside India within the Kushan Empire, namely Khotan and parts of Bactria, had been converted to Buddhism long before the beginning of the Mahāyāna movement. Having been converted to Hīnayāna, they remained loyal to that tradition, although sectarian differences and the mountainous geography between them separated them from their Hīnayāna brothers on the southern slopes of the Himalayas. Furthermore, the dividing line between the two "Vehicles" was not yet clearly defined.

We can therefore safely conclude that the second-century Buddhist mission to China was mainly an effort by the Kushans to win the friendship of those Chinese people who were inclined toward religion. Its members came from countries outside India that had long been Buddhist and had recently come under the rule of the Kushans. While it contained the beginnings of Mahāyānism, it was primarily Hīnayāna.

The next thing that strikes us is the very basic nature of the Hīnayāna Buddhism that these men taught. There are some extremely elementary treatises among the Sūtras translated—short works, for instance, on the Four Truths, the <term>Twelvefold Chain of Causation</term>, the causes of pain, duty toward parents, the punishments for sin, and the rewards of virtue. The publication of these tracts seems to show that the Buddhist missionaries were doing pioneer work on untouched ground. The previous mission of Kaśyapa Matanga and Dharmaraksha (if indeed it had been a Buddhist mission at all) had evidently died out completely, and these men had to start over. Only this can explain the necessity of publishing these elementary treatises. It has been no more than fifty years since the re-introduction of

Another <term>Mahāyāna</term> trace can be found in the *Sūtra on the Use of Images of the Buddha*, attributed to Lokaraksha.<note>Nanjo, "Catalogue of the Tripitaka," No. 289.</note> The fact that images representing the Buddha and other prominent figures were not made until the beginning of <term>Gandhāra Buddhism</term> is shown in Japan by the use of the term <term>Image Law</term> to denote the second phase of their religion. They say that for five centuries after the <term>Nirvana</term>, the <term>Upright Law</term> continued. This was to be followed by a thousand years of the <term>Image Law</term>, after which would come the <term>Age of the Destruction of the Law</term> in which we currently live. It was, apparently, the image worship of the Buddhists that prompted the <term>Confucianists</term> to create images of their own revered master. The Buddhists were inspired by Gandhāra art; that art was Greek and Roman in its ideals, and so it happened that the art of China, and eventually that of Japan, has drawn its inspiration from Antioch and Alexandria.

Another trace, again, of the <term>Mahāyāna</term> teachings may be found in the presence of Buddhas and <term>Bodhisattvas</term> other than S'akyamuni. One of these is <term>Akshobya</term> and another is <term>Amitābha</term>—the one representing the East, the other the West. The first represents that perfect wisdom which is immovable because it rests firmly on the thought of Buddha; the second represents that same perfect wisdom which has finished its course and resolved its doubts, and so is at rest. # THE MISSIONARIES OF THE HAN

Lokaraksha reappears in a literary form, fully developed. Asvaghosha and Nagarjuna, being natives of India proper, would only have known him by reputation; however, Anshikao and Lokaraksha, coming from Central Asia, knew him more fully.

The doctrine of Amitābha is now more fully developed. When Shakyamuni consoled the Queen of Bimbisara, he merely pointed her toward Amitābha, whose mercies are infinite and who is ever near to comfort the distressed.<note>1. Found in the *Amitāyur-dhyāni Sūtra*, *Sacred Books of the East*, vol. 49. He has (again in a Buddhist manner) been euhemerized, so to speak; his genealogy is provided, and he is practically God Almighty. Yet he was once a man, and his current high status as the Lord of the Western Paradise—the Father and Savior of those who trust in him, the ψυχοπομπός <note>A psychopomp, or guide of souls.</note> meeting the soul at death and placing it in the mansion prepared for it—is entirely the result of a vow made countless centuries ago by a mere human. This vow was pursued diligently through many lives until it resulted in the creation of a Paradise and the opening of salvation through faith for those who invoke his name.

And, again significantly strange, more than a century after the Christian revelation—in a region where Jews, Israelites, and Christians lived side by side with Buddhists and others—Amitābha appears in literary form, developed into the first member of a quasi-Trinity. He is accompanied by his son, Avalokiteshvara, the bisexual expression of his mercy, who in many forms and as many persons was manifested upon earth to save the suffering.<note>2. I have a small Japanese *Catechism of Kwannon* which states the doctrine about this deity very succinctly.</note>

## CHAPTER XIV

### DHARMAGUPTA <note>1. I take this chapter mainly from Gyōnen’s sketch of the Eight Buddhist Sects in Japan ("Revue de l'Histoire des Religions," vol. xxv. p. 341).</note>

ONE of the most important services that Sakyamuni provided to his immediate disciples, as well as to future generations, was to supply them with a set of disciplinary rules of life. This discipline, known as the *Vinaya*, was not given in any formal manner. As the occasion arose, the Master spoke his mind, and thus, little by little, during the long years of his ministry, there was formed, as it were, a *corpus* of various rulings delivered without any definite plan or system. Yet there was no contradiction among these rulings, for it was one mind that gave them all, and that mind was a singularly consistent and clear-sighted one.

What the *Vinaya* rulings lacked in system was, furthermore, more than compensated for by the definiteness which came to them from the fact that in every case they were based on some real fact or some concrete difficulty. If the Sūtras—those I mean, such as most of the Agamas, which can be distinctly traced back to the life of the Master—give us a true picture of Sakyamuni's life, we cannot but conclude that his mind wavered at times between two or more alternative sets of speculative doctrines. Is there a god? Is there such

<summary>This page introduces the Vinaya, the collection of disciplinary rules established by Sakyamuni, which developed pragmatically over his life rather than through a systematic plan. The author notes that while these practical rules are consistent, the speculative doctrines found in the Sūtras suggest that Sakyamuni's mind may have wavered on certain metaphysical questions.</summary>

a thing as a soul? Does the physical universe really exist, or is it all a mere illusion? On these points, he spoke in such a way as to leave his followers the greatest room for speculative differences. If we are inclined (not being specialists in metaphysics) to impatiently dismiss the speculations of Sarvāstivādins, Sautrāntikas, and all the chatter of Hīnayāna sectarianism—if we find it difficult to see how the term "Buddhism" can be stretched wide enough to cover all the variations of the so-called Mahāyāna—we must remember that it was the deliberate vagueness of the Master's own teaching that gave his followers the boldness to wander so far afield in the daring of their later speculations.

From all this vagueness of the Sūtra Pitaka, the Vinaya Pitaka was spared. When the Master gave rules to his communities for the Sabbath meetings, for the confession of sins, for the admission of women, for the regulation of dress, and so on, he was obliged to be concise, clear, and definite. The Vinaya rules, therefore, give us a more trustworthy picture of the Master's mind than any of the Sūtras do. They make us feel that we are dealing with the real Buddha and with the real community of monks.

It fell to the lot of Upali, the barber, to record from memory at the orthodox Council at Rājagṛiha the disciplinary decisions of his Master and to form them into a connected whole. His collection was well received, was adopted, and for more than a century was the authorized canon of discipline enforced by the successive Patriarchs—Kaśyapa, Ananda, Madhyantika, Śānavasas, and Upagupta. Upagupta was a contemporary of Asoka, and we know from some of Asoka's monuments that many corruptions had entered Buddhism by then, and that the monks were beginning to form cliques and

Dharmagupta, Upagupta's successor, whom we place, therefore, somewhere around 240 B.C. or a little later, reformed the *Vinaya* by a new recitation,¹ and thus formally withdrew his followers from communion with the others. This, says Gyōnen (p. 343), was the first schism.

After this, the process of sect formation proceeded very rapidly. As each sect felt justified in drawing up its own modified discipline, it was not long before there were twenty disciplines where originally there had been only one.

We need not stop to inquire what these twenty disciplines were. Only four of them reached China, and these four were ultimately merged into one; the survivor was a reformed edition of Dharmagupta's reformed code.²

According to the Dharmagupta system of discipline—a system which is still largely in use in Japan, although the old *Vinaya* or *Ritsu* sect has long ceased to have its own separate corporate existence³—the faithful here on earth are divided into seven classes. At the bottom of the scale come (i) the *Ubasoku*, and (ii) the *Ubai*, laymen and laywomen, who desire to lead a religious life without leaving their homes. These individuals were required to keep the five precepts—not to kill, not to steal, not to be guilty of any form of

Furthermore, on the Sabbath day,¹ the prohibition of sexual immorality became a prohibition of even lawful sexual intercourse, and prohibitions were added against the use of perfumes and oils, dances and public spectacles, and luxurious couches—in short, against anything that might incite the passions. Added to these, as a recommendation for spiritual perfection, was the rule not to eat at unusual hours.

Above the *Ubasoku* and *Ubai* were (iii) the *Shami* and (iv) the *Shamini*, whom we might call the Buddhist *Endeavorers*.² These persons undertook to keep all the above rules permanently. They also added a rule forbidding them from receiving gold, silver, or precious objects of any kind; that is, they made a vow of perpetual poverty. Higher up in the scale were (v) the *Shiki Shamana*, a higher grade of ascetics, who added what are known as the Six Doctrines. They would not kill even a mosquito; they committed to being scrupulously honest, even regarding the smallest sums of money; they would not touch a woman; they would not tell even a white lie; they never drank fermented liquors; and they never ate meals outside of prescribed times.

Finally came the full-fledged monks and nuns, (vi) the *Biku* and (vii) the *Bikuni*. As the Vinaya became increasingly influenced by Mahāyāna ideas, these individuals were seen as candidates for the rank of Bodhisattva. Consequently, they were called upon to undertake the *Bosatsu Kai* or *Gusoku Kai*—the rules of the Bodhisattva, also known as the Complete Rules.

Another set of sins, thirteen in number, are considered very grave, though they do not altogether destroy the spiritual character of the sinner. They are (i) self-defilement; (ii) coming into contact with a woman; (iii) slander; (iv) self-praise, intended to increase one's alms; (v) acting as a matchmaker to arrange a marriage; (vi) speaking ill of the clergy; (vii) slandering the clergy; (viii) disobeying the orders of a religious superior; (ix) inciting another monk to such disobedience; (x) visiting the house of a layperson to cause quarrels; (xi) disregarding the wishes of the community and causing divisions. Two more rules (xii and xiii) concerned building a house with one's own money or with the contributions of the faithful.

Another set of offenses against the law of poverty could only be resolved by purification ceremonies. These concerned the prohibition of having two coats, the single garment that must always be worn even at home, unnecessary dishes, persistence in asking for alms, etc.

But the Han translators had apparently been content with merely sowing the seeds of Buddhism—another indication of the fact that they were truly the pioneers of the faith. They said nothing about discipline, and they had made no attempt to introduce the monastic order into China.

The great Han dynasty came to an end in 214 A.D., having held China in one way or another under its continuous rule since 206 B.C.<note>The Former or Western Han were in power from 206 B.C. to 25 A.D.; the Latter or Eastern Han from 25 A.D. to 214 A.D.</note> The assassination of the last Han ruler led to a prolonged civil war, at the conclusion of which we find China divided into the kingdoms of the Wei, the Wu, and the Shu. Several practical reforms should be noticed. In A.D. 335, a monk named Buddhoganga persuaded King She-hu of the Posterior Chow dynasty to institute ordinations and allow Chinese natives to take monastic vows.<note>² I touch on this again in my chapter on Heian Buddhism.</note> This permission greatly changed the nature of Chinese Buddhism. In India, it had been the custom for kings to support the Order through royal charity, and the custom was practiced at first in China also, thus keeping the Order as a foreign and aristocratic institution. But when Chinese natives took the vows, the Order increased very rapidly, and Buddhism became something belonging to the people rather than to the sovereign.

<note>They may (must?) have been Buddhists before entering Europe. (See Flinders Petrie on "Migrations" in the *Journal of the Anthropological Institute*.)</note>

For countless tribes of the enemy had initially crossed over the borders, and more were continuing to cross, with no one to stop them. In the midst of such great evils, it seemed like a genuine profit to accept bribes from the enemy. Each tribe brought their ancestral sacred objects from home, along with their priests and priestesses. However, they were extremely secretive and maintained an unbreakable, adamantine silence regarding these matters; their public pretense and acting were carefully calculated to deceive the enemy. They dressed some of their people as "bishops" in an impressive costume and hood, and by making them act with great cunning like foxes, they sent them forward into the middle. Everywhere they undermined security through oaths that were held in contempt by the barbarians but were strictly observed by the [Roman] emperors. There was also a class among them called "monks" who imitated those found among the enemy. This imitation involved nothing difficult or practical; it was enough for them to wear dark robes and tunics to be regarded as holy and to be trusted. The barbarians quickly realized that what was admired among the Romans could be used for deception. For in other respects, they guarded their ancestral sacred rites with the most profound and hidden secrecy, both nobly and sincerely. Despite this, people fell into such foolishness that those who seemed to have sense were clearly and easily convinced that they were Christians and were following all the rites.

In the extract above, note: (i) that the religion is *ta patria hiera* (ancestral rites), a faith brought with them from Central Asia; (ii) that the institution of quasi-bishops seems to be spoken of as a recent innovation, and that it corresponds in time with what we know of Chinese ordinations; (iii) that *black* (*phaios*) matches what we know of Shinshū and Jōdo monks; (iv) that it corresponds with what we know from other sources about the confusion between Buddhist *arhats* and Christian "saints." The purpose of the trick was to deceive the Romans into believing that the barbarians were already Christians. The work of Ulfilas came later, at least in terms of its influence, and his institutions could not be described as being "ancestral rites" of the Goths.

->MANICHAEISM<-

But the Magians did not want to see Babylonia aroused to national enthusiasm by the preaching of a new national faith, and Manes was driven into exile. His exile, followed later by his martyrdom, changed his system from a merely local cult to one of world-wide significance. He wandered as an exile through the countries north, north-east, and east of the newly constituted Persian kingdom, from which he was an outcast; and when, venturing to return to Persia, he was cruelly put to death by his enemies, his disciples seized upon his memory with enthusiasm and carried his teachings far and wide through Europe and Asia. Manichaeism was for many centuries a serious menace to the Christian Church.

Manichaeism may most properly be described as the completion of the Gnostic systems. It seems to have swept them all together and to have joined them into one cohesive whole. We hear no more of Gnosticism after the rise of Manichaeism. It was not a Christian religion, yet it had its Christian side. It could speak to Christians in Christian language, and it claimed for Manes that he was the Paraclete, the Comforter whom Christ had promised. We have only to read the anti-Manichaean treatises of St. Augustine, or any of the notices of Manichaeism in the Greek or Latin Fathers, to understand that Manes could talk, when he pleased, as a Christian. But he faced many ways, and in China the Manichaean clergy seemed rather to aim at identifying themselves with the Buddhists.

Manichaeism did not, like Christianity, "present itself to man as a power to save him by cleansing his heart from sin; but, like Gnosticism, it simply proposed to...

The personality of God comprises five spiritual and five material sub-elements, a division clearly corresponding to the five Dhyāni Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. “But God is not alone in the light: His fullness encompasses an air of light, an earth of light, and numberless glories and magnificences. Upwards and sideways this realm of light is unbounded; but from below it is met by the realm of darkness, the Cloud.” Thus “Light resting on the Great Cloud” becomes the symbol of the Manichaean system. The term is found in China and Japan, often as a name for temples. I believe that in every case it can be traced back to a Manichaean origin or connection.

<margin>| |</margin>
The ethical system of Manichaeism is more clearly allied with Buddhism. Whether Manes, coming to India, found the Dharmagupta system at work and incorporated it into his own, or whether the later Vinayists borrowed from the Manichaeans, I cannot tell. It all depends on the date to be assigned to books like the Brahmajāla Sūtra. But there is no doubt that the “Perfect” of the Manichaean system are remarkably like the candidates for Buddhahood who take upon themselves the 250 Rules of the Bodhisattva. In both systems there is the same threefold arrangement of sins according to whether they concern the hand, the mouth, or the heart. In both there is the same prohibition of marriage and of every sort of sensual pleasure; Bodhisattvas and the “Perfect” are alike forbidden

It is impossible to deny the influence that Manichaeism exerted upon the adaptable Mahāyāna tradition. From the middle of the third century onward, the two religions were constantly side by side, and whatever person we consider after that date, we must always take into account the fact that they most probably knew something of Manichaeism. Zoroastrianism also comes into account, but the Zoroastrians were not a proselytizing community like the Manichaeans, and it is not until the Tang period that we find them side by side with Buddhism.

Manichaeism did not set itself to work to preach Christ, but it had its Christian aspect; and wherever in Central Asia we find—as we often do—a Manichaean temple almost side by side with a Buddhist monastery, we may safely infer that there must have been some indirect knowledge among the Buddhists of the historical existence of Christ.

## CHAPTER XVI

### CHINA IN THE THIRD, FOURTH, AND FIFTH CENTURIES

It is very difficult to form a clear mental picture of China from the middle of the third century A.D. to the middle of the sixth. The three kingdoms of Wei, Wu, and Shu, which I mentioned in a previous chapter, came to an end in A.D. 265. At that time, Szuma I established himself as the first ruler of the Tsin dynasty upon the ruins of Wu and Shu, which he annexed to Wei. The Tsin dynasty officially united China under a single sovereign, but this unity was more apparent than real. There were many semi-independent principalities that were extremely reluctant to acknowledge the supremacy of the Dragon Throne, and the unification of the empire was not achieved without considerable difficulty. Many of these border principalities were Buddhist, and it was from them, even more than from India, that the overwhelming flood of Buddhist books and translators came, which has contributed to making the history of Buddhism in China such a hopeless chaos. Many of these translators brought their books from Khotan. Around the year A.D. 270, Khotan was a semi-independent state that paid tribute to China, with which it shared very close trade relations. Buddhism was practically the only religion of the country; the common language was an Indian dialect, and the script was a form of Sanskrit known as Kharoshti. There were other principalities of

The limited interaction with India proper can be inferred from the fact that, during the years 317–439, out of thirty-six translators mentioned by Nanjo, twelve came from the western regions (including Khotan), eight from Kubhâ (Kabul), ten from various parts of China proper, two from Turkestan and Bukhara, and only four from India.

The Emperor Wu-ti (for this was the name that Szuma I assumed upon his accession) was an extremely capable ruler. He not only unified the country and saved it for a time from foreign invasion, but he also did much for literature and the general development of the empire. He encouraged travel (we read of a Chinese scholar, Tsushi, or the "Red Teacher," being sent to India), and in the year 284 he received at his capital (more likely Nanking) an embassy from a Roman emperor. It was the year of Diocletian's accession: the embassy, which may have been traveling for some time, must have been sent by Probus (276–284), or by Aurelian, the "Restorer of the World" (270–276). It is possible that it was not an embassy at all, but merely a group of traders whom the vanity of the Chinese raised to the dignity of ambassadors.

Wu-ti died in 290 and was succeeded by his son Hweiti, a simpleton "who could not distinguish beans from wheat," and who was entirely controlled by an unprincipled wife. The country was immediately engulfed in rebellion from one end to another, and the Tartars on the frontier established a rival kingdom in Shansi, with a claimant to the throne who alleged descent from the great Han family. The Han had not yet been forgotten, and the great Wu-ti, after all, had only been a successful usurper. The weak Hweiti was poisoned in 306; his successor was killed in battle against the Tartars in 311. Mingti, who succeeded him, was compelled to remove his

The White Lotus Society still exists in China, I am told, and its members sing hymns that are difficult to distinguish from Christian ones.¹

With Kumarajīva begins the period of <term>Saddharmapundarika</term> influence. That remarkable book (the connection between which and one of the Gnostic books I have already pointed out) may be described as a type of Buddhist Apocalypse.

The Master, on the Vulture Peak, awakens from his trance to show his listeners that, although people may think there are three forms of saving doctrine, there is really only one. The apparent differences arise from the fact that the One Truth must be adapted and modified to suit the needs of those to whom it is delivered. This is illustrated by various parables, and the listeners have the lesson impressed upon them that the ultimate goal of all endeavors must be to reach All-knowingness. And to know everything is the same thing as knowing nothing.

The Master is endowed with all knowledge and all power. He knows the past—the long record of his own existences—and the future—the destinies of his listeners—both of which he describes. His knowledge is so great that even the Buddhas made Perfect in the past are anxious to hear his Wisdom, and he offers himself, united with a great Buddha of previous times, for the adoration of the congregation.

Then he sends out his disciples to preach his gospel. He promises them his protection and encourages them by showing the wonderful success of their preaching. It will really be He who preaches, and not they. Every one of their countless millions of converts has been his personal disciple at some point in time. At the head of the groups of those who will believe are four great <term>Bodhisattvas</term>. Later chapters lead us to infer that "the Four" are Yakushi, Kwannon, Fugen, and Myō-On.¹ Nichiren claimed that he himself was one of the Four. Whoever they are, they are beings of great power who stand around the Master, who is supreme and unlimited by time or space.

If Professor Takakusu is right, we must place the two brothers Asangha and Vasubandhu in this period, as they play such an important part in the development of the <term>Mahāyāna</term>. Takakusu places them around A.D. 445 and explains his reasoning for doing so. However, on the list of <term>Mahāyāna Patriarchs</term> provided by Nanjo, Vasubandhu appears exactly halfway between Nāgārjuna and Bodhidharma. We know Bodhidharma's date was A.D. 520; if we place Nāgārjuna around A.D. 120, we find that a halfway date would place Vasubandhu around A.D. 300, which fits better with the observable effects of his work. Vasubandhu, like Nāgārjuna, is claimed by many sects. He belongs to the <term>Kusha</term>, the <term>Hossō</term>, and the <term>Jōdo</term>; the latter, especially, considers him to be one of the most powerful advocates of faith in Amitābha and rebirth in the <term>Pure Land</term>.

His brother, Asangha, who was a Mahayanist before him, is regarded as the founder of the <term>Hossō</term> or

He was delivering a series of lectures at a preaching-place in Ayodhya, where he lived. The lectures were not his own. One day a student doubted his word. “You must not do that,” the professor said; “what I am giving you I obtained from the <term>Tushita</term> Heaven, from <term>Maitreya</term> himself.” With a skepticism that would have done credit to a class of Japanese students, his audience refused to believe him. “Very well, then,” said <term>Asangha</term>, “I’ll bring my <term>Maitreya</term> with me next time!” And the lessons delivered in this way were the foundation of the doctrines of the <term>Hossō</term> Sect!

## A. NOTE ON THE CHINESE SECTS.

The following notes on Chinese sects will be useful for reference, as some of them will appear again in the Japanese chapters. Many of them were extremely superstitious and corrupt; few professed much real reverence for the teachings of <term>S'akyamuni</term>, and in none, except in the <term>Jōdo</term>, do we find any of the enthusiasm that inspires its followers. I derive my information mainly from <term>Nanjo</term> and <term>Murakami</term>.

1. The <term>Abhidharma</term> sect. In India, this was considered one of the twenty sects of the <term>Hinayāna</term>. It was based on the Commentary on the <term>Abhidharma</term> treatises written by <term>Kātyāyaniputra</term>, and was brought to China about A.D. 394 by three Indian monks: <term>Sanghadeva</term>, <term>Dharmanandin</term>, and <term>Sanghabhūti</term>. It seems to have flourished until about A.D. 440. I have found no traces of it in Japan.

2. <term>Jōjitsu</term>, based on <term>Harivarman's</term> “<term>Satyasiddhiśāstra</term>” (<term>Nanjo</term>, No. 1274), and brought to Singanfu by <term>Kumarajiva</term> in 401. It was opposed to the doctrines of the <term>Sarvāstivādins</term>. It flourished in China until the beginning of the <term>Tang</term> period, when it was absorbed by the <term>Tendai</term>. It appeared in Japan only to disappear again.

3. <term>Sanron</term>, based on three <term>S'āstras</term>, two by <term>Nāgārjuna</term>, one by

<keywords>Asangha, Maitreya, Dharmalakshana, Hossō Sect, Abhidharma Sect, Jōjitsu Sect, Chinese Buddhism, Buddhist history</keywords>

<page-num>164</page-num>
<header>THE CREED OF HALF JAPAN</header>

Deva, with commentaries by <term>Asangha</term> and <term>Vasubandhu</term>. It was deeply metaphysical and was held in high esteem in China during the Sui dynasty (589–618). Under the Tang it lost its prestige. It was brought to Japan during the time when Sui influence was strong, and its first recognized head was <term>Ekwan</term> (624), but it was ousted from favor by the <term>Hossō</term> and <term>Kegon</term> sects.

4. Nirvana (<term>Nehan</term>). This sect may be said to have flourished from <term>A.D.</term> 386 to <term>A.D.</term> 589, first among the Liang, and afterwards at Nanking under the earlier Sung. It was one of the first sects to construct a "Harmony" of the numerous <term>Sūtras</term>. It divided <term>Shaka</term>'s life into five periods, and considered the <term>Sūtra</term> of the Great Decease (<term>Nehangyō</term>) as representing the highest and final teachings of the Master. The <term>Saddharmapundarika</term> and most of the <term>Amida</term> books had not yet become prominent in China when this sect was started. It was absorbed under the Tang by the <term>Tendai</term> sect, and reached Japan under that name.

5. <term>Jiron</term>, based on the <term>Das'abhūmika</term>, with <term>Vasubandhu</term>'s (not <term>Nāgārjuna</term>'s) commentary. Introduced by <term>Bodhiruci</term> <term>A.D.</term> 508, it flourished under the Northern Wei (386–534). It was eventually absorbed by <term>Kegon</term>.

6. <term>Jōdo</term>. This sect is an effort at simplification. It tries to present *one object of Faith to its followers*. Its best-known teacher is <term>Zendō</term>, a contemporary of the Nestorian missionaries at Singanfu. He advised his followers (and in this he was followed by the Japanese <term>Hōnen</term>) to throw away the other books of the Canon, and to pin their faith on the central clause of <term>Amida</term>'s vow. His writings contain some wonderfully striking echoes of scriptural phrases, *e.g.*, "the turning of the hearts of the children to the Fathers, and *vice versa*," and the warning against adding to or taking from the words of his book. Haas ("Amida Buddha unsere Zuflucht") gives quotations from his works, as well as from those of <term>Donran</term> and <term>Dōshaku</term>.

7. <term>Zen</term>, another effort at simplification. <term>Bodhidharma</term>, who arrived in China in <term>A.D.</term> 527, advised his followers to throw away all books, and to strive to attain enlightenment by way of meditation. <term>Bodhidharma</term> taught in the Kingdom of the Liang, and afterwards among the Northern Wei. This sect, like the <term>Jōdo</term>, has had a great influence in Japan. I have a chapter on it in my "Wheat among the Tares." See also "Sermons by a Buddhist Abbot," published by the Open Court, Chicago. It was not taught much at Singanfu, and was consequently slow in reaching Japan.

8. *Ritsu*, founded as a separate organization by Dōsen at the beginning of the Tang period. However, the Vinaya discipline had been taught long before that time and arrived very early in Japan (see the chapter on Dharmagupta). "If a person does not practice Dhyāna and Samādhi <note>meditation and contemplation</note>, they cannot understand the truth. If they do not keep all the precepts, they cannot accomplish their excellent practice." This would seem to show that the Ritsu is in some ways an expansion of Zen. In Japan, the sect was ultimately merged into the Shingon.

9. *Hossō*, which means "the sect that studies the nature of things," is also known as the Dharmalakshana or Yoga sect. This is the doctrine contained in the lectures given by Maitreya for Asangha, to which I have already alluded. It was established in China by Hiouen Thsang about <term>A.D. 640</term>. It was brought to Japan in 653 by Dōsō, who transmitted it to Gyōgi, and again independently in 712 by the notorious Gembō. It was the Hossō that introduced the system known as <term>Ryōbu Shinto</term> to Japan. It cannot be credited with doing much to improve humanity in Japan.

10. *Tendai*, named after the mountain where its chief founder, Chisha Daishi, had his monastery. It is based on the <term>Saddharmapundarika</term> and is one of the harmonizing sects. Emon (<term>A.D. 551</term>) was the first man to grasp the full significance of the <term>Lotus Scripture</term>. He was assisted in his work by Eshi and Chi-ki; the latter, under the name of Chisha Daishi, became the actual founder of the sect. This sect intends to be all-embracing. Its supreme Buddha is Vairoc’ana, who transmitted his teaching to S’akyamuni, who transmitted it to Maitreya, and thus through Asangha’s lecture hall to the world. It divides the period of S’akyamuni’s life into five parts. It accepts Amida as another name for Vairoc’ana. It practices Yoga and charms, as the Hossō and Shingon do, but rejects the Shingon claim of a revelation to Nāgārjuna through the sage of the Iron Tower. Chisha Daishi died in <term>A.D. 597</term>.

11. *Kegon* (<term>Avatamsaka</term>). The fundamental scriptures were translated in <term>A.D. 418</term> by Buddhabhadra (Kakugen). It was very popular under the Tsin (557–589) and throughout the Tang period. It arrived in Japan later than the Hossō but was swallowed up by the Shingon (see below on Namudaishi) and Tendai.

12. *Shingon*. We have seen that this sect (as well as the Tendai) contains doctrines very similar to those of the Gnostics of Alexandria. The Secret Shingon was not, however, brought to China

¹ Regarding the earliest surviving Chinese translation of this work, made by Lokaraksha in A.D. 147, it is worth noting that Hōzō Biku—the earthly phase of Amida—makes his vow there not before the last, but before the first of his eighty-one predecessors. 3. *Amitāyur-dhyāna-sūtra* (Japanese *Kwammuryōjukyō*), translated by Kalayaśas in 424 A.D., eight years after Eon's death. These are: (i) worldly goodness, such as filial piety, loyalty, respect for parents, etc.; (ii) morality of that internal and unworldly kind which is the first foundation of the religious life; and (iii) the goodness of practice, which includes the practical application to life of the Four Great Truths and the Six Pārāmitas, or Cardinal Virtues. A good seed produces good fruit in abundance. If we sow the seeds of the three types of goodness, we shall reach, as fruit, the ninefold bliss of the Pure Land.

## CHAPTER XVII

### BUDDHISM REACHES JAPAN

BUDDHISM reached Japan from Korea, and not initially from China.
Korea, in the period we have been considering, was not as large a country as it is now. The entire region from the Yalu River, which forms the current boundary of the Korean Empire, to the Tatong River, halfway between Wiju and Seoul, belonged to China. The rest of the peninsula was divided into three independent kingdoms: Koma, which occupied the eastern slopes from the Tumen River in the north down almost to the extreme south of the peninsula; Kudara, which occupied the whole of the western slopes from the Chinese frontier to the extreme south; and the small kingdom of Shiragi in the southeastern corner of the peninsula, on the side nearest to Japan. The southernmost province of Shiragi was the province of Mimana, which may be said to have been at one time practically a Japanese colony.
Buddhism had reached the kingdom of Koma in 372 A.D., the missionary having been sent from Singanfu by the ruler of the Former Thsin (350–394 A.D.). A ruler of the Eastern Tsin (317 to 420) had sent an Indian priest, Marananda, to preach the Gospel of Buddha in Kudara in the year 384. Shiragi had received the doctrine from the neighboring kingdom of Koma in

### BUDDHISM REACHES JAPAN

<margin>A.D. 424.</margin> The well-known tendency of the Buddhist priesthood for political intrigue and amateur statecraft makes it highly probable that the rival rulers of the Thsin and the Tsin, searching for any means to support their failing dynasties, used Buddhist missionaries for political purposes to gain allies in Koma and Kudara, both of which kingdoms bordered the Chinese frontiers. We have no accurate information regarding the exact nature of Korean Buddhism at this time. The division into sects in China was still new, and sectarian boundaries were not very clearly defined. The doctrine still maintained its Indian and predominantly Hinayanistic character; <term>Vasubandhu</term>, <term>Asangha</term>, and other great teachers of <term>Mahāyāna</term> had possibly not been born when Buddhism reached Korea.¹ There are indications showing that much attention was paid to the <term>Vinaya</term> discipline, and that whatever speculation existed followed the lines established by the <term>Kusha</term>, <term>Sanron</term>, and <term>Jōjitsu</term> sects (see Chapter XVI.).

Korea and Japan were by no means strangers to each other. As early as 32 B.C. (if the early records of Japan can be trusted), the small province of <term>Mimāna</term> or <term>Kara</term>, oppressed by <term>Shiragi</term>, had appealed to Japan for help. The reigning emperor, <term>Sujin Tennō</term>, became its protector, and the prestige of the Japanese name was so great that Japan was able not only to turn <term>Mimāna</term> into a Japanese dependency, but to keep it as such for several centuries. Korean influence upon Japan may have begun even then; for in the reign of the next emperor, <term>Suinin</term>, around the dawn of the Christian era, we find the beginnings of rice culture in Japan and an attempt to elevate and ennoble the native worship of the <term>Kami</term>, which may have been due to the influence

...of <term>Nintoku</term> with deep respect as a man of singular virtue and nobility. <term>Nintoku</term> introduced <term>sericulture</term> (silkworm breeding) into Japan, and it is a significant fact—suggesting a possibly earlier existence of <term>Buddhism</term> in this country—that in the silk districts, the patron deity of <term>sericulture</term> is the Buddhist saint <term>Ashvaghosha</term>.<note>See "Bukkyō Mondō Shū," pp. 14–24.</note>

In the year A.D. 522, a Chinese priest named <term>Shiba Tatsu</term>, a subject of the <term>Liang</term> dynasty (502–557), made an attempt to establish a mission in <term>Yamato</term>, which failed. The <term>Liang</term> ruled in southern China. Their first emperor, <term>Wu-ti</term>, was a powerful ruler who extended the dominions of his house to the eastern seacoast and did much to foster trade and commerce. In his reign, the Chinese began to be a seafaring people, and Chinese ships visited the Bay of Bengal, <term>Ceylon</term>, the west coast of India, and even penetrated as far as the Persian Gulf. During the earlier years of his reign (502–549), <term>Wu-ti</term> was a great patron of <term>Confucianism</term>; in his later years, he alienated his Confucian subjects by his zeal for <term>Buddhism</term>, which he adopted with all the ardor of a convert. In northern China, his most powerful rival was the kingdom of the <term>Wei</term>, ruled over by a queen named <term>Hushi</term>, who, like <term>Wu-ti</term>, was a zealous Buddhist. This was much to the disgust of her Confucianist subjects, who objected to the worship of <term>Shakyamuni</term> on the grounds that he was only a deified man and not a god like <term>Tientei</term>, the ruler of Heaven. In the end, they dethroned their queen and threw her into the <term>Hoangho</term> (Yellow River).<note>Kaeuffer, "Geschichte Ostasiens," vol. ii. p. 397.</note>

The <term>Wei</term> influence<note>There were three Wei dynasties, all in northern China: (1) Northern Wei, 386–534; (2) Western Wei, 534–557; (3) Eastern Wei, 532–550.</note> (386–584) would naturally be great in the Korean states which touched their boundaries.

## THE CREED OF HALF JAPAN

<term>Shiba Tatsu</term> passed through <term>Korea</term> on his way to <term>Japan</term>. It is highly probable that he came on a semi-political mission which failed. Neither <term>Korea</term> nor <term>Japan</term> cared for an alliance with the distant <term>Liang</term>, whose fortunes were apparently bound up with the personality of one man. <term>Wu-ti</term>’s death in 549 was practically the end of his house and dynasty.

But <term>Shiba Tatsu</term>’s mission may very possibly have suggested a reason why the Korean kingdoms should seek to strengthen themselves by an alliance with <term>Japan</term>. <term>Korea</term> was practically a <term>Buddhist</term> realm. Both <term>Wei</term> and <term>Liang</term>, though ruled over by sovereigns with <term>Buddhist</term> propensities, had powerful aristocracies which were strongly anti-Buddhist. Had either of these kingdoms gained the ascendancy in the peninsula, a grievous persecution would have followed, ending perhaps in the overthrow of Korean dynasties.<sup>1</sup> <term>Japan</term> was as yet neither <term>Buddhist</term> nor <term>Confucian</term>. If she could be won over to the faith, the immediate future at least would be secured from danger.

Accordingly, in 545, and again in 552,<sup>2</sup> King <term>Seimei</term> of <term>Kudara</term> sent presents to the Emperor of <term>Japan</term>—images of Buddha and sacred books—together with a recommendatory letter in which he pointed out the virtues of the <term>Buddhist</term> religion, as well as its evident destiny to travel constantly eastward from the land of its origin. The presents received only a doubtful welcome.

The object of <term>Buddha’s</term> teaching was to destroy error and establish the truth: one implied the other, for the destruction of error left truth in its place, and when all errors were destroyed, truth would have the field to itself. But to set to work to establish positive truth would necessarily involve the establishment of error. <note>There can, therefore, never be such a thing as a positive and infallible Revelation of Truth.</note> Truth was of two kinds, absolute (真) and apparent (俗), and error, though infinite in its possibilities, might all be summed up under eight great heads. Speculations such as these, the products of the hair-splitting Indian mind, had no appeal for the practical Japanese intellect, and the <term>Sanron</term> sect<note>For the meaning of Sanron, see the previous chapter.</note> was never more than a shadow among the Buddhist denominations in Japan. If it had not been for the simple faith of the Japanese women, who took the <term>Buddha</term> of the <term>Vinaya</term> books as their model—with his plain, straightforward directions regarding the religious life of the believer—it is possible that Buddhism might have had to wait some years longer before gaining the attention of the Japanese people. This is a lesson that should not be ignored.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### THE CROWN PRINCE SHŌTOKU TAISHI

Emperor Kimmei, who had received from Korea the gifts of Buddhist images and sacred vessels that had caused so much disturbance among his subjects, died in A.D. 570. His reign had not been very happy or glorious. In addition to the domestic confusion arising from the introduction of the new religion, there had been disappointments in the country's foreign policy. His ally, King Seimei of Kudara, had been defeated by the troops of Shiragi and taken prisoner (around 557), a Japanese army in Korea had been defeated by the Shiragi armies in 562, and the province of Mimāna had been entirely lost to Japan. When Kimmei lay dying in 570, he charged his successor, Bidatsu, not to rest until Mimāna had been recovered.

It was not Bidatsu's good fortune to recover the lost province, and when he died in A.D. 585, he gave his successor, Yōmei, the same solemn command that his predecessor had given him. But the year following his accession, the wife of his brother Yōmei gave birth to a son who was destined to restore the country's fallen prestige. The child born was at first called Umayado, "the Stable Prince," a name which has been explained by the story (surely a fiction) that his mother, while making the rounds of her house and grounds, was suddenly seized by labor pains and gave birth to her son in the stable.

He had another name, Toyoto-mimi, which may refer to his physical appearance; but in any case, personal defects had no effect on his intellectual powers, and he was recognized early for both his wisdom and his virtue.

His early youth was a troubled one. Bidatsu continued to receive presents (and appeals for help) from the King of Kudara, who was hard-pressed by Shiragi and scarcely able to defend himself. Without becoming a convert, the Emperor did everything in his power to help the new religion. To give just one instance, he established the practice of releasing animals on the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth of every month—a practice not unlike the early *uposatha*, or the Christian and Jewish Sabbath. No civil disturbances marked his reign; but once, when a plague broke out shortly after the construction of a pagoda—built to house a Buddhist relic that had reportedly been found in some rice—there must have been many doubtful heads shaken over the unfortunate event. But the Buddhists were not to be moved. They met the plague with the weapon of prayer, and when the Emperor himself miraculously recovered from an attack of the illness, they felt that they had triumphed.

In 586, Prince Umayado’s father, Yōmei, ascended the throne, and the Prince became, in expectation at least, the Heir Apparent. Yōmei went further than any of his predecessors, for he was the first Imperial convert to Buddhism and the first emperor to be baptized with the Buddhist ceremony of *Kwanjo*. His conversion possibly cost him his life, for he died in the following year, and his death was the occasion for the outbreak of a civil war. This war ended with the Battle of Shigisen, in which Prince Shōtoku and his loyal friend, Soga

It would seem that the Prince’s Buddhism was of too pronounced a type for him to be a suitable occupant of the throne, which went to his uncle Sujun, a younger brother of Bidatsu and Yōmei. Sujun must have been the candidate favored by the conservative <term>Kami</term> worshippers, or at least acceptable to them. He made preparations for an expedition against Shiragi, but he was apparently unable to preserve the loyalty of the advanced party of the Buddhists, for he was murdered in 592 by the ally of the Prince, Soga no Umako.

The Prince was again passed over—voluntarily, it would seem. Sujun’s successor was his elder half-sister, Suiko, the widow of Bidatsu—for marriages between half-brothers and half-sisters were always allowed in ancient Japan. Suiko reigned from 593 to 628; for all but the last seven years, her nephew, now known as Shōtoku Taishi, acted as her deputy and regent, so that what was nominally the reign of the Empress Suiko was in reality the reign of the Crown Prince Shōtoku.

Shōtoku’s life work falls under three headings. We must judge him by his foreign policy, his domestic administration, and his religious achievements.

His foreign policy was eminently successful. His uncles had dreamed of conquering Shiragi, and an expedition was actually on the point of starting when the Emperor Sujun was murdered. Shōtoku tried a more conciliatory line of policy, and one more in accordance with the religious professions of a Buddhist. He sent embassies to Shiragi in 597, and again in 600, with the result that tribute was sent to Japan, not only from Shiragi, but from Mimāna as well, showing thereby that, thanks to the Regent’s wise policy, Shiragi had recognized the independence of the state of Mimāna protected by the

Japanese. Shōtoku went even further in asserting the dignity of his country. He dared to claim an equal imperial status for Japan with China, which Wen-ti of the Sui Dynasty had recently reunited under a single rule. Wen-ti had expanded his territory from the borders of Koma in the east to the Turkic kingdoms in the west, and his successor, Yangti, who ruled from 606 to 618, had extended his power even further. Shōtoku’s Korean policy brought him into conflict with Yangti, who also had designs on the peninsula. In 609, the Japanese Court received a letter from the Chinese sovereign. Shōtoku answered it, but in a tone of equality: “The Eastern Emperor respectfully addresses the Emperor of the West.” The Chinese Court did not entirely appreciate the tone of the letter; however, Koma sent gifts to the Japanese Court in 610, as did Shiragi in 616. Bluffing—or rather, the proper assertion of dignity—is sometimes a very effective policy for a statesman to adopt.

Shōtoku’s domestic administration is primarily associated with an attempt made in 603 to organize the official ranks of government service according to the model of the Chinese Court,<note>The grades are as follows: *Daitoku*, *Shōtoku*, *Daijin*, *Shōjin*, *Tairei*, *Shōrei*, *Daishin*, *Shōshin*, *Daigi*, *Shōgi*, *Daichi*, *Shōchi*. *Toku*, *Jin*, *Rei*, *Shin*, *Gi*, and *Chi* (virtue, benevolence, propriety, sincerity, justice, and wisdom) are the fundamental Confucian virtues.</note> and the Constitution of the Seventeen Articles issued the following year. These newly graded official ranks were named after Confucian virtues, as if to remind the officials of the supreme importance of virtue above all else. In the Constitution, we find traces of Confucian influence along with an outspoken advocacy for Buddhism, which the author—at least in his own mind—considered the only religion for a wise man to follow.

The seventeen articles of the Constitution shed significant light on the national conditions that Shōtoku sought to improve. It was a period of disunion and discord, likely dating back to the days before the introduction of Buddhism, but also probably worsened by it. The results of this discord were visible in the loss of Mimāna and nearly all influence in Korea, as well as in the stagnation of Japanese culture. In his first article, Shōtoku appeals to the country for the sake of harmony; in the second, he points his countrymen toward what he believes to be the best and truest way of achieving it—the sincere acceptance of Buddhism. We cannot help but admire the boldness of his words, considering the ongoing opposition to foreign doctrines. Nor can we forget that, at nearly this same time, an Emperor of China was concluding that whenever a ruler showed himself too partial toward the doctrines of Buddhism, he always brought ruin to his dynasty.¹ In Shōtoku's eyes, Buddhism appeared very different.

In Article III, Shōtoku emphasizes the dignity of the Emperor, who stands above his people, offering them protection just as the heavens stand over and protect the earth below. This article was likely directed against the nobles, whose respect for the sovereign during those days of civil strife and confusion was not always as great as it should have been. Furthermore, the article must be read in reference to the murder of Emperor Sujun by Shōtoku's ally, Soga no Umako. Had Shōtoku felt himself in any way to be blamed for his continued friendship with the man who had committed that deed, he would hardly have ventured to speak as he did regarding the respect due to the Emperor.² It would seem as though

Sujun had been a usurper, possibly with the aid of those who opposed Buddhism; Soga no Umako, as the supporter of Shōtoku’s claims, had opened the way for the Prince to succeed, but the Prince, declining to take the throne in this manner, instead secured the nomination of his aunt. He was conscious of his own rights as the son of Yōmei, yet he stood back so that he might be in a position to speak with greater emphasis on the duty that a subject owes to their sovereign. It is evident from this Article that Shōtoku did not share the later formulated and now officially accepted doctrine regarding the origin of the Imperial House.

The following Articles deal with the duties of ministers and officials. If subjects have certain duties toward their rulers, rulers and magistrates have certain responsibilities toward those beneath them, which must be carried out with decorum and the maintenance of due proportion. Such behavior cannot fail to have a good influence on the country at large (Art. *iv.*). But if, on the other hand (Art. *v.*), the magistracy allows itself to be bribed with gifts, if the judge is negligent in the administration of justice, if he gives his decisions to suit his own interests or without clarity, the poor will no longer know whom to turn to for support, and the country will lose its prosperity. Lying and flattery (Art. *vi.*) have been evils in every country and age; Shōtoku’s age was certainly not free from them. It was also exposed to another danger, that of hereditary office (Arts. *vii.* and *viii.*). Men were promoted to ranks and high positions, not for any special abilities they had shown in lower positions, but because these offices were considered to be the privileges of certain families. And the hereditary office had all too often been treated as a

In Articles x–xiv, the evils arising from a lack of responsibility on the part of these hereditary office-holders—who treated their positions almost as sinecures—are laid out in more detail. A magistrate might allow himself to lose his temper on the bench and bully the accused or the witnesses. He should remember that it is always possible that he himself is not the pinnacle of wisdom; it is also possible that the prisoner in the dock and the witness under cross-examination are reasonable men (Art. x). He should listen, therefore, to the opinions of others, deliver his decisions with solemnity and caution, and be very careful to dispense praise and blame in strict accordance with the results of a rigorous and impartial investigation (Art. xi). He should be careful not to levy any arbitrary taxes on his own authority in the district he was called to rule, so as not to provoke the people to resistance (Art. vii). He should know the workings of every detail of his own office, as well as the diligence or negligence of his staff. If something went wrong because a subordinate was absent from his post, the head of the department must not excuse himself by claiming he did not know the man was absent. It was his duty to know it and to ensure that the public service was properly maintained (Art. xiii). Mutual jealousies have often brought ruin to a state. Saints and sages appear only rarely in the world; jealousy and envy are the main obstacles hindering their more frequent emergence. And what would become of the government of a country without sages or saints? (Art. xv). In his judgment, it was perfectly suited to provide his countrymen with the firm ethical basis that the Shintoism of the time lacked, as well as the religious enthusiasm that comes from a definite theological system. We will now move on to the consideration of Shōtoku’s religion.

Shōtoku has been much blamed by modern Shintoist writers as lacking in patriotism, because he laid no stress on the national gods of the land, and because, in the second article of his Constitution, he emphasized Buddhism as the only religion worthy of being adopted by his subjects. It is true that the saying once commonly attributed to him—that the religion of Japan was like a tripod standing on three legs: Buddhism, Confucianism, and Shinto—cannot be supported. As Dazai truly observes, Shinto did not exist (that is, it was not organized into a system) until long after the Crown Prince’s time.¹ But it is also true that there is no sign of him having forced his beliefs on the consciences of his people against their will. He confined himself to preaching the faith which he had adopted with all his heart and soul; for other forms of faith and religion, he had no thoughts left.

He had no reason to love the Kami-worshippers. The followers of that system were not only religious conservatives, but probably obstructionists in the way of popular progress, and they were opposed not only to Buddhism but to Confucianism as well. His entire early life had been embittered by the opposition of a Conservative party which was not even loyal to the throne; it is hardly surprising if, upon his rise to power, he did

He did not go out of his way to recommend a system that had always obstructed the reforms and progress he was so eager to initiate. Furthermore, the Shinto of his day required no recommendation from him. It was already well-established in the hearts of the people. It had not yet been systematized—that came later, as a result of the opposition to Buddhism—nor had the amalgamation between the two religions yet occurred. But we can well imagine that Shōtoku saw no reason why it should not be quietly absorbed by the all-encompassing Buddhism that he preached. There was no need to mention the subject. He would preach Buddha and trust future events for the result.

Shōtoku, like Ashoka, whom he closely resembled in character, was a preacher. This fact makes the historian's task easier, for we fortunately know the texts from which he preached to the ladies and gentlemen of his aunt’s court. In the year 606, two years after the issuance of his Constitution, he lectured in his palace at Naniwa on three books: the “Saddharmapundarika Sūtra,” the “Vimāla-Kīrtti-nirdesa-sūtra,” and the “S’rimāladenī-simhananda-sūtra.” <gloss>1</gloss> In the same year, he decreed the observance of Shakyamuni’s birthday. We may summarize the three Sūtras by saying that the first provided Shōtoku with a manual of theology; the second, with texts on the duties of the devout layman; and the third, with sermons on the duties of faithful women. On these three Sūtras, he preached and also composed commentaries.

Shōtoku was also a man who believed in the power and efficacy of prayer. Shōtoku’s limitations were due to his exalted position. # CHAPTER XIX
## BUDDHISM DURING THE NARA PERIOD¹ FROM A.D. 621–782

The activities of Kumarajiva seem to have led to the fragmentation of the Mahāyāna, which, despite the variety of doctrines it contained within its broad scope, had previously managed to maintain a united front. The sectarianism of Chinese Buddhism was fueled by the troubled state of the Chinese Empire, which was broken up into many kingdoms, each striving for dominance. We have seen some of these rival states searching for allies and trying to gain support for themselves in the Korean peninsula and in Japan. We have seen Korea similarly divided into warring kingdoms, some of which—Kudara and Mimāna—looked to Japan for help, while Shiragi, relying on Chinese support from the Wei kingdom, boldly resisted Japanese intervention. Koma, too weak for independent action, remained undecided and wavered between Japan and Shiragi, depending on its interests at the time. Finally, we have seen Japan under Shōtoku Taishi gradually leaning more and more toward following China's lead, adopting the Sui Empire (590–618) as its model in both religion and secular politics.
