Shōtoku died in 621. Three years before his death, the Sui dynasty in China—with its costly ambition and magnificence—had been forced to make way for the Tang family. The Tangs ruled until 907 and began a period of greatness and prosperity that China had not known since the fall of the great House of Han in 220 A.D.

The Tang dynasty began poorly for Buddhism. <term>Kaotsu</term> (618–627), their first ruler, dismantled Buddhist monasteries everywhere and sent 100,000 <term>bonzes</term> back to secular life where they would be forced to work. Neither his successor <term>Taitsung</term> nor his wife <term>Ch'angsun</term> <note>When Ch'angsun was dying, she spoke to her son with words to this effect: “Our life is in the hands of Heaven, and when it decides that we shall die, no mortal power can prolong it. As for the Taoist and Buddhist faiths, they are heresies and have been the cause of injury both to the people and to the State. Your father had a great aversion to them, and you must not displease him by calling on them on my behalf.” She requested to be buried with great simplicity, urging her son to associate with good men and to avoid extravagance, especially in hunting and building.</note> had any sympathy for the faith. However, the Buddhists knew how to win back favor within a few years, and the Tangs had not been on the Chinese throne for fifty years before <term>Buddhism</term> was once again in full force, and on a far more magnificent scale than before. Under the Tangs, it became essentially a Chinese faith; it had, so to speak, discarded its Indian loincloth and adopted the flowing robes of the Chinese.

In the same year that <term>Shōtoku Taishi</term> died, the first <term>Zoroastrian</term> temple ever built in China was erected at <term>Singanfu</term>, which was the capital at that time. The Tangs owed much to the support of the Turkish tribes on the western frontier of China during the period when they were busy winning their crown, and it was probably due to this—

# BUDDHISM DURING THE NARA PERIOD

It was through the connection between the Empire and the tribes on its borders that the Magians took the opportunity to preach in China itself. Singanfu, which lies in the province of Shensi, is not far from the then-current homes of the Turkish tribes; indeed, it was once suggested to Kaotsu by some cowardly advisers that he should move his capital to a safer spot in the province of Honan, where he would be free from the danger of raids by the barbarians.

The year of Shōtoku’s death was also the year of the Hejirah—the year in which Mohammed fled to Medina and announced his divine mission to the astonished world. Ten years later, Izdegerd, King of Persia, was fighting for his very existence against the victorious Arabs who had gone forth to conquer. By the year 640, the whole of Persia—along with Merv, Balkh, Herat, and everything as far as the Indus and the Oxus rivers—had submitted to the sword of this new religious enthusiasm. It is well known that Persia, in the throes of her final crisis, appealed to China for help. After Izdegerd’s death in 651, his son fled into Turkestan, from where he made his way to China. He succeeded in persuading the Chinese to take over the administration of the entire country between their frontier and that of the Arabs. It was as the Chinese Viceroy of that district that he was attacked and defeated by the Arabs in 670 and forced once more to flee to Singanfu.¹

Was it chance, or was it the design of Heaven, that in the year 636—shortly after Izdegerd had entered into his last fatal war against the Arabs—a Christian mission from Persia arrived in Singanfu?

In Singanfu and its neighborhood, there was also a renewed Buddhist zeal, stirred by a sense of new dangers. The Buddhists had allowed the luxury of the Sui dynasty and many of the rulers of the illegitimate states to go uncensured. Indeed, they had profited from the distractions and evils of the era, securing wealth, status, and tax exemptions as the price for supporting luxurious and ambitious princes. All of this brought upon them the hatred and contempt of the educated classes. The open hostility of powerful sovereigns, such as Kaotsung and others, must have warned them to set their house in order if they wished to maintain their previous prosperity. We can see many signs of this reform movement born of fear: the new school of translation established by Kumarajīva, the suggested merging of Buddhism with Taoism, the new revelations (for they essentially were) of the Hossō and the Kegon, and the comprehensive system established by Chisha Daishi of the Tendai all point to the same conclusion.

Only Bodhidharma and Zendō¹ aimed at simplification,

He was the popular preacher of the hour, and the popularity of his preaching drew the hostility of the other sects upon him. Tendai, Hossō, and Kegon have always been the enemies of the simple faith preached by Zendō. They have always treated it as something alien to Buddhism—and perhaps it was. At any rate, it existed in Singanfu, side by side with many foreign faiths, during that momentous half-century which meant so very much for the religious development of the Far East.

It was probably about this time also that the Manichaean missions reached China proper. They had been in the Turfan and Khotan districts long before this time, but they probably never reached China itself until the time of the Tangs. Recent discoveries by German and other explorers are likely, in a short time, to add so much to our knowledge of Manichaeism that it is not worth speaking at length on the subject here. Let us be content with noting that Manichaeism was in China and was one of the rivals of Buddhism.

Magians, Christians, and Manichaeans were three rivals, in addition to the old enemies, Confucianism and Taoism. With Kaotsu and Taitsung on the throne of the united empire, suppressing Buddhist monasteries with a strong hand, things looked very dark indeed for the Chinese Mahāyāna. Hiouen Thsang was the man who saved it during this crisis. Born in 602 and admitted to the priesthood in 622, Hiouen Thsang determined to travel to India and collect accurate information and materials from the original home of Buddhism for the defense of the faith, which he saw threatened from both within and without. It is quite possible that he mistrusted the Central Asian traditions...

Starting in 629, he made a tour of those Buddhist countries in Central Asia that had not yet fallen prey to the Arabs, and in India, where he was royally treated by the great king Siladitya Harsha, one of the last of its Buddhist sovereigns. When he returned to China, the movement hostile to Buddhism had for the time spent its strength, and when, about 646, he published translations of some of the new books he had brought with him, the Emperor himself deigned to write a preface. <note>Hiouen Thsang gives us the best contemporary picture we have of Buddhist India. If it were not for him and the other Chinese pilgrims who visited India, we would know nothing of the history of that country for several centuries. Hiouen Thsang, in addition to his own contributions to the theology of Buddhism, brought back the materials with which the purely Chinese sects, such as *Tendai* and *Kegon* (*Avatamsaka*), were afterwards established.</note>

Hiouen Thsang, the Max Müller of his day, was in direct relations with Japan. In 655, about the time of the accession of the Empress Saimei, a priest from Kawachi, a Sōzu <note>*Sōzu* is a Japanese ecclesiastical title equivalent to our canon or archdeacon. There, meeting with Hiouen Thsang, he learned from him the Hossō or Dharma-lakshana doctrines, which the great doctor was preaching. Five years later, in the same reign, two more priests, Chitsū and Chitatsu, crossed to China in a ship of Shiragi, and were initiated into the Hossō mysteries by Hiouen Thsang and his coadjutor Jion daishi. Although the Hossō sect, as a formal organization, disappeared shortly after the end of the Nara period, it left permanent traces in the country's religious history. This is because Dōsō and Chitatsu had as their principal disciple the celebrated Gyōgi Bosatsu, <note>Gyōgi Bosatsu was a famous Korean priest (670–749) who held great influence in Japan. If we trace this teaching back to its earliest origins, we shall see what it meant and how powerfully it was likely to affect the situation in Japan. We shall also see, incidentally, how far Mahāyāna Buddhism had traveled by this time from the simplicity of Shakyamuni's original teachings.

---

One of the natural consequences of adopting the system known as *Ryōbu* ("two parts") was that by treating the native gods of Japan as merely incarnations of one or another of the Buddhas—and therefore entitled to the worship of Buddhists—the Japanese were able to introduce many non-Buddhist elements into their faith. Thus, Amida and Vairoc'ana, both of whom are symbolized by the Sun, came to be identified with Tenshōkōdaijin, the "Heaven-shining-mighty goddess" from whom the Imperial house claims descent. (The change of gender is unimportant, for many of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, such as Kwannon, are bisexual.) In this way, too, Buddhism, which strictly forbids the taking of life, gained a "Buddhified" god of war in Hachiman. As a result, Buddhist monks who worshipped the god of war could go to battle with a clear conscience. Nichiren (*Seigoroku*, p. 132) speaks of Tenshōkōdaijin and Hachiman as the true lords of Japan, who were revealed in later times as Buddhas. Hideyoshi, who openly declared his desire for deification, even built a temple for himself where he intended to be worshipped after his death as Shin Hachiman, the "New God of War."

This transformation allowed Buddhism to integrate into Japanese culture, even reconciling its pacifist roots with the worship of war gods like Hachiman.</summary>

### BUDDHISM DURING THE NARA PERIOD 199

The Hossō sect traced its origins back to the brothers Asangha and Vasubandhu, whom we may place at the beginning of the fourth century A.D. It was an age of syncretism and eclecticism. Mani, the founder of Manichaeism, had already developed his great religion, which was destined to spread so widely and to have such an extended and varied influence; Mani had labored in India, as well as studied in Alexandria and Babylon. The Buddhists in India, hard-pressed by the arguments of Hindu philosophers, such as the formidable Sankarāchārya, were searching for new ways of presenting their principles to the Hindu world. The <term>Dharmalakshana</term> or Hossō teachings of Asangha and Vasubandhu were intended to build a bridge between Hinduism and the <term>Mahāyāna</term>, in such a way that the Buddhist might, as it were, invade the territory of Hinduism and conquer without appearing to do so.

The teaching was based, as I have said, on a revelation or quasi-revelation. While Asangha was lecturing in Ayodhya (modern-day Oude) in India, he received a heavenly visitor: the great Bodhisattva Maitreya, <note>For more on this, see the chapter on *Hossō* in volume 1 of *Bukkyō Kakushū Kōyō*.</note> the disciple of Shakyamuni, who had received the promise of becoming the future Savior of the world and who was waiting in the celestial regions for the fullness of time to come. Maitreya, appearing in the lecture hall, explained to Asangha a secret and mysterious doctrine which he had been commissioned to deliver. He had come from a Buddha greater and wiser than Shakyamuni—from the great Buddha *Loc’ana*, or *Roshana*, whose colossal statue is now known as the Daibutsu of Nara. This figure is not to be confused with the *Vairoc’ana* of the *Shingon* sect, which was introduced later by the *Kegon* scholars and *Kōbō Daishi*.

Roshana, said Maitreya, was the Supreme Being—invisible but all-powerful. When He showed Himself upon earth, it was through the personality of two great spiritual Beings: Maitreya himself and Manjuśri, the powerful Bodhisattva of China. <note>¹ It is interesting to note how the different schools of the Mahāyāna nearly all present us with a triad or trinity. Between this trinity of Locana, Maitreya, and Manjuśri, and the Pure-land trinity of Amitābha, Avalokites'vara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, there is only a difference of names. The concepts are identical.</note>

One of the keynotes of the Hossō teaching (it would require a large volume to describe it all) is the doctrine of Oneness, from which the other name of the sect, the *Yuishikikyō*, or Oneness sect, is derived. A Christian would say, "God is One, and besides Him there is no other." But the Hossō sect (if we may use the word "God" for Buddhist speculations) would put it a little differently: "God is One, and besides Him there is nothing." The Universe, or God (for the two were treated as identical), was looked upon as a mighty ocean, unfathomable and unlimited, and the phenomena of nature and life—trees and plants, birds and beasts, sun and stars, men, angels, and even the gods whom men worshipped—were but the waves which appear for a moment on the surface, vanish, and reappear in a different shape. The wave I look at now is but a rearrangement of the drops in the wave which appeared in a different shape in another part of the bay. The god I worship now, on the Himalayan slopes, I call by the name of S'akyamuni; rearrange the particles that compose him, and he will appear presently on the plains of the Ganges as the Hindu Vishnu. The name and the form have been changed, but the essence, which is a part of the great Ocean of the Universe (which is God), is unchanged and remains identically the same. Thus it happened in India that men passed from one cult to

This was the doctrine that enabled Gyōgi Bosatsu and other leading priests of the Nara period to propose the doctrine of Ryōbu-Shinto (or *Ryōbu-Bukkyō*, as it is also called). According to this doctrine, the ancient gods of Japan—Amaterasu, the Sun Goddess, and the other divinities whom the Japanese had brought from their unknown original homes on the Asian continent—were not independent spiritual beings. Instead, they were merely fresh incarnations of that same divine Essence which had moved for a time on the surface of things, manifesting as various great Bodhisattvas and Buddhas of the Indian religion. Buddhism had not come to destroy Japan's faith, but to strengthen it with the additional light shining from India and China. One may doubt how far this was a popular movement. The common people counted for very little in those days; it was an oracle, issued from the Temple at Isé, that authoritatively proclaimed the identity of Amaterasu and Vairoc'ana.¹ A few years earlier, in the year 616, the great god of Miwa² had very obligingly let it be known throughout Japan that the Buddhist clergy were the proper ministers to take charge of funeral rites.³ This practically amounted to an official endowment of Buddhism.

Another sect that appeared in Japan during the Nara period was the Kegon, or Avatamsaka sect, which was introduced in 736. It was of purely Chinese origin, although the books on which it was based came originally from India. It had been founded at the end of the Sui and the beginning of the Tang dynasties, between 600 and 660, by a priest whose name the Japanese pronounce as Tojun (杜順). At the time it arose, it represented one of the latest developments in Chinese Buddhist thought (it came into prominence shortly after the Hossō). The Japanese have always wanted to have the very latest ideas in every department of human thought.

Like the Hossō, the Kegon traced its origins back to the very beginnings of the Mahāyāna. Legend says that when Nāgārjuna, in his travels, reached the Himalayas, he was taken to the Dragon Palace under the sea, from which he brought back the wonderful book known as the *Avatamsaka Sūtra*,<note>See Nanjo, No. 87.</note> which was to form the basis of the new sect. It is a very difficult and long book; many earlier translators had attempted it, but they had only produced fragmentary versions of individual chapters.<note>The list of *Avatamsaka Sūtras* provided by Nanjo gives us data for determining the age of Nāgārjuna. One of the chapters was translated by Lokaraksha of the Han Dynasty, who reached Loyang in 147 A.D. It follows that Nāgārjuna must have lived before that date. Furthermore, all Buddhist authorities in Japan place him 600 years after the Parinirvana. If we set that date at about 500 B.C., we find Nāgārjuna’s date to be about 100 A.D., which aligns very well both with the translation by Lokaraksha and with the year assigned by Eusebius and other writers for the starting point of Gnosticism.</note> Now at last, in the Tang period, a complete version was finished. The project received the most enthusiastic encouragement from the Court, and one of the Tang empresses in the early eighth century not only sent to Khotan to obtain a complete copy of the Sanskrit *Sūtra*,

Sakyamuni therefore set them aside for a while and did not return to them again until toward the close of his ministry, when his disciples were sufficiently advanced to receive them.

At their core, the three sets meant much the same thing, and the ethics of Buddhism were much the same whoever preached them; but the three represented sectarian differences, and rivalries quickly emerged between jealous monks competing with one another for the favor of the court and nobility. This was one of the characteristics of the Nara age.¹

Any student who has the time, inclination, and opportunity to further investigate the study of this period will find it full of very valuable historical material which sheds significant light on the present life and thought of the Japanese people. Among a number of sovereigns of no special importance, Kōtoku Tennō (645–654) is distinguished for the zeal with which he worked according to the lines of political and civil reform established by Shōtoku. The Taika reforms (so called from the *Nengo*¹ or year-period in which they were issued—an institution then first borrowed from China) brought the institutions of Japan very close to the Chinese models. The old offices of the *Ōmi* and *Ōmuraji*² were abolished, and three new officers with Chinese titles—*Sadaijin*, *Udaijin*, and *Naidaijin*—were appointed to take their place. Exact reports were demanded from the governors of the provinces regarding the conditions and needs of the people; a simple but (for the time) sufficient Court of Appeal was instituted in the form of a box placed at the palace gates to receive the complaints of the people; provincial boundaries were fixed; and the *Handen shuja-hō* was established. This law, while providing that each peasant family should have a minimum allotment of rice land (two *tan* for a man and a little more than one *tan* for a woman), also provided for the revenues of the State by taking one-twentieth of the produce for State purposes. Thus, the State became the universal landlord, and the people paid a single tax that included rent. The reforms were not carried out without opposition. Soga Ishikawa-maro, who held the office of Udaijin, was falsely accused

The Nara period also saw the publication of the two great chronicles of ancient Japan—the *Kojiki* and the *Nihongi*.<note>There is a translation of the *Kojiki* by Chamberlain (*Asiatic Society of Japan*, vol. x, Supp.); a translation of the *Nihongi* into English by Aston (*Japan Society, London*, Supp. I); and one in German by Florenz (*Mitteilungen der deutschen Gesellschaft für Natur und Völkerkunde Ostasiens*, Tokyo).</note> The *Kojiki* was published in 712 and contains the history of Japan from its creation to the end of the reign of Empress Suiko (A.D. 628). The *Nihongi* was published in 722 and covers much of the same history. In assessing their value, one must remember that they are chronicles rather than formal histories. Even so, the writers were clearly motivated by a desire to claim an ancient origin for Japan—and therefore a level of dignity—equal to that claimed by the empire of the proud Tang dynasty. Therefore, the lives of early sovereigns have in some cases been extended beyond all bounds of probability, and

In other respects, the era was uncritical, superstitious, and therefore credulous. When the Kegon Scriptures were being explained in the palace, a pink cloud hovered over the building, which was taken to signify the presence of a heavenly audience. A priest in the mountains of Tamba, who served a temple dedicated to Kwannon, was snowed in one winter day; being cut off from the outside world for nearly a week, he was in danger of starving. As he prayed, he heard a sound on the veranda, and, going out, found a joint of venison placed there. He ate it and survived, though by eating it he broke the laws of Buddhism. Sometime after this, while cleaning his temple, he discovered the source of the venison. From the thigh of the statue of Kwannon, a piece had been cut—wood, shall we call it, or flesh?—the exact size of the venison that had been placed on the veranda.<note>I especially note this particular instance because the mention of venison seems to connect it with the deer Jātaka, which reappears in Christian folklore as the legend of St. Eustathius, and later as that of St. Hubert.</note> The deity himself, at the cost of a painful self-sacrifice, had saved the life of his worshipper.

A sense of wonder was in the air; therefore, when the Goddess of Ise proclaimed her identity with Amitābha or Vairochana, it was believed. Likewise, when the strange tales of the *Kojiki* were published, they were also accepted in faith. It is easy to sneer at an age of credulity; it would be wiser, perhaps, to look back at the strange stories current in Europe during the same period, which our forefathers

#### Kōmyōji (光 明 寺).

In the year 614 A.D., a boy was born in China. I do not know the precise name his parents first gave him. Judging by the examples of other men in similar positions, he had many names at different periods of his life. The name by which he was last known was Zendō (善 導), but that was almost certainly not his childhood name. His family name was Shu (朱), and he was born in the district of Shishū (泗 州).

When he was born, the Sui<note>The Sui dynasty ruled in China from 589–619 A.D. They came to power at the end of a long period of division; the Empire had previously been divided into many small kingdoms, with Chinese rulers south of the Yangtze and Tartar or Turkish chieftains in the northern districts. These included the Wei (Tartars), the Hsia (Huns), the Northern Yen (Tartars), the Western Liang (Turks), and the Western Tsin (Tibetans). These smaller kingdoms are of great importance in the history of Buddhism, for it was in them, rather than in China proper, that Buddhism flourished before the Tang period. The Sui family had only two sovereigns—Wen-ti (589–606), who united China and carried the Chinese name far among the Turks in the North and East; and Yang-ti (605–617), a man of violent temper, prone to debauchery and extravagance, who brought the Empire to the verge of ruin. He was overthrown by Li-yüan of the Tang family, who ascended the throne in A.D. 618 as Kaotsu.</note> dynasty was tottering toward its fall and had, in fact, only four more years of life. We may believe that the Duke of Tang, on the extreme northwest boundaries of the Empire, was already conspiring with Turkish and other chieftains and contemplating that great *coup d’état* which put his master at his mercy and seated himself firmly on the Celestial

Some reform was certainly needed. In the year 618, the Duke of Tang deposed his master and took his seat on the Imperial throne as Kaotsu, the founder of the Tang dynasty. One of the most striking events of his reign was the submission of a petition to the throne against Buddhism. It was presented by leading men among the *literati* and Confucianists and was strongly worded.<note>Kaeuffer, "History of East Asia," vol. ii. p. 659.</note> Kaotsu accepted the petition and acted upon it. He ordered a general dissolution and suppression of Buddhist monasteries and returned 100,000 monks and nuns to secular life. It was probably a necessary measure. The monks were very numerous and very powerful, and they claimed exemption from State control. Various abuses are likely to arise in institutions whose members claim they should not be treated on the same footing as ordinary citizens.

Zendō entered the Buddhist order at a very early age. I cannot determine whether it was before or after the suppression of the monasteries by Kaotsu, but it was most likely before that event. His teacher was a certain Shōshō (明 勝) of Misshu (密 州), a prominent person in the then newly formed Sanron sect. This sect, which is also called the *Ichi-dai-kyōshu*, or "Sect of the Teachings of Buddha's Whole Life," made it a feature of its teachings that it professed to accept every one of the many thousand volumes of the Mahāyāna Canon as having equal authority, without assigning to any single one a pre-eminent place among its peers. What he learned from these teachers led him to adopt a rule of life known as *han shu sammai* (般舟三昧), which reads almost like the stern rule of a Christian ascetic, or perhaps even more like that of a Manichæan fanatic. *Mi tsune ni butsu wo haishi, kuchi tsune ni butsu wo tonae, kokoro tsune ni butsu wo omou.* “His body ceaselessly engaged in the worship of Buddha, his mouth ceaselessly engaged in the recital of Buddha’s praises, his heart ceaselessly meditating on Buddha.” With this in mind, he retired to the Temple of Goshinji (悟眞寺) in Shunnan, where, amidst beautiful mountain scenery and in the solitude of retirement, he “beat out his music.” It is quite evident that this retirement, which lasted for several years, was of great value in the formation of his religious ideas. The name of the temple signifies, appropriately, the “Temple for the Instruction of Truth.” He remained here until his twenty-ninth year, returning to Singanfu in the year <term>A.D.</term> 643.¹

The book which he placed in <term>Zendō</term>'s hands was the *<term>Larger Sukhāvati Vyūha</term>*, the book which gives the account of <term>Amida</term>'s life, of His incarnation in the person of <term>Hōzō Biku</term>, His labors undertaken for the salvation of men, the successful accomplishment of His Great Vow, and His return to glory as King of His Western Paradise. This doctrine <term>Zendō</term> accepted and preached. He may be said to have carried the doctrine a stage further. The followers of <term>Hōnen Shōnin</term> (otherwise known as <term>Genkū</term>) form three communities: (i) the <term>Shinshu</term>, founded by <term>Shinran</term>, and (ii) and (iii) the two sub-sects of the older <term>Jōdo</term> sect, the <term>Chinsei-ha</term> and the <term>Seizan-ha</term>.² The <term>Chinsei-ha</term>, agreeing in this respect with the <term>Shinshu</term>, differ from the <term>Seizan-ha</term> in the matter of reciting the <term>Nembutsu</term>. The latter community treats the <term>Nembutsu</term> as an act of adoration addressed to all the <term>Buddhas</term>; the <term>Chinsei-ha</term> and <term>Shinshu</term> treat it as addressed to <term>Amida</term> alone, as being the only <term>Buddha</term>, and the one to whom everything else is subordinate and subservient; and this practice, according to <term>Murakami</term>,³ is due to the teachings of <term>Zendō</term>. Zendō's biographers relate how, when the patriarch was on the way to visit Dōshaku, his road lay through forests and mountains so rough and impassable that, at last, worn out with fatigue, he had to lie down to rest in a cave. He was fainting from hunger and weariness, and it was two days before he could raise himself. Then it seemed to him that a voice sounded in his ears: "Pull yourself together and struggle on; your difficulties will disappear." We may perhaps inquire what these difficulties were and how they disappeared.

Dōshaku is said to have died in the year <term>A.D.</term> 637. The date cannot be implicitly trusted, for it is also said that Zendō was twenty-nine years old when he visited Dōshaku and accepted <term>Amidaism</term>—an impossible age if Zendō was born in <term>A.D.</term> 614. The explanation will probably be found in another statement to the effect that Dōshaku died five years after Zendō’s visit. That would make Zendō twenty-three years old when he visited Dōshaku, and we may easily believe that the conversion to Amidaism, as he came to learn it, may have been a slow process, not fully accomplished for several years. But, whichever way we look at it, Zendō’s conversion to the full faith in Amida must have taken place around the year <term>A.D.</term> 636 (if anything, a little later than that year), and in, or near, the capital city of Singanfu. From that date, and in that city, he began his preaching activity.

China under the <term>Tang dynasty</term> had many dealings with Central Asia. The ruling family, as dukes of the dependent principality of Tang, had been heavily involved with Tartar and Turkish tribes, and it was apparently by their help that the family had been seated on the throne of China. From the moment, therefore, that the Dynasty was established, the new Empire became the focus of Central Asian attention.<sup>1</sup> A Persian mission was sent by Chosroes II requesting an alliance, and in 621 the first <term>Zoroastrian</term> temple was erected in Singanfu. The leader of this mission seems to have been a <term>Magian</term> named Holu ("the son of fire," as P. Gaubil calls him), who was very active in inciting China against the <term>Mahometans</term>. There seems to be no mention of <term>Manichæans</term> in China proper for many years to come,<sup>2</sup> but in 636,

After 636, then, we find two men in Singanfu preaching nearly identical doctrines: one preaching them in connection with Christ, the other in connection with <term>Amida</term>. It is further said of <term>Zendō</term>’s work that he was constantly assisted by a mysterious priest who visited him every evening and helped him with his commentaries (see Tada, "*Shoshingekōwa*," p. 359). This mysterious collaborator may have been a Christian; if so, the strange coincidences and the almost Pauline echoes constantly found in <term>Zendō</term>’s writings would be fully explained. 

Nor is this a baseless assumption. We have one clear instance of such collaboration between a Buddhist and a <term>Nestorian</term> about a century later, when the <term>Nestorian</term> priest <term>King Tsing</term> (or Adam, as he is called on the Singanfu monument) collaborated with the Indian monk <term>Prajna</term> in the translation of a book on the Six Cardinal Virtues (*Shat Parāmitā Sūtra*).<note>1 This can be found in the Buddhist Canon; see Nanjo’s Catalogue, No. 1004.</note> The original was not in Sanskrit, but in the Hu (胡) language—that is, Persian or, more probably, Uigur. At any rate, not much came of this attempted collaboration, which likely caused much jealousy and opposition. After a while, it was forbidden by the Emperor <term>Taitsung</term>, who, in a published decree, ordered the <term>Nestorian</term> <term>King Tsing</term> to confine himself to the teachings of <term>Mishiho</term> and to leave the followers of <term>S'akyamuni</term> to propagate the teachings of their master.<note>2 Professor Takakusu drew attention to <term>Prajna</term> in his translation of I-Tsing’s “Record of the Buddhist Religion” (Oxford, 1896). <term>Mishiho</term> means Messiah. A phrase that <term>Zendō</term> uses more than once is <term>Fushi Sōgō</term>, “the turning of the hearts of parents and children to one another,” a phrase which immediately suggests the book of Malachi. <term>Zendō</term>’s phrase was later made the title of the well-known Japanese <term>Jōdo</term> book, the *Fushi Sōgō*. I am much indebted to Dr. Haas of Heidelberg for calling my attention to this matter.</note>

Strangely, the Nestorians—who had been well received and honorably treated by Taitsung and Kaotsung—fell into disgrace and were persecuted as soon as Kaotsung’s death left supreme power in the hands of the Empress-Dowager Wu-hu and her advisor Hwai-yi. The persecution of the Nestorians was instigated by the same people who opposed the followers of Zendō, and much the same excuses were used. Moreover, the persecution of the two groups continued for the same period, and relief came to them at the same time. Regarding the Nestorians, we read that Huantsung (723–756), succeeding Wu-hu, rebuilt the “Temple of Felicity,” as the Nestorian Church was called; that Huantsung’s successor, Sutsung (756–763), coming into a troubled inheritance, recovered Singanfu (which was held by rebels) and erected “luminous” temples in various parts of his empire; and finally, that the Emperor Taitsung (763–780)—the same ruler who discouraged the

When the Nestorian mission first arrived in China in AD 636, they obtained from the Emperor Teitsung a decree authorizing the erection of a *Tatsin* (that is, a Syrian) temple. This name, however, may have led to confusion, for both Zoroastrians and Manichæans might conceivably have claimed the title (loosely construed), and in fact did so. When Huantsung, soon after 713, rebuilds the Nestorian Church, it is called a “Temple of Felicity.” When Sutsung, in 756, recovers Singanfu, the Nestorian Churches are “luminous (景) temples,” and this name has come to be identified with Nestorianism ever since, both in China and Japan.

When Zendō died, the Emperor Kaotsung (650–683) granted to the temple in which he resided the honorific title of Kōmyōji (光明寺), which is only another form of “luminous temple.” The popular explanation of this name is obviously a fanciful one. Bright rays of light do not come out of the mouths of even the most eloquent preachers of any faith, nor do books, however holy and moldy, glow with a phosphorescent light. Yet that was what Shōkō is said to have seen issuing from the works of Zendō preserved in the library at the White Horse Monastery.<note>See Nanjo, “Short History of the Twelve Buddhist Sects,” p. 107.</note> Kaotsung was an enlightened monarch, and if he gave the title of Kōmyōji, it must have been for the quality of the doctrine and not by reason of any doubtful miracle. This view receives considerable support from Japanese history. Shōtoku Taishi, whom the Shinshu honor as the first of their Zenchishiki or Saints, died in 621, shortly after the start of the Tang Dynasty. Buddhism was, therefore, in full swing in Japan when, in 636, the Nestorian Mission arrived at Singanfu and Zendō began his preaching; there were many Japanese students being sent yearly to China for study.<sup>1</sup> Not only that, but there were many Chinese families residing in Japan and naturalized there (*ayabito*), and it has been noted that most of Emperor Kōtoku’s Taikwa Reforms (A.D. 645–654) were worked out for him by these *ayabito*.<sup>2</sup> The entire Nara period was an age in which Japan was especially sensitive to Chinese influences, and particularly to the influences of Chinese Buddhism.

This influence seems to have reached its peak during the reign of Emperor Shōmu (724–748) and his Consort, Empress Kōmyō (the very name, a posthumous one, is in itself significant). Emperor Shōmu was a very zealous Buddhist. He founded hospitals and charitable institutions, and his Empress distinguished herself by personally undertaking the nursing of lepers<sup>3</sup>—a truly Christian work. Japan was in no position at the time to undertake hospital work unaided. Foreign doctors had to be employed, and the diligent research of Japanese students has recently shown the presence of a Nestorian Christian at the Court in Japan (the Nestorian Christians were famous all

Mr. Tachibana, who provided me with the materials for this note, bases his information on an article by Dr. Takakusu in "Shigakuzasshi," vol. iii. No. 7, and on Dr. Kume’s "History of the Nara Epoch." That Rimitsu was a Christian was shown some time ago by Mr. Saeki. He could not have been a Manichæan, since the Manichæans discouraged doctors.</note>

In 781, the Singanfu monument was erected, and shortly before or after, the Chinese Emperor found reason to prohibit such collaboration. In 782, Emperor Kwammu ascended the throne of Japan. The Buddhists had been putting on airs for some time, and the ambitious priest Dōkyō, intriguing with Empress Shōtoku (765–769), had assumed the title of *Hō Ō*, or "religious emperor"—a kind of pope! Kwammu decided to put an end to the political intrigues of the Nara clergy, moved his capital to Kyoto, and sent Kōbō and Dengyo to China to study religion. They returned, one with the Shingon, the

Gyogi Bosatsu was the spiritual director of Shōmu and his Empress Kōmyō. He was an advocate of Kōmyō doctrines, very practical, and very charitable. He was a syncretist and first originated the <term>Ryōbu</term> doctrine in Japan, stimulated to do so by the example of the Buddhists and Taoists in China.

But the light still shone, despite the opposition of the Tendai. Zendō's books came over to Japan, Mr. Tada tells us, at different times between 796 and 858, and several monks, such as Kūya and Eikwan, kept the faith in Amida alive. They invoked His name on Hieizan or wandered from province to province disguised as traveling priests or horse dealers (*umakata*), preaching a simple faith to country peasants.^1 And finally, the great Hōnen (Genkū), breaking with the Tendai as so many others had done in order to return to the teaching of Zendō, founded a temple at Kurodani. This temple is still known as *Konkai Kōmyōji*, "the Illustrious Temple of the Golden Precept," and it remains to this day one of the chief seats of the Chinsei sub-division of the Jōdo sect. It is this Chinsei-ha which preserves Zendō's rule of making the Nembutsu an invocation of the Great Amida alone, excluding all others.

# CHAPTER XX

## HEIAN BUDDHISM¹

It was in the year A.D. 767, in the first year of the period known to the Japanese as *Jingo Keiun*, that a child was born in a village in Ōmi, not far from the shores of Lake Biwa, who was destined to exercise a great influence on the Buddhism of his country. The father, a Confucian scholar and yet also a man of religion and piety, had often prayed for a son, and, having received his desire, showed his gratitude to Heaven by the care he bestowed upon his son's education. Saichō (the name by which the son was later known) grew up a well-trained lad with a liking for books and a wisdom a little (possibly) beyond his years.

His father was a man of religion and piety; it was no wonder that the son should follow such a close example. Buddhism was at the height of its popularity during the eighth century, and the Court—dissolute and luxurious, and yet, like the Athenians, prone to superstition—encouraged a very magnificent system of ritualism as a counterbalance for its moral and ethical deficiencies. It was very natural that the boy's imagination should be caught by the outward splendor of the worship he saw around him, and that his favorite pastime should be

<margin>Vertical pencil line marking this paragraph</margin>
It was in the midst of these events that Saichō was born. And things did not go much better as time went on. Shōtoku was succeeded by Konin (770–781), but the change of sovereign brought no relief to the country. The Fujiwaras were reinstated in office, it is true, and the meddling Pope Dōkyō was banished to a safe distance in what was then the remote province of Shimotsuke. But the Nara monks were not pleased to see an end put to their temporal power. In the next reign, that of Kwammu (782–805), an insurrection of the Ebisu in the north—one of a series of similar outbreaks, and therefore possibly traceable to Dōkyō's sinister influence—gave the authorities a vast amount of trouble. Kwammu resolved that, at whatever cost, the interference of the Buddhist clergy in matters of state must come to an end; accordingly, he removed his capital, first to Uda, and eventually to his new city of Kyoto, or Heian.

He was an advocate for foreign missions and often spoke on the subject to his students. At last, one day he presented the matter very strongly to them and asked for volunteers. Not a single student answered the call. The next morning, he told them after his lecture that, since no one had volunteered, he would go himself. The superiority of example over instruction was immediately shown by the ready response of over twenty men, who had been willing to follow but did not feel themselves competent to lead.

But it was easier to volunteer than to go. Storms, pirates, shipwrecks, and being cast away on a distant and inhospitable shore all combined to delay the journey. Nearly ten years passed before Ganjin reached Japan; when he finally did, he had already lost his eyesight through the hardships of his adventures, and it was sheer grit that pulled him through. But merits like these were not likely to go unnoticed. Ganjin was given an honorable post at one of the Nara temples, where his undeniable sanctity was highly revered by many who could claim no such virtue themselves. He was put in charge of the *Kaidan*, and thus became the minister of ordination for the monks. He died before Saichō's admission to the Order, but the books he brought with him influenced the course of Saichō's life.

Saichō was fortunate (we might almost, I think, add farsighted) in his selection of a site for his monastery. Hiyeizan dominates the plain of Kyoto, and it was only five years after the consecration of the chapel with its image of Yakuō that Kwammu Tennō forsook Nara and established his capital at Heian (794). The following year, Saichō, whose fame for sanctity had spread very widely, was the celebrant at a great *Dai Kuyō-e*, or High Mass, at which the Emperor himself was present, as well as a large number of priests from Nara and the south.

Kwammu remained faithful throughout his life in his admiration for Saichō. He encouraged him to travel from place to place lecturing on the <term>Hokekyō</term>, and one of the last acts of his reign was to commission him to go to China to consult the <term>Tendai</term> authorities at their primary seat. This was intended to complete what was lacking in the system that Saichō had been instrumental in establishing in Japan.

Saichō set out in 802 as a chaplain (if we may call him that) in the suite of Fujiwara Kadomaro, the Japanese Ambassador to the Court of the Tang Dynasty. Storms delayed the party, and it was not until the following year that he reached China, heading straight for the great monastery of Tientai in the province of Chekiang. Here, he pursued his inquiries with the energy of a man who knows exactly what he wants and can go straight to the point, and he was soon ready to return to Japan. His studies had touched upon the doctrines of <term>Zen</term> and <term>Shingon</term>, but his main interest had been the perfecting of his own <term>Tendai</term> system by the acquisition of proper authority under the <term>Vinaya</term>, or Rules of Ecclesiastical Discipline. At this point, let me digress for a moment to summarize the chief points of the <term>Tendai</term> system.

It will be remembered that the earliest form of Buddhism in China was non-sectarian, as the early missionaries were content to call themselves Buddhists without any further sectarian distinctions. From the year 265 to 589, we find Indian sects—<term>Abhidharma</term> or <term>Kusha</term>, <term>Jōjitsu</term>, <term>Sanron</term>, <term>Jōdo</term>, and <term>Nirvana</term>—some of which have already been summarized. field. We have already spoken of Kegon; the Tendai school was founded in 538 by Chisha Daishi, who nevertheless had predecessors and claimed to derive his specific tenets from the long-suffering Nāgārjuna, who is regarded as the founder of nearly every heresy or sect in Northern Buddhism.

<margin>aspects</margin>
The fundamental principle of Tendai may be called introspection (*Kwanshin no hōhō*), but it is also a system of harmonization through which an attempt is made to create a sense of harmony and order out of the bewildering chaos of the Buddhist Scriptures. Its teachings are divided into two great divisions or gates: the gate of teaching (*Kyō*) and the gate of meditation (*Kwan*). It claims that a person can attain Enlightenment by following either the teachings found in the Scriptures or the practice of meditation and contemplation. It distinguishes three Vehicles instead of two: the Hīnayāna (or *Shojō*), the Apparent or Quasi-Mahāyāna of the Jōdo and Indian sects (*Gondaijō*), and the true Mahāyāna of the sects which originated in China—Zen, Shingon, Kegon, and itself (*Jitsudaijō*).

It embraced the entire collection of the Mahāyāna books, which it divided into five periods. It was said that S’akyamuni had begun his ministry by preaching in heaven, to angels and men, the transcendent doctrines of the Kegon. Because these were too difficult for ordinary, sinful people to understand, he descended to Benares with the practical teaching of the Agon Scriptures. As time passed, the teachings were “developed” (*vaipulya*) in the Hodo books, as the next category was called. From development to wisdom (*prajñā*) was the next step; from wisdom to the final perfection of the Saddharma pundarika Sūtra was the natural conclusion. Thus, the doctrines of S’akyamuni numbered 84,000.

beginning with extreme simplicity and ending in the clouds of mysticism. In delivering these many doctrines, Shaka used many teaching methods: *ton*, or suddenness, letting the truth burst with full brilliance upon the minds of his hearers; *zen*, or gradual advancement from strength to strength; *himitsu*, or esoteric symbolism; and *fujō*, or parabolic uncertainty. He adapted his sermons for all listeners and arranged them so that, in a single sermon, the same words conveyed Hinayana doctrines to some and Mahayana to others who were capable of understanding them. He had indeed become "all things to all men."

The Tendai system, which embraced everything, included many elements that were not Buddhist at all. Its doctrine of *shō aku no hōmon*, or inherent evil, is dualistic; it asserts that in *Shinnyo*, which is the pantheistic deity, there is an evil principle as well as a good one, and that the two are equal in duration and power. Manichaeans¹ and Magi both held that doctrine, but it was hardly a Buddhist principle. It must have been a very difficult task to make such mutually antagonistic doctrines as those of Zen and Jodo coexist within the same religious tradition.

But what Saichō primarily wanted was spiritual and ecclesiastical authority. The Chinese Tientai school seems to have had little hesitation in granting this, and Saichō soon returned to Japan, holding a native episcopate in his own hands.

*Kaidan* is the name given to a platform or dais used for the distribution of certificates and diplomas to successful candidates for the priesthood. Its existence in any particular temple implied the right of that temple's authorities to confer Orders, and the Buddhist monk is as jealous of his Apostolic succession as is the highest High Churchman among ourselves.<note>2. Thus, when a Buddhist priest is ordained, he receives "letters of orders" on which are given the principal names of the priests through whom the succession has come down to him from the Apostles of Shakyamuni. It seems impossible to trace this practice earlier than 250 A.D., before which date it was not considered necessary in China. It is therefore quite possible that the Buddhists may have learned the practice from Christian neighbors in Central Asia. The only exception to this rule is the insignificant sect of the *Yūdzūnembutsu*, who trace their succession, not to Shakyamuni, but to the Vision of Amida granted to their Founder in the twelfth century.</note> There had been no ordinations of monks in China before 250 A.D., prior to which the simple taking of the "threefold Refuge"—in Buddha, the Law, and the Community of Monks—had been considered sufficient. The first regular ordinations had been held about 350, the custom having been brought into the country by an Indian monk named Buddhoganga. These ordinations had been of the *Hinayana* type (mainly connected with the old Indian sect of the Dharmaguptas); they had found their way to Japan, where *Kaidan* had

But a new line of succession had been inaugurated by the Tientai in China, and Saichō, having received the necessary authorizations, erected a new *Kaidan* at his monastery on Hiyeizan at which ordinations were to take place according to the Chinese Mahāyāna discipline. Saichō likely had his good reasons for taking such a serious step; but his action set the whole of the South into a blaze of indignation and excitement. In the midst of this, Kūkai returned to Japan.

Which side would Kūkai take? He was a Southerner by birth, for he hailed from Sanuki; and by education, for he was at the time attached to one of the great temples in the ancient capital. A feeling of loyalty prevented him from turning against his old friends in the South. At the same time, he was, like Saichō, convinced of the necessity of reform, and he had, moreover, a great friendship for Saichō, who had received baptism at his hands.

Both sides appealed to him, and he was at a loss how to act. He resolved to steer clear of the controversy altogether and went off on a series of missionary journeys throughout the land. His first journey was to the Kanto districts, and all the way to Shimotsuke and beyond. He was more than a mere preacher; he planned roads, suggested the construction of bridges, encouraged agriculture and education, and simplified the writing of Japanese. The traveler will find his posthumous name of Kōbō Daishi in all parts of the land: he was the "Apostle of the North," and the pacification of the troublesome northern tribes was much facilitated by his efforts. When he returned to Kyoto, the *Kaidan* controversy was still raging. So he

On his next visit to Kyoto, Saichō, now known as Dengyō Daishi, had died, and Kōbō felt that he could at last hope to publish his own views of Buddhist doctrine without going against those of the friend for whom he had such a warm affection. He retired in the year 816 to his new monastery at Mount Kōya (Kōya San), in the province of Kii, and there wrote his "Sangōshiki," "Jūjūshinron," and the other treatises in which he develops his system. He died in 835, a venerable and revered man. Buddhist Japan hardly believes him to be dead even now. He is said to be sitting in his tomb on Mount Kōya, waiting for Maitreya to come and convert the world. Then he will go forth from his place of waiting and join in the glory of victory.

In the first of the two works that I have just mentioned, the "Sangōshiki," Kōbō Daishi works out a comparison of the three great religions of the East as he understood them—Confucianism, Taoism, and Buddhism. All three were found in the Japan of his day. Confucianism (of the ancient, unreformed variety) had been there longer than Buddhism, and the Confucian scholars had joined hands with the Kami worshippers in opposing Buddhism, just as they had done with Taoism in opposition to the same religion in China. Kōbō seems to have treated the Shinto of Japan as almost identical with the Taoism of China (etymologically, the two words are the same), and with very good reason. The inter-

The intercourse between Japan and China had been going on for over three centuries, during which period much had come into Japan besides Buddhism and Confucianism. The original *Kami*-worship had been elevated, as it were, into a system by the very fact of its early controversies with Buddhism, and Dr. De Visser¹ has recently shown us how much Taoism lurks in the Shinto-based folklore of Japan. <insert>(</insert>Confucianism, Buddhism, and Taoism formed in Kōbō’s mind the three legs of a tripod on which the cauldron of the State might securely rest. During the Tang Period, in the first half of the eighth century, a certain number of men arrived in China, mostly from Southern India and traveling by the sea route,² who brought with them a new and evidently very late form of Buddhism. This form had practically captured Tibet—then a leading kingdom of Asia—and because of its novelty, it was likely to captivate the imagination of the novelty-loving Japanese. Kōbō developed this system in his “*Jūjūshinron*,” or “Treatise of the Ten Grades of Existence.”

It is a world peopled by spiritual beings, but very much like our own, with good and bad in it. The least in the kingdom of Buddha is higher than the Buddhist heaven.</note> The spiritual world consisted of those who were called out from the natural world to follow the truth. Its lowest grade was the *S'ramana*, who strove for, and the *Engaku* or *Pratyekabuddha*, who realized, the salvation of his own soul. That included the whole range of Buddhist believers, but there was an election within the election—the doctrines of *Hossō*, *Tendai*, and *Kegon* offered three successive steps, each higher than the last, for their respective devotees, and at the top of all stood the *Shingon*.

My readers will perhaps remember that in my earlier chapters I spoke of *Vairoc'ana*, the supreme Buddha—a reflection, as it were, of *Osiris*, whom we found in the Alexandrian Gnosis. *Vairoc'ana* is honored as supreme by the *Hossō*, *Tendai*, and *Kegon*, and the order in which *Kōbō* places these sects seems to depend on the amount of honor which they were disposed to give to *Vairoc'ana*.<note>2. Both *Hōnen Shōnin* and *Nichiren* criticize *Kōbō's* arrangement of the order of precedence assigned to the sects—the latter with considerable harshness, as is his habit. It was from *Nichiren* that I got the allusion to *S'akyamuni* not being, in *Kōbō's* opinion, fit to be the cowherd of *Vairoc'ana*. *Nichiren* aptly says that if *Vairoc'ana* is a figure of such great importance, his existence should be proved as *S'akyamuni's* has been, and he bluntly charges *Kōbō* with being a liar (*dai-mōgo*) for trying to pass off fictitious Buddhas on his countrymen.</note>

A distinction is sometimes made between the *Roshana* of the *Hossō*, *Kegon*, and *Tendai*, and the *Vairoc'ana* (*Beroshana*) of the *Shingon*. It is for this latter that *Nichiren* seeks proof. The fact seems to be that there are, as it were, two strains of cryptic teaching regarding *Vairoc'ana*. The one (*Roshana*) came overland, or from North-Western India, and is probably connected with Syrian Gnosticism. The second (*Beroshana*) came from Southern India and has Alexandrian affinities.

I fear I must repeat myself here a little to make things clear.

There are two Buddhisms: one is of a plain, simple sort, quite good enough for the practical purposes of this world; that is the Buddhism taught by Shakyamuni, whether in the Hinayana or the Mahayana. The true spiritual Buddhism is that proclaimed by Vairocana, <margin>{</margin> a Being so high that Shakyamuni (with a pun on his family name) "was not worthy to be his cowherd." This secret teaching had been delivered to Nagarjuna by one who had received it from Vairocana himself, had been secretly handed down through the ages, and had finally been published in the fullness of time.

Like the gods of the Manichaeans and Gnostics, Vairocana is fivefold, and is represented by the five great statues of the Five Dhyani Buddhas. To the mystic five correspond the five elements, the five senses, the five colors, the five planets, and many other groups of five. But they are really six, for just as Vairocana, besides occupying his seat of honor in the midst of the Five, overshadows and embraces all his colleagues, so there is a sixth sense, a sixth element, etc., which overshadows and embraces everything (*alaya shiki*). The five are represented by five Chinese characters, representing the sounds A-ba-ra-ka-ki, and to these is added a sixth syllable,

<margin>| ✓ The Japanese Tendai has its *mantra* or magic formulas (Jap. *darani*), as well as the Shingon. But it has no *mudra*, or manual gestures. These are peculiar to the Shingonism brought in by Kukai, or Kobo. Neither does the Tendai accept the secret books said to have been found by Nagarjuna at the Iron Tower in Southern India. It gets its mantra and dharani from the Dragon Palace books, and from Maitreya's lectures in Asangha's lecture hall.</margin>

There were always certain differences between Syrian and Alexandrian Gnosticism. It is interesting to find them cropping up in Japan. They throw a flood of light on the obscure Book of Iao.

The one world is good, the other evil, and thus—as with the Manichaeans—evil and good are equal and eternal with one another.

In the Womb World, there is a constant struggle; from the Diamond World, where the Everlasting Powers dwell—whose sum total represents the Mandala or Pleroma of God—there come forth countless rays of various light, incarnated or manifested in many shapes and forms of angels and gods, to aid man in his struggles. No lasting value need be attached to these forms. They are but the transient appearances of Vairocana the Invisible, who alone is unchangeable and everlasting.

# CHAPTER XXI

## “NAMUDAISHI”

The title of this chapter is the title of a Japanese poem on the life of the great Kōbō Daishi: “Glory to the Great Teacher.”

Kōbō Daishi’s life, as it has been preserved in the religious traditions of Japan, is full of wonders. It is true that the present generation scoffs at these wonders and tries to write biographies of the distinguished monk with all the miracles removed. These rationalized biographies do not suit the popular imagination. It is as the wonder-working Apostle of a new form of faith that Kōbō Daishi lives in popular tradition, and the religious historian cannot afford to leave out the miracles which adorn or characterize his life. The miracles are part and parcel of the religious history of the country.

The poem “Namudaishi” is a religious ballad, written in the ordinary 7.5.7.5 meter of the Japanese <term>wasan</term>. It is not a great poem, but it gives a good summary of Kōbō’s life as it appears to the ordinary Buddhist believer in Japan. And it has never yet been presented to the English-speaking public.<note>There is an English translation published in 1909, in a volume on Kōbō Daishi titled “Namudaishi.” However, it was produced by a Japanese writer who knew very little English and had no English friend to correct his translation. It requires some knowledge of “English as she is spoke” to understand it.</note>

---

<note>¹ Ac'ārya is an Indian word unknown to the earliest periods of the Mahāyāna. Its use denotes a long association between Brahmans and Buddhists.</note>
<note>² The Mandara is, in one sense, the *pleroma*—that is, the sum total of the divine personalities that constitute the Godhead. The word is also used (and here, according to the Japanese commentary) to denote a magic ring or circle used in sorcery. We must never forget the significant role that sorcery plays in the Shingon, just as it did in Egyptian Gnosticism and the related Cabbala.</note>
<note>³ The Ryōbu doctrine is that there are two worlds, of which one, the world of ideas, is fixed and eternal. The material world corresponds to the world of ideas, with this difference: that a single Idea in the Ideal World may have many material counterparts in the world of matter. Thus, the gods of India may be taken as the corporeal counterparts of the incorporeal Truths which the Eternal Buddhas represent. The same, however, holds true for the gods of China and Japan. And things which are equal to the same thing are equal to one another.</note>
<note>⁴ Shingonism has undoubtedly always been a most powerful stimulant of art.</note>

29. In the second month of the second year of the Kōnin era (February 811 A.D.), along with Emperor Saga, he received the <term>Kwanjō</term> of the gods <note>1</note> from the hands of Ōnakatomi, the famous ritualist.

---

<note>1. This was evidently the formal inauguration of <term>Ryōbu Shinto</term>. The Emperor, Saga Tenno, and Kōbō were baptized (<term>Kwanjō</term>) into the Shinto community by the chief ritualist of that faith. And the Shintoists, in their turn, were baptized into Buddhism by Kōbō. The agreement was reached on the assumption that the Buddhas and <term>Bodhisattvas</term> were essentially the same beings as the Shinto gods, and that the two religions meant the same thing, even if they used different languages. The <term>Shingon</term> commentator, in praising the *Scripture of the Lotus of the Good Law*, says it does not matter whether one says in Sanskrit, *Saddharmapundarika sūtram*, or in Chinese, *Myō Hō Renge Kyō*, or in Japanese, *Tayenaru nori no hachisu no hana no minori*. The meaning and the effect are identical in each case.
Regarding Emperor Saga, Murdoch says (*History of Japan*, vol. i. p. 227) that he was "undoubtedly a highly accomplished man of brilliant parts . . . deeply versed in Chinese literature; that he did everything to encourage its study, and exerted himself to complete the Sinicization of the country." However, it was the splendor and magnificence of the Chinese Court, rather than its solid virtues, that appealed to him. Luxury and ostentation crept in, and the nobles found it difficult to meet the expenses of court life; consequently, relief had to be granted to them by exempting their domains from Imperial taxes. This impoverished the Court, created great semi-independent baronies, and brought about exactly the state of affairs that <term>Kwammu</term> had worked so hard to avoid when he tried to break the power of the great Nara monasteries.</note>

The messenger never forgot that feeling as long as he lived.<note>This story can be found in Satow and Hawes’ “Handbook to Japan,” p. 416 (2nd edition).</note>

60. The Emperors Kwampyō and Shirakawa, the retired Emperor Go-Uda, and several others of our rulers had such faith in the Sage’s merits that they made pilgrimages to Kōya to worship at his sanctuary.

There is a second list. Vairocana and Vajrasattva, they say, must not be counted, as very little is known about them. The eight patriarchs must be counted as: (1) Nāgārjuna, (2) Nāgabodhi, (3) Vajrabodhi, (4) Subhakarasinḥa (Jap. Zenmui), (5) Amoghavajra, (6) Keikwa, (7) Ichigyō, (8) Kōbō.

It must be noticed—

(i) that Nāgārjuna receives his information from Vajrasattva, who receives it from Vairocana. It does not, therefore, represent a very old teaching. Nāgārjuna is considered the thirteenth Patriarch of the Zen sect; he is at most only the *third* Patriarch of the Shingon. And if we assume Nāgārjuna to have lived about the middle of the second century, the conclusion is almost unavoidable that Vajrasattva and Vairocana cannot date from much before the middle of the first century.

(ii) The Shingon Patriarchs, Vajrabodhi, Amoghavajra, and others, reached China via the sea-route during the sixth and seventh centuries. They came from South India and Ceylon, in both of which places there were Egyptian colonies.

(iii) I have already in a previous chapter given many instances showing the close connection between Egyptian Gnosticism and the Shingon. I will now give another.

In the commentary to the last verse of Namu Daishi, the writer says that the Shingon is different from other forms of Buddhism. It has had no great changes, no violent reformations, and no developments. Its doctrine has been handed down from generation to generation of the faithful by the transmission of what is called the “Seal of Vairocana.” The “Seal of Vairocana” is said to be the secret meaning of the letter A in the Sanskrit alphabet. <term>A-ji</term>, as it is called, is a very sacred thing to a Shingonist. “The paths which must be walked when visiting the buildings of Kōya San,” say Satow and Hawes (*l.c.*), “together form the Sanskrit letter *A*, which is regarded as the symbol of the Taizōkai”<note>The author identifies the Taizōkai as the Diamond World or World of Ideas; however, Taizōkai is typically the Womb Realm, while the Diamond Realm is the Kongōkai.</note> (that is, the Diamond World, or World of Ideas, of which Vairocana is the center and the life). In “Pistis Sophia” (Schmidt’s edition, p. 81) there is a note given by a later hand. According to this, the Seal of the Undying One (<term>ἀθάνατος</term>; in Shingon, Amida is always <term>amṛita</term>) is *aaa*. He who sits on the throne (that is, Christ the “First Mystery”) is *aaa*; the interpretation of the whole Name of God is *aaaa*, *aaaa*, *aaaa*. <term>Ὁ μὲν πρῶτος οὐρανὸς φθέγγεται τὸ Α</term> (“The first heaven sounds the A”), says Irenaeus regarding the Gnostic Marcus (Iren., lib. i. cap. xiv. 7). The Gnostics, it is well known, stole the Christ of the Christians. The Shingon, possibly without knowing it, have for centuries been the receivers of stolen goods.

# CHAPTER XXII

## THE BUDDHISM OF THE GEMPEI PERIOD <note>1</note>

It is very difficult to describe in a short paragraph, or even in one long chapter, the complicated period of Japanese history centered on the fierce wars waged with such relentless bitterness between the rival Taira and Minamoto families and their respective factions. It would be beyond the scope of this work to attempt to do so. We must satisfy ourselves with a brief mention of some of the leading features of the period, as far as they concern the history of Japanese religion.

During the ninth and tenth centuries, supreme power in Japan lay practically in the hands of the great Fujiwara family, who, under various titles, monopolized all the great offices of state and kept the emperors—always their tools and often connected to them by marriage and kinship—in a state of absolute subjection. Occasional attempts were made to destroy the Fujiwara monopoly. Sugawara Michizane, <note>2</note>

and innocent ways. The luxury that the Fujiwara family encouraged was no mere wanton display, nor a simple search for pleasure. It was adopted with a practical goal in mind, and besides succeeding in its immediate purpose, it led to other far-reaching results. The Fujiwaras became liberal patrons of the arts and letters. The pictures for which Japan is so justly famous—her music, poetry, and dramatic art, those creations that are held to portray so vividly the character of the sentimental yet strangely matter-of-fact Japanese people—all owe their development mainly to the artistic instincts of this gifted and powerful family. For these things, at least, Japan owes them a lasting debt of gratitude.¹

It should be noted here that the arts and letters of early medieval Japan are all Buddhist—or, at least, are so thoroughly impregnated and saturated with the spirit of that religion that it is impossible to understand their inner beauties without some knowledge of the faith that inspired the artists. Emperor Kwammu had moved his capital from Nara to Kyōto to be free from the intervention of the meddling priesthood in matters of state, and Dengyō had founded his monastery upon Hieizan in the hope of finding a quiet spot where he might be free from “earth’s many voices.” The outcome was the exact opposite of what either of these men expected.² The Tendai reforms turned Japanese Buddhism into a widespread organization with far-reaching ramifications. The Fujiwaras knew how to use that organization for their own ends, and the Buddhist

When the "captain of the ship," as sometimes happened, began to know too much and to grow restless on his soft cushions, some monastery would provide a convenient desert island upon which the restless captain might be marooned.¹

Sometimes a captain, more far-sighted than the rest, did not wait to be marooned, but shut himself up voluntarily in his own cabin, as it were, and continued to direct the ship of State from the safe shelter of some monastery. He did this through the person of some infant son or grandson whom he put on the throne instead of himself, and for whom he acted as guardian or regent. Such was the course adopted, for example, by the Emperors Shirakawa and Toba,² and it seemed quite natural in a country like Japan, where the "power behind the throne" has always been such a potent reality. An ex-Emperor, living in a monastery and from there directing the affairs of State in the name of his immature son or grandson, would seem to be an ideal state of affairs from the point of view of an ambitious priesthood. Monasteries were jealous of the new-fashioned growths on the slopes of Mount Hiei; the Hieizan household was encouraged to engage in domestic feuds. The appointment of a *Zashū*, or Archbishop, of the Tendai community—chosen not from the monks of the Mother House of Hieizan, but from the residents of the daughter institution at Ōtsu, the Onjōji or Miidera—gave the signal for a strange civil war within the fold of the Tendai itself. Hieizan and Miidera became the headquarters of two warring armies, with a military organization of *tera-samurai*, or temple knights, and bands of fighting men. The other large temples followed suit, and the lay people of Japan had the undesirable privilege, several times during these centuries, of witnessing armies of “religious” persons engaging in fratricidal strife—killing, burning, and laying waste.

In the meantime, an upper-middle class was growing up in Japan, closely connected with the aristocracy and yet independent of them, corresponding very nearly to our English gentry.

It had been the practice of both the Fujiwara and also, from time to time, the Emperors themselves, to raise money for political or religious purposes by the sale of certain patents known as *shō-en* (not unlike the baronetcies of King James I). These conferred upon their holders the privilege of possessing their estates free from Imperial taxation and exempt from the jurisdiction of the provincial governors. Some of the Emperors, such as Go-sanjo (1069), had opposed this practice; but needy and religious-minded rulers, such as Shirakawa (1073) and Toba (1108), had been very lavish in the granting of these patents, and the holders of these privileges became an important element in the State. They formed the main support of the rival factions of Taira and

The Minamoto, even after Yoritomo’s formal and successful organization of their scattered members, continued to be—as *<term>samurai</term>*—the true backbone of the Japanese nation down to our own times.

Independent, freedom-loving, reasonably well-educated, and devoted to martial exercises and the outdoor sports that have been the pastime of country gentlemen in all ages and climates, these men felt nothing but contempt for the sickly sentimentalism of the fashionable priests, with their legends, repetitive prayers, and their somewhat hypocritical prohibitions against hunting and fighting. We shall see in another chapter that they were not lacking in religious feeling. For now, let us simply note that they were rising to prominence as a social and religious force, capable of exerting a decisive influence on the destinies of their country.

In a previous chapter, I have already referred to the social miseries of the country during the period that many writers describe as if it were the golden age of Japanese history. We might just as accurately speak of the reign of King Stephen, or the long-suffering miseries of the Wars of the Roses, as having been the golden age of our English history. The suffering of the common people—naturally ignored by chroniclers whose eyes were fixed only on the precincts of the Imperial Palace—was truly immense. It could not have been otherwise.

In my last chapter, I also spoke of the pathetic figure of the *<term>Odori-nembutsu</term>*, the poor, half-witted, princely priest, dancing his way through the country with the monotonous *<term>nembutsu</term>* constantly upon his lips, in the hope

It may interest some of my readers to know that since the end of 1910, I have been working with some Buddhist friends in Tokyo on a translation of early Buddhist documents that may lead to some interesting developments. Our current immediate goal is to complete a translation into a European language of all the Indian books translated into Chinese during the Han period, specifically between 147 A.D. and 220 A.D. When these have been translated (which will take several years to accomplish), we hope that we shall be able to provide the world with a reasonably complete picture of what Buddhism was like when it was first introduced into China. We also hope to shed some light on <term>Gnosticism</term> and the development of Christian heresies during the second and third centuries.

However, more interesting material for translation will probably be found in the works of Japanese theologians of the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth centuries—a field still untouched by European research. Today, we are learning to see that Christ's work was far greater than anything our ancestors of even a century ago ever imagined. We are coming to understand that each nation will contribute, and is currently contributing, its part to the "Perfect Temple of the Future," and that no spiritual building can be considered final if it does not make adequate room for the glory and honor of all nations to be brought into it.

In ages incalculably remote, he appeared in various forms among men, all his incarnations being intended to bring salvation to mankind. In his last incarnation, he appeared as the <term>Bhikshu Hōzo</term> (<term>Dharmakāra</term>), and as such registered a vow that should the Perfect Consummation of the <term>Buddhahood</term> ever be in his power, he would not accept deliverance unless such deliverance should also mean the salvation of suffering mankind. In fulfillment of that vow, he endured much suffering and many agonies, but he triumphed in the end, and the fruit of his labors has been the opening of a Paradise in a <term>Pure Land</term>, into which all may enter who call upon his name with Faith.<note>1</note> Other Buddhas also have spoken of Paradise;<note>2</note> <term>Amida</term> alone can speak of it as *my* Paradise.

<term>Amida</term> is <term>Ichi-butsu</term>, the One Buddha, and besides Him there is none, for all the other Buddhas and <term>Bodhisattvas</term> and gods, in whom men trust, are but temporary and partial manifestations of the Great Father, whose Vow (a Christian might call it his *Will*) is that all mankind should be saved—saved from the miseries of existence, from all those universals of misery which <term>S'akyamuni</term> disclosed to a suffering world, and placed in that Paradise where there is nothing to hinder or to hurt the soul on its upward path to that Perfection which comes from the <term>Beatific Vision</term> of <term>Amida</term> Himself.<note>3</note>

<term>Amida</term> is One and Indivisible, but He has several names, and two of the names by which He is known among men have become personified with a quasi-separate existence as His Sons, and sit, the one on His right, the other on His left, in His Kingdom. The right represents His Wisdom, the left His Mercy; the latter is occupied by His Son <term>Avalokites'vara</term>, or <term>Kwannon</term>, "the Lord who looked down," incarnate again and again for man and his salvation; the former, personified as <term>Mahāsthāmaprāpta</term>, or <term>Seishi</term>, whose gift to man is, significantly, not salvation, but life.<note>1 I learned this in conversation with a Buddhist priest. I can only repeat here what I have said elsewhere: that the Ophite Gnostics, who appeared in the same locations and at the same time as the original Amida Buddhists, used identical language regarding Christ.</note>

To grasp this salvation, achieved for man by <term>Amida</term>, and brought to him by <term>Kwannon</term> and <term>Seishi</term>, nothing is needed but Faith—no works of the Law, no austerities, penances, or devotions, no resolutions of amendment, no futile strivings, no repentance—nothing but Faith. It sounds like an immoral doctrine, a kind of <term>antinomianism</term>, yet it is not exactly immoral as expounded, at least by its latest preachers, the school of <term>Shinran</term> and his disciples. For faith brings salvation; the realization of salvation arouses the gratitude of the heart, and the grateful heart, knowing what it is by nature and what it has become by grace, becomes so filled with the expansive power of a deep love that it turns good deeds, austerities, and devotions from being fruitless attempts at obtaining a salvation which is practically beyond man's attainment into the joyful formulas through which the new life imparted to the soul finds its expression.

He then devotes another series of chapters to considering seven great names that <term>Shinran</term> had selected to represent the entire history of <term>Amidaism</term> from its first beginning to <term>Shinran</term>’s time. Having thus surveyed all the ground covered by the *<term>Shōshinge</term>*, he proceeds to base a concluding exhortation to his readers regarding their present duties and prospects on that foundation.

The names are selected from India, China, and Japan. The Indian patriarchs are <term>Nāgārjuna</term> and <term>Vasubandhu</term>; those from China are <term>Donran</term>, <term>Dōshaku</term>, and <term>Zendō</term>; and those from Japan are <term>Genshin</term> and <term>Genkū</term>. Two chapters are devoted to each name—one biographical and one doctrinal—and the author has cleverly constructed his doctrinal chapters in such a way as to show that there has been a regular and consistent development all the way from <term>Nāgārjuna</term> to <term>Shinran</term>, who brought the system to its perfection.<note>1 Mr. Tada gives the dates of the seven as follows: (1) <term>Nāgārjuna</term>, about A.D. 150; (2) <term>Vasubandhu</term>, around A.D. 440; (3) <term>Donran</term>, around A.D. 356; (4) <term>Dōshaku</term>, A.D. 553; (5) <term>Zendō</term>, A.D. 614; (6) <term>Genshin</term>, A.D. 943; and finally <term>Genkū</term> (<term>Hōnen</term>), A.D. 1130-1213.</note>

Thus, in <term>Nāgārjuna</term>, the doctrine is vague: no mention is made of the <term>Sūtras</term> that tell of Amida, but <term>Nāgārjuna</term> died with his face set toward the <term>Western Paradise</term>, and there are passages in his works that foreshadow the doctrine. In <term>Vasubandhu</term>, we take a step further: the mystic teacher knows of the book that contains the description of Paradise and, while not giving himself up entirely to the worship of <term>Amitābha</term> to the exclusion of every other cult, still places <term>Amitābha</term> at the top of the Buddhist pantheon. In the chapters on the Chinese Patriarchs, we are shown how one of them was attracted to <term>Amidaism</term> by its simplicity. The complexity of the doctrines in the other books had confused his mind; here was something easy, intelligible, and within his reach. The other had been long seeking for the Elixir of Life and had dabbled in...

And what are we to say of <term>Kūya’s</term> answer, when questioned about the glory of the life to come: “What I shall be I do not know now; I shall know hereafter”?
