Or of <term>Kakuhan’s</term> definition of *<term>Butsu</term>* (佛): “He is higher than the territorial prince, higher than the Emperor, higher than the Brahma, and He is a *Trinity*”? Or of <term>Myōe’s</term> refusal of an offer of wealth: “I have food and clothing; I am content”? The spirit of Christianity breathes in these men; there was a spiritual affinity even if there was no physical contact. The whole of <term>Shinran’s</term> system—his permission for clergy to marry and his hereditary episcopates—strongly suggests <term>Nestorianism</term>.</note>

# CHAPTER XXIII

## THE BUDDHISM OF KAMAKURA

<term>Kamakura</term> is associated with <term>Yoritomo</term> and the Regents of the <term>Hōjō</term> family. <term>Yoritomo</term>, the first of the <term>Minamoto</term> <term>Shōguns</term> (1147–1199), was the son of that <term>Yoshitomo</term> who, after allying himself with the <term>Taira</term> against his own clan and taking up arms against his own father, ended by breaking with the <term>Taira</term> because of their lack of gratitude. He died miserably at the hands of one of his own retainers, who hoped to earn the favor of <term>Kiyomori</term> by sending him the head of his misguided master.

His wife, <term>Tokiwa Gozen</term>, who had once been a consort of the <term>Emperor Konoe</term> and had escaped with her three children from the massacre in which her husband had died, sacrificed herself to the vindictive <term>Kiyomori</term> in order to save the three children she had borne to <term>Yoshitomo</term>. One of these children was <term>Yoritomo</term>; another was <term>Yoshitsune</term>, the favorite hero of Japanese history and romance.

<term>Yoritomo</term> was about thirteen years old when his father died. His mother’s self-sacrifice persuaded <term>Kiyomori</term> to spare him, but he was banished to <term>Izu</term>. He did not behave very well there, though he managed to win the affections of his guardian’s daughter, the beautiful and capable <term>Masa-ko</term>. She ran away from home to join her lover at the start of his war against the <term>Taira</term> and may be said to have laid the foundations of the <term>Hōjō</term>

The <term>Zen</term> sects (there are three in Japan) owe their separate existence to a famous Indian priest, <term>Bodhidharma</term>, who arrived in China in the year 526 A.D., just two years before the foundation of the <term>Benedictine Order</term> in Europe.

It was a period of religious conflict and confusion in India. The Hindus were vigorously and successfully protesting against both <term>Mahāyāna</term> and <term>Hīnayāna</term>, and were gradually absorbing into their own systems everything that was good in the Buddhist religion.<note>It was this absorption of Buddhist elements into <term>Hinduism</term> that enabled it to overcome the faith of <term>S'akyamuni</term>. To the present day, a great deal of Buddhism can be found remaining in the popular cults of India, and the Japanese Buddhist feels more in agreement with the Hindu than he does with his fellow Buddhist in <term>Ceylon</term>.</note> A great opposition (which we might better call a persecution<note>For example, the one started by <term>Mihirakula</term>.</note>) was being raised against the "sons of <term>S'akyamuni</term>," and many Buddhist priests found it convenient to leave India and seek refuge abroad. Many of them found their way to China, which was then divided into two rival kingdoms: the north under the <term>Wei</term> and the south under the <term>Sung</term>, along with several minor principalities. Both dynasties favored the Buddhist religion, partly, it can be assumed, for political reasons, and many embassies came from India and Central Asia to ask for the assistance of China, the leading Buddhist power in Asia. <term>Bodhidharma</term> was no ordinary priest. His visit to China had much the same significance as the visit of an <term>Archbishop of Canterbury</term> who might undertake a "mission of help" to the <term>Anglican Missions</term> in Japan.

*Zazen*, as the Japanese call it, is a very difficult course of contemplations, with suggestions from the spiritual director that provide topics and hints, but nothing more. When the postulant has finished the course, he may have obtained Enlightenment, or he may not; he has, at any rate, gone through a course of mental discipline which has given him, to some extent, the mind of a soldier.

Such was the Buddhism that the Hōjō Regents called to their aid when they were engaged in making Kamakura the military center of a reformed Japan. The Contemplative Teaching had, it is true, been in the country for some time under the name of the Busshinshū, or "Sect of Buddha's Heart," but it had been too puritanical to find favor with the courtiers of Nara or Kyōto. The Zen system closely touches the philosophical thought of India. It also has many points of contact with Confucianism. It recognizes a supreme Being but absolutely refuses to personify Him. To personify God, says the <term>Zen</term> follower, whether as <term>Vairocana</term>, as <term>Amida</term>, as <term>Sakyamuni</term>, or as Jehovah, is to limit Him. He cannot be tied down to any form; He transcends the widest, highest, and deepest conceptions of the human mind. Yet Zen does not blame those who thus personify God and, by personifying Him, limit Him. It recognizes that for certain minds personification is a necessity. The Infinite mind must become finite in order that the finite mind may grasp it. But a personified God is nothing but a *<term>hōben</term>*, an adaptation of the Truth to the weakness of the human intellect. Such personification, it has been observed, always serves to narrow the mind and make it intolerant. The Jew, the Muslim, the Christian, the worshipper of <term>Amida</term>, of <term>Sakyamuni</term>, of <term>Vairocana</term>—all in turn have become dogmatic, intolerant, and uncharitable, and all for the same reason. They start from a personal, and therefore an imperfect, conception of God.

In the same way, <term>Zen</term> possesses no Canon of Scripture. The Christian has his Bible, the Muslim his Koran, and every sect of Buddhism has formed its own little Canon of Holy Books out of the unwieldy mass of the <term>Tripitaka</term>. The formation of a canon leads to loss of

charity. Certain books are taken as representing a divine revelation; all other books of religion are judged by this arbitrary standard, and whatever does not agree with it is rejected. The letter of Scripture has always proved to be a fruitful mother of controversy and dissension. <term>Zen</term> has no special list of Sacred Books. It does not reject any <term>Sutras</term> or <term>Abhidharmas</term>; it reads and values them for all the truths they contain, but it sets up no books as being infallible or beyond criticism. It criticizes freely all the Sacred Books of <term>Buddhism</term>; and it accepts, with equal freedom and reverence, the good books of all countries.

It has been said already that <term>Zen</term>, while rejecting a personal God, accepts with reverence a "Something Beyond Knowledge," which lies at the back of phenomenal existence. We can never know that Being in its entirety, but we can reach to Him in three ways—"feeling after Him, and, perhaps, finding Him." We may look into our own hearts, by introspection and meditation, and there we shall find Him. We may look into the hearts of others by means of the Word, spoken or written, and there we shall find Him. We may look at Nature, in all its manifestations, romantic or commonplace, and there we shall find Him. For my heart is <term>Buddha</term>; and the heart of my brother whose books I read, is <term>Buddha</term>; and Nature in its entirety, the Infinitely Great, the Infinitely Small, every star or comet, every mountain range or ocean, every insect, every leaf, is <term>Buddha</term>.

Such is the faith of the <term>Zenshuist</term>. For his daily conduct he accepts no infallible guide but his own enlightened conscience, which is one with the enlightened conscience of the universe. For the details, however, of his behavior he will follow <term>Confucius</term>, <term>Sakyamuni</term>, <term>Epictetus</term>, anything that will help him to lead his daily life in a manner worthy of a religious philosopher.

Zen, as taught by its Japanese founders, Eisai and Dōgen, and as fostered by the wise counsels of the Hōjō regents, was quite a different religion from the miracle-mongering, worldly, and intriguing parody of religion which the Hossō, Kegon, Tendai, and Shingon sects had been passing off on the country to the obvious disgust of the warrior and the man of action. It was very different, again, from the pietistic <term>solifidianism</term> <note>the doctrine of salvation by faith alone</note> of Honen and Shinran, with its contempt for this world and its fixed gaze upon the joys of the Western Paradise. Zen fired the imagination of the warrior, the statesman, and the man of letters; and if Japanese art drew its inspiration from the wild fancies of Kegon and Shingon <term>Buddhology</term>, Japanese poetry drew it from the solid quietude of the Zen monasteries. In those places, it was taught to look "within"—into the heart and into the innermost shrine of Nature—and there to be comforted by the One, Omnipresent, Heart of Buddha, whom man can feel but not know.¹

## CHAPTER XXIV

### NICHIREN AND THE EARLIER SECTS

In the year 1257, Japan was struck by a very terrible earthquake. After the earthquake, in 1258, a destructive hurricane arrived, which overthrew much of what the earthquake had left standing. In 1259, as a natural result of the two calamities already mentioned, there was a famine throughout Japan, along with the pestilence which always seems to follow in the wake of famine. The distress was so great, says Nichiren in one of his letters, that men prayed for death rather than to remain alive in the midst of the universal misery. The government was at its wits' end, not knowing how to relieve the general suffering; supplications and prayers were ordered to be offered up in all temples throughout the land. But months passed by without any signs of relief or decrease. At last, in 1260, Nichiren began preaching in the public streets of Kamakura, after having submitted his newly written treatise, entitled *Rissho Ankoku-ron*, to the Regent and his retired father. In the same year, Kublai Khan, the grandson of Jingis Khan, established his capital at Pekin, or Khambalik, where he received a visit from the Italian traveler, Marco Polo. These few facts will serve, I trust, as a sufficient introduction to this chapter.

Nichiren was born in 1222, in a remote village on the coast of Awa. He was in the habit of describing his

father as an outcast, from which some have inferred that he was of low descent. This was not so, however; his father had been the retainer of a high noble at the Court of Kyōtō and had been banished, according to the custom of the time, for some fault that had displeased his master. What the fault was is not mentioned; if the father was at all like the son, we may infer that it was that outspoken plainness which men of high position do not always like. The family, which consisted of the father, the mother, and the only child born to them in exile, lived alone and apart in the fishing village, shunned by the locals because they were in disgrace and holding little interaction with their neighbors. The child—sensitive, tender-hearted, high-spirited, and fearless—grew up solitary and alone, the target of the fisher boys, but devoted to animals, especially to those that were injured and maimed.

In 1234, when he was about twelve years old, he was taken by his parents to the Temple of Kyosumidera, not far from his native village, and there placed under the care of an old Shingon priest, who was the resident head. In Japan, it has always been the course pursued in dedicating a child to the priesthood to take him to some worthy priest to be trained and educated, and to let him serve as an acolyte and personal attendant to his master until such time as he is ready to take the vows of the order upon himself.

Nichiren took his life seriously. One of his first acts after entering the Kiyozumi Temple ¹ as a student was

to slip away by himself into the Temple Oratory, and there, before the image of Kokūzō Bosatsu, to offer a prayer that he might grow up to be a good priest worthy of the name; and as he went on with his studies in the quiet seclusion of that country monastery, he felt the early signs of his great calling. He realized that the Buddhism of the Kamakura period had strayed far from the primitive Buddhism of its Indian Founder; he saw that it was hopelessly divided by sects, schisms, and varieties of contradictory doctrines, and that, being so, it was inevitably unable to accomplish the good in the world which its Founder had intended. The condition of Japan was miserable; the Buddhist sects, whether of Kyōtō, Nara, or Kamakura, were powerless to resist the growing evils: a Buddhism purified, revitalized, and united might and would save Japan from dangers both external and internal. He determined to be the man who would accomplish this great design.

Those who know the early maturity of Japanese youth will not be surprised that Nichiren formed this plan before he was twenty years of age. The idea seems to have been suggested to him by reading that very remarkable book, the "Saddharmapundarika Sutra." <note>¹ I have already written at some length on the "Saddharmapundarika" in my book, "The Wheat among the Tares." Having read it and interpreted it for himself, he became quite confident in his mission, and with characteristic energy he set to work preparing to execute it. He left the quiet Temple of Kyosumidera and spent several years traveling throughout Japan to study every existing form of Buddhism. When he had thus finished his survey of the entire field, he felt himself in a position to formulate his own views on religion and national life. Nichiren has often been described by those who knew him only superficially as a mere dreamer and fanatic. A more careful study reveals him as a man of very decided opinions and someone who was extremely outspoken. But he was always able to give a reason for his conclusions, and those reasons were sane and persuasive; and in putting his views into practice, he constantly showed that if he dared to denounce error in severe tones, his courage came from reflection and not from mere impulse.

For more than twenty years, Nichiren devoted himself with great diligence to the study of Japanese Buddhism. He told us in one of his letters that from the age of twelve to thirty-two, he gave himself up to the comparative study of all Buddhist sects in his country—Kusha, Jojitsu, Ritsu (Vinaya), Hossō, Sanron, Kegon, Shingon, and the Tendai-Hokke, which was the official designation of the sect founded by Dengyo Daishi at Hieizan. To these he—

<insert>The Nichiren sect, which professes to base all its teaching on this Sutra, confines itself mainly to the Shakumon section.</insert>

It was Nichiren's claim that the true meaning of the *Hommon* had been revealed to him, which had been concealed from former ages and kept for revelation in the last "millennium" of the "Destruction of the Law." The *Shakumon*, according to him, must be interpreted in light of the *Hommon*, which is the truly important part. The essence of the whole is to be found in the syllables *myō-hō-ren-ge-kyō*, which serve simultaneously as the object of adoration, the protective charm, and the *Kaidan*, or Ordination Vow of the sect. One sub-sect considers only two chapters of the *Hommon* to be truly genuine and authentic.

My readers will have noticed, in the previous chapters of this book, that Buddhism, whether in India, China, or Japan, has always shown an ingrained tendency to shield itself under government favor and patronage. Kings were its protectors and patrons in India, where, under Ashoka, Kanishka, and like-minded rulers, it had flourished and become a mighty tree. When royal patronage was withdrawn and Hinduism asserted itself once more, the zeal of the Indian Buddhist lost its passion, and the Faith maintained itself only in those lands where the rulers were Buddhists. We see the same phenomenon in China, where the personal creed of the ruling house had a great deal to do with the successes and failures of the religion of Shakyamuni.

The Nara priests were nearly all courtiers who, though they might intrigue at times against the government, still intrigued only as courtiers, in the interests of one faction against another. The Heian clergy, followers of Dengyō and Kōbō, had become the subservient courtiers of the dominant Fujiwara family; the pietists of the Gempei period had been the favored ones of emperors like Toba and Shirakawa in their resistance to the gloved hand of the Fujiwara; the Zen had become political tools in the powerful grasp of the Hōjō Regents. <margin>pencil line</margin> Nichiren could see no hope of social or political improvement from the sect-based Buddhism of his time. Religious and political Japan were, in Nichiren's eyes, both suffering from a dangerous disease.

He therefore constantly condemned the already existing sects of Buddhism. He denounced them in his first sermon; he continued his denunciations to the very end. *Nembutsu wa mugen no gō.*<gloss>1</gloss> The Nembutsu was consistently criticized as a practice which leads men to the lowest of the hells. Nichiren never treated Amida as being in any sense a Buddhist divinity. He looked on him, in the form which the <term>Shinshu</term> made him wear, as an unauthorized importation from somewhere outside of Buddhism, and his Paradise as a pure fancy. At the very best, he held him to be but a partial manifestation of Shakyamuni, the One and Eternal. It was unlikely that the peculiar <term>Jōdo</term> tenet of salvation by faith alone, without repentance or works, would appeal to Nichiren’s mind.

*Zenshū wa tenma ha-jun no setsu.* "The Zen," he continued, "is a doctrine of demons and fiends." We are familiar with the illustration of the man whose house, "empty, swept, and garnished," stood open for the return of a company of evil spirits larger than the one that had been cast out. The Zen house was in exactly that position. <term>Bodhidharma</term> had cast out of his Buddhism all the superstitious books and doctrines with which the miracle-mongering <term>Mahāyānism</term> of Central Asia and China had covered over the original simplicity of Shakyamuni's teaching. He had put nothing in its place, and had commanded his followers to look within to see what form they should see, and to listen for what voice they should hear, coming to them from the empty chambers of their own minds. *Daishō no Kairitsu wa seken ōwaku no hō* (or, as it is found in a shorter version, *Ritsu Kokuzoku*).

> "The Vinaya sects, whether of the Small Vehicle (connected with the *Kaidan* at Nara) or of the Great Vehicle (those connected with the *Kaidan* at Hieizan), are brigands that disturb the peace of the country."

We have seen how ambitious priests in the Nara period interfered with the Imperial succession in the cases of, for example, the Empress Shotoku and the Emperor Junnin. We have also seen how, after Kwammu moved his capital to Kyōto to be free from priestly interference, the *Tendai* priesthood still managed to become the allies of the Fujiwara in their manipulation of Emperors to suit their own policy. We have also seen how the *Kaidan* question, which was mainly one of discipline and therefore deeply concerned the Ritsu sects, caused a schism between Hieizan and Nara, and later, a schism and civil war between Hieizan and her daughter temple of Miidera. When we think of the Fighting Temples, with their militias and men-at-arms, we can see some reason for Nichiren's denunciation of the "brigand" sects that "throw the world into confusion."

Shingon he described as *bōkoku*, or "traitors to their country," probably referring to their adoption of a lord other than S'akyamuni, the rightful lord in spiritual matters in Japan, and their constant reference to India as the seat of authority in matters of religion. His language regarding Vairoc'ana, or Dainichi, was even more contemptuous than that which he had used for Amida.

He argued that there was no evidence at all for the existence of Vairoc’ana, unlike the case of the historical S’akyamuni; that the story of Nāgārjuna finding the Shingon books in the Iron Tower in Southern India was a complete fabrication; and that Kōbō Daishi was the “greatest liar in Japan” (*Nihon no dai mōgo*).

As for the images of Amida, Kwannon, and the others, he was accused of recommending that they should be thrown into the fire or the sea. In his judgment, they had caused enough mischief in Japan.¹

Nichiren first expressed these views in a sermon preached near his native village, which he visited again at the end of his studies in 1254. He then took up residence near Kamakura, where he built a small hermitage for himself in the village of Nagoye, as there was no temple in the capital of the Hōjō Regents that would accept him as a resident.

---

¹ <note>“Nembutsu is the karma of hell; the Zen sect is the teaching of the Heavenly Devils and demons; the Vinaya of the Great and Small Vehicles is a law that deceives the world; the images of the traditional objects of worship, such as Amida and Kwannon, should be thrown into the fire or cast into the water” (“*Seigōroku*,” p. 774).</note>

It is interesting to note that there is no idol on the main altar in a Nichiren temple, although the side altars are often decorated in this way. In, for example, the Temple of Myōhōji at Kamakura—the oldest of all Nichiren shrines—there is a literal *stūpa* or tabernacle, such as those found in the ancient *chaityas* of India, which symbolizes the *stūpa* that descended from heaven in chapter 14 of the “*Saddharma pundarika*.” In front of this tabernacle is the usual “table of prothesis” <note>an offering table used for preparing the elements</note> found in all Japanese Buddhist temples, and in front of that is what might be called the choir, with desks for the monks. Over this section, which is located near the middle of the building, is a canopy or umbrella from which hang strings of flowers made of thin brass; the whole arrangement is intended to symbolize the “Pentecostal” shower of celestial flowers with which the story of the “*Saddharma pundarika*” begins. Interestingly, S’akyamuni is distinguished from the glorified but invisible Buddha who is believed to reside within the tabernacle. For the historical S’akyamuni, there is a separate building in another part of the grounds. This is, I believe, the universal practice.

There was also no pulpit for him to occupy, except for the one that has always been open to the agitator and the reformer: the street corner. He became an outdoor preacher, and his sermons—plain, simple, and full of conviction—soon attracted a great deal of attention. The earthquakes, the famines, the plagues, the fruitless prayers offered in the temples, and the shadow of the terrible Mongol power creeping closer to Japan all served to give point to his oratory. He was rapidly gaining popular favor; the priests of the official sects were conscious that power was slipping from them. The Regent had reason to be annoyed at the boldness with which the hermit <margin>/</margin>of Nagoye addressed him in his semi-political, semi-religious pamphlet on the "Reformation of Religion and the Pacification of the Country." Nichiren's enemies combined to bring against him a formal accusation of inciting rebellion and spreading heresy. He was arrested, brought before the Regent's Court, found guilty, and banished to Ito in the peninsula of Izu. This was in 1261; in 1264 he was once more in Kamakura, more outspoken than ever. Another great calamity was impending—a long-continued drought hung over the land and threatened a failure of the rice crops. <margin>✓</margin>The official priesthood was praying for rain, but there was no one to answer. Nichiren laughed at their vain efforts. At last he took his turn at prayer: Heaven answered, and the people were convinced that he was a prophet.

But he had, in the excitement of his preaching, allowed himself to use unseemly expressions. He had told the people that the late Regent, the well-meaning and devoted Saimyoji, was in hell, suffering torments, and that the current Regent, Tokimune, was preparing to follow him. The words were seized, twisted, and exaggerated. His enemies procured his arrest and dragged him before the

the Regent's Court, where, after an eventful trial which his followers today read with something of the reverence with which we listen to the telling of the familiar story of the Passion of Christ, he was condemned to death and led out for execution on the sands of Tatsu no Kuchi,¹ halfway between Kamakura and Enoshima.

But the Regent must have felt that Nichiren was in the right. His conscience troubled him after he had passed the death sentence, and he sent a messenger in great haste after the executioner's procession to revoke the condemnation, changing the sentence to one of banishment to the distant island of Sado. The messenger arrived only just in time. The mats were already spread for the prisoner to kneel on while waiting for the fatal stroke; the prisoner was already kneeling on the mat, and his faithful disciples believed then, and have ever since, that their master was given back to them from the dead. Legend has been busy embellishing the story. The executioner, it was said, had already lifted his sword when a flash of lightning from a cloudless sky rendered the blow harmless. Before he had recovered for a second stroke, the messenger from the Regent had arrived and the danger was past.

The exile in Sado was not of long duration. Nichiren returned in 1272, busy warning the nation about the danger of the Mongol invasion. "discerning the face of the heavens."¹ He now led a charmed life and was quite secure in the affection of his followers. His later years were devoted to Minobu and Ikegami, the two monasteries especially connected with the memories of his personality, and at the latter he passed away in the year 1282. His had been an eventful life. He still has, among his countrymen, many friends and many critics. To the outsider, who studies him impartially, he will always appear as a fearless man who had the courage of his convictions.

Now let us turn to the theological remedy which Nichiren proposed for the ills of both Church and State.

It was his great idea to restore S'akyamuni (not in his temporal manifestation in fleshly form, but as the Eternal and Infinite) to his proper place in the Buddhist Heavens. False brethren, calling themselves Buddhists, had given to S'akyamuni a place of inferiority. They had spoken of him as only a temporary manifestation of a part of the glories of some other Buddha, Amitābha or Vairoc'ana, greater than himself, and the simpler Sūtras of the Hīnayāna they had despised as containing a simplified Gospel watered down to suit the intelligence of the ill-instructed. Nichiren reversed this position. He had been much shocked on one of his journeys to find some children playing with an idol of S'akyamuni which had been discarded from the temple to make room for a new-fangled image of Amida, and he was resolved to make reparation for the insult which had thus been offered to the lawful Lord of Buddhism. "S'akyamuni," he said,

in one of his extensive writings,¹ "is the lord of this <term>Saba-world</term>, for three reasons—firstly, because he is the World-honored One for all sentient beings; secondly, because he is both father and mother of all sentient beings in this <term>Saba-world</term>; and thirdly, because he is the original and first teacher of all sentient beings in this <term>Saba-world</term>." Everything that the Jodoist said about Amida, Nichiren said about S’akyamuni. S’akyamuni was uncreated, without beginning, without end, and unlimited in every aspect. S’akyamuni was the Light of the World, had always been so, and would always remain so. Whatever teaching existed in the world, whatever hope there was for man’s ultimate perfection, all came to him from S’akyamuni, whose mercies were over all the world, but more especially over the fortunate inhabitants of the *<term>ichi-embudai</term>*²—India, China, and Japan—which had embraced his faith.

S’akyamuni’s teachings are summed up, said Nichiren (following here the teachings of the Japanese Tendai), in the *Hokekyō* or *Saddharmapundarika Sutra*, spoken on the Vulture’s Peak during the last few years of his earthly life.³ But he interpreted this sutra in a new manner, with great ingenuity.

<header>THE CREED OF HALF JAPAN</header>

The <term>Hokekyō</term>, in Nichiren's interpretation, was an Apocalypse containing a forecast of the things that would happen in <term>Buddhism</term> after the death of its founder. It deals with the "Millenniums" of <term>Buddhism</term>—the three periods, one of five hundred years and two of one thousand years each, which should cover what might be called the present dispensation. This conception is quite familiar to the entire family of Japanese <term>Buddhism</term>.

In the <term>Hokekyō</term> itself, the scene is set on <term>Vulture's Peak</term>, the favorite haunt of <term>Shakyamuni</term> in his later years. The Master, now an old man, is weary from teaching and has fallen into a trance. "His body was motionless, and his mind had reached perfect tranquility. As soon as the Lord had entered his meditation, there fell a great rain of divine flowers, covering the Lord and the four classes of hearers... and at that moment, a ray issued from within the circle of hair between the Lord’s eyebrows. It extended over eighteen thousand Buddha fields in the Eastern quarter." Nichiren took this trance as signifying the <term>Parinirvana</term> of <term>Shakyamuni</term>. Then comes a period of silence—the same period we have already noticed in our historical review of the Buddhist Church. This period is much longer for the Northern Buddhist, who knows nothing of <term>Ashoka</term> and passes directly from the <term>Vaishali Council</term> to the one held under <term>Kanishka</term>.

In the *<term>Seigōroku</term>* (p. 645), after listing the early patriarchs of Northern <term>Buddhism</term>, Nichiren adds that during their terms of office, not even the name of a single <term>Mahayana Sutra</term> (*sho-Daijo Kyo wa myoji mo nashi*) is to be found. On the following page, there is another passage in which he describes the astonishment and perplexity of the <term>Hinayana</term> doctors when <term>Ashvaghosa</term> and <term>Nagarjuna</term> began to propose their <term>Mahayana</term> doctrines. Nichiren’s thought was that the <term>Hokekyō</term>, as a type of Apocalypse, was far too advanced for the immediate disciples of <term>Shakyamuni</term>. For this reason, it lay fallow for several centuries, gradually winning recognition as the spiritual intelligence of the Buddhist communities increased.

<summary>Nichiren interprets the Hokekyō (Lotus Sutra) as a prophetic text that outlines the future eras of Buddhism, explaining that its delayed recognition was due to its advanced spiritual nature. The text describes the sutra's miraculous opening scene on Vulture's Peak and the historical transition from Hinayana to Mahayana doctrines.</summary>

## CHAPTER XXV

### "RISSHŌ ANKOKU RON"

The "Risshō Ankoku ron" is the title of Nichiren's essay which, when presented to the Kamakura Regent, brought upon its author all kinds of persecutions and troubles. It was Nichiren's warning against the evil paths which were bringing his country to decay. It has by no means lost its prophetic value today. In the last few months, I have come across two new Japanese editions of this essay, which Nichirenists tell us is as applicable to the Japan of today as it was to the Japan of Nichiren's time. To the best of my knowledge, the essay has never been translated into any European language until now.

It is written in the form of a dialogue. The reader should imagine the master of a house—who must be Nichiren himself—seated before his books in his study. The house is likely the hermitage that Nichiren built for himself among the sandhills behind Kamakura, where he gathered his earliest disciples and where he actually composed this historic treatise. A visitor comes to him and immediately dives into the subject closest to his heart.

*The Visitor.* We have seen many signs in the heavens and on the earth: a famine, a plague; the whole country is filled with misery. Horses and cows are dying on the roadsides, as are people, and there is no one to bury them.

<summary>This chapter introduces Nichiren's "Risshō Ankoku ron," a prophetic treatise written as a dialogue that warns of national decay and describes the suffering caused by famine and plague in 13th-century Japan. The author notes that the work remains highly relevant to modern Nichirenists and has not been previously translated into European languages.</summary>

<keywords>Nichiren, Risshō Ankoku ron, Kamakura Regent, Japan, prophecy, famine, plague, dialogue, Buddhism</keywords>

> “the seven troubles come merely as a matter of rotation, soon to be followed by the seven forms of prosperity,”⁵

Regarding the other forms of Buddhism and other Sūtras, including even the *Saddharma pundarika* and the Sūtras of the Shingon tradition, he uses four words to describe what our attitude toward them should be. “Give them up,” he says, “close the books, set them aside, and throw them away.”² Through this doctrine, he has misled thousands of his followers, both laypeople and clergy.

The *Kegon* was delivered in the heavenly regions; (ii) *Agon*, the elementary truth of the Agamas for ordinary mortals; (iii) *Hannya*; and (iv) *Hodo*, periods of apparent truth—that is, absolute truth adapted to the circumstances and capabilities of the listeners, or “accommodations”; (v) *Hokke-Nehan*, “absolute truth.” The controversy between Amidaists and others is over which Sutras most truly represent this final period: the *Saddharma-pundarika* or the Amida books. It is very difficult to decide; it is also very difficult to fit the three Amida Sutras into any specific place in the Canon.</note> Donran, Doshaku, and Zendo, however, seized upon an apparent truth and forgot the absolute truth that was still to come. They did not understand the full truth of Buddhism. Honen was worse than they were; instead of merely following them, he went even further and advocated for the giving up, closing, laying aside, and flinging away of all the many thousands of works in the Mahayana Scriptures, as well as all the innumerable Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and gods. However, there is no doubt about the joy with which the common people received this simplified doctrine, regardless of its source.</note>

# CHAPTER XXVI

## THE MONGOLS

In the year 1282, Nichiren, reviewing his own life, said that there were three things for which he considered himself deserving of recognition. <note>“Seigōroku.”</note> He had published his treatise, *<term>Risshō Ankoku</term>*, and presented a copy to the Regent at great personal risk to himself, thereby calling the Regent’s attention to the evils of the State and the only apparent remedy for them. Next, some years later, he had dared to tell the same exalted figure that the only safety for the State lay in adopting the doctrines which he himself so earnestly advocated. This boldness had almost cost him his life. And, lastly, not content with general warnings about the <term>Mongols</term>, he had foretold the exact time when the much-dreaded invasion was going to take place, and events had fully justified his prophecy.

We have spoken of Nichiren’s famous writing; we have also discussed the doctrines which he preached constantly. It remains for us to speak of the <term>Mongols</term> and their attempted invasion of Japan.

Central and North-Eastern Asia was for centuries the cradle of fierce and barbarous races which started out on careers of conquest and acquired permanent homes for themselves in the fertile and more favored districts of Europe. Scythians and Goths, Alans and Huns,

<summary>Nichiren reflects on his life, highlighting his bold warnings to the Japanese government and his accurate prediction of the Mongol invasion. The text begins to describe the historical background of the Mongol tribes emerging from Central Asia.</summary>

<keywords>Nichiren, Risshō Ankoku, Mongols, Japan, Scythians, Goths, Alans, Huns, Seigōroku, prophecy</keywords>

--- Page 344 ---

Bulgarians and Cumani, Yuëtchi and Uighurs, were merely “reshuffles of the same cards,”<note>H. E. Parker.</note> different layers, as it were, of the same peoples, going out from their homes in Central Asia to harass the civilized nations of two continents.

In the twelfth, thirteenth, and fourteenth centuries, it was the Mongolian power that made itself feared throughout the world.<note>I have consulted D'Ohsson's *History of the Mongols*, Karamsin's *History of the Russian Empire* (German translation), and Black, *Proselytes of Ishmael*.</note> The Mongols and the Tartars were, essentially, the aristocracy and *common people* of a large semi-barbarous tribe of nomadic herdsmen, hunters, and warriors, whose home lay to the north of China proper, around the Gobi Desert, by the banks of the Amur river, and among the mountains south of Lake Baikal. Here in the year 1162, in the tent of the tribal chief, a child was born who was given the name Temujin—a name later exchanged for that of Genghis Khan, or the "Perfect Warrior."<note>Some Japanese writers have chosen to identify Genghis Khan with Yoshitsune, the popular hero of the Minamoto, who disappears from Japanese history in the year 1189 at the age of thirty-one. No proof can be given for this assumption. It is based on the Sinico-Japanese reading of the name Minamoto Yoshitsune, which is *Gen Gikyō*, a fair approximation of *Genghis Khan*. Yoshitsune certainly had the same adventurous spirit found in Genghis Khan and his descendants, and the suggested identification is very flattering to some Japanese minds.</note> Genghis Khan in due time succeeded to the leadership of the Mongol and Tartar tribes (1206), and then began a series of victories, campaigns, and conquests, which truly overshadows the exploits of Alexander and Napoleon. The Mongol conqueror had this advantage over his two European rivals: he was able to pass his power and military genius down to descendants who were just as remarkable

<page-num>331</page-num>
->THE MONGOLS<-

and as talented as himself. The first conquests of the Mongols were in Northern China; their next exploit was the overthrow of the Chowaresmian Kingdom <note>The Khwarazmian Empire.</note>, which reached from India to the Caspian Sea, with its capital at Bokhara. From the Caspian to Russia was but a step; in 1237 (only thirty years after Genghis Khan's election), his grandson Batu, at the head of a Mongol army, had subdued Russia, burned Moscow and Khiew <note>Kyiv.</note>, and compelled the Russian princes to do him homage and pay tribute to the Great Khan, his uncle Octai <note>Ogedei Khan; spelled Octaï in the original.</note>, the son of Genghis, who ruled at Karakorum, somewhere halfway in a straight line between Pekin <note>Beijing.</note> and Lake Baikal. Entering Poland and Silesia, they were met by a German army at Wahlstatt in 1241, and, although victors in the battle, they pushed their advances no further in this direction. Instead, devoting themselves to the strengthening of their dominions in South Russia, they pushed their conquests into Hungary, drove the king of that country to take refuge on an island off the coast of Dalmatia, and advanced to within two days' march of Vienna. Their line of march was everywhere marked by terrible traces of vindictive cruelty. They spared neither age nor sex, neither town nor country, neither palace nor church. They had no respect for, and even less fear of, the chivalry of Europe. They knew that Christendom was a conglomeration of states hostile to each other; they knew, also, that the best elements in Christendom were frittering away their strength in vain attempts to recover the Holy Sepulchre. So long as it pleased Western Europe to keep up the Crusades, they did not trouble themselves much about attacking the Saracens. Nevertheless, in 1258, their Asiatic armies overthrew the Caliphate of Baghdad and destroyed that city; and when, between 1274 and 1279, Kublai Khan, the grandson and fourth successor of Genghis Khan, added the whole of China

When Kublai Khan was in the midst of his conquests in China, having already overthrown the Kin <note>The Jin dynasty.</note> dynasty, and being then planning the subjugation of the rival Sung <note>The Song dynasty.</note> dynasty, he remembered the Empire of Japan as having been at one time in the habit of sending presents to the Tang Emperors, which those rulers accepted as tribute. At once, in 1268, he sent an arrogant letter to the Regent, demanding the submission of Japan to the rule of the Mongol Khans, and the delivery of tribute in recognition of that suzerainty. We know the nature of that letter. The Mongols had for several years been sending the most insulting and arrogant letters to the Russian princes, the Kings of Hungary and France, the Emperor of Germany, and even the Pope, and the letter to the Regent of Japan was written in no less arrogant language than the other messages. But Hōjō Tokimune was a match for the Tatar Khan (were they not all chips off the same block? and might not Japanese blood have been mixed with that of the Mongol chiefs?), and he well understood the art of meeting arrogance with arrogance. The first letter was left without an answer. A second letter, sent with an embassy in 1271, was returned unopened. In 1274 Kublai sent a fleet of 150 ships, which ravaged Tsushima and Ikishima, and successfully landed at Imatsu in Chikuzen, an expedition which might have been very serious had not the Mongol commander been killed in battle and a large part of the fleet destroyed by a typhoon. The Regent was running tremendous risks in opposing a Power whose rulers openly boasted that they were lords over the whole earth; yet he never swerved from the line he had taken up of meeting arrogance with pride. In 1276, Kublaï sent an ambassador to Kamakura. Tokimune had him led out to Tatsu no Kuchi (the same spot that had witnessed the attempted execution of Nichiren), and there beheaded him. Two others, who came on the same errand, were beheaded at Hakata in Kyūshū as soon as they landed on Japanese soil. Further hostilities were now unavoidable. In 1279, Tokimune ordered the Daimyōs of Kyūshū and the West to prepare to resist a hostile invasion. In 1281, an Armada, carrying 100,000 Mongols and 10,000 Koreans, appeared off Dazaifu in Kyūshū, having ravaged the island of Iki on the way. The invaders landed at Goryū-san in Hizen, where they met with strenuous resistance. At the end of a week’s fighting, neither army could claim to have gained much advantage. Then came one of those terrible storms that from time to time visit the shores of Japan; the invaders were forced to look to the safety of their ships. They were literally “between the Devil and the deep sea,” and, being in that difficult situation, were practically annihilated. Of all the medieval nations of Asia and Europe that were forced to face those terrible conquerors in the heyday of their power, Japan was the only one that scored a complete victory. It was also probably the only one that absolutely refused to be cowed by Tartar bluster.

But we must not forget that our present concern with the Mongol invasion of Japan is its bearing on the religious history of that country.

Secondly, it is a certain fact that the religious world of Europe took a great deal of interest in the conversion of the Great Khan of Tartary to Christianity, and that several embassies were sent from Europe for that purpose. The matter was brought before the Council of Lyons in 1245 by Pope Innocent IV, and a resolution was reached that the Pope should send missionaries to the Mongol Emperor, urging him to abstain from further bloodshed and to turn to the true faith. In consequence of this resolution, Innocent IV sent two embassies, which left Rome the following year. All the accounts describe the Mongols as monotheists. There is one God in Heaven, the Ruler and Judge of all, and there is one Sovereign on Earth, whose privilege it is to rule over the whole world. "God in Heaven, the Khan upon Earth" was the motto they engraved

One result, however, must have followed from this strange fraternization—the various religions must have learned a good deal about one another from their close proximity at the Court.

Another fact, about which all the writers are agreed who have written about the Mongolian Court under the three or four immediate successors of Genghis Khan, is that, in addition to priests and monks of the various religions, there was a considerable number of laypeople from many countries. # CHAPTER XXVII

## THE BUDDHISM OF THE MUROMACHI AGE

The Hōjō Regents fell in the year 1333. Their downfall was due to many causes and had been in development for some time. The immediate and final cause was the combination of a genuine, significant grievance, which alienated the sympathies of the people, with the fact that the Imperial throne was occupied at the time by an Emperor of exceptional ability—the unfortunate Go-daigo (Daigo II).

The grievance was caused by the greed of Nagasaki Takasuke, the Minister of Hōjō Takatoki, the last of the Kamakura Regents. Takatoki was a very different person from the Saimyōji who resigned his high office to study the needs of his people, or the Tokimune who organized the forces that repelled the Mongols. He was a weak, vain man, preoccupied with intrigues against Shoguns, Barons, and Prelates, and he found no time to attend to the details of administration. He left all such unpleasant matters to Nagasaki Tadasuke, and the minister profited from the freedom his master gave him by selling rice to the people at very high prices during a period of famine. What made this outrage even more scandalous was that the rice had been stored by the earlier Regents for the purpose of free distribution in times of need.

The resulting unpopularity of the Regent gave

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the fall of the Hōjō Regents, picking up from the previous page's discussion of how the Regent’s unpopularity provided Emperor Go-daigo with the chance to attempt an Imperial restoration.</meta>

Go-daigo saw an opportunity for restoring the Imperial House to its rightful position in the country. The design was not accomplished at one blow; but Go-daigo had staunch supporters in Kusunoki Masashige, Nitta Yoshisada, Ashikaga Takauji, and other loyalist knights and barons, and with their help Kamakura was destroyed, and the Hōjō Regency overthrown. It had been an unconstitutional usurpation from the very beginning, but it had done good service to the country in the earlier years of its existence.

Unfortunately, however, Go-daigo quickly offended his chief supporters by the grants of land and fiefs that he made to unworthy parasites and favorites, instead of to the warriors whose arms had placed the reins of administrative power in his hands. The men who had, as it were, made the Emperor, felt, perhaps, that they could also unmake him, and Ashikaga Takauji, seeing an opportunity for turning the discontent against the Emperor to his own advantage, raised the standard of revolt and proclaimed himself Shōgun in the place of Moriyoshi, the newly appointed Shōgun of the Imperial Blood,¹ whose scandalously luxurious life had quickly shown him to be unfit for his office.

The Civil War that was thus commenced was a terrible one for Japan. It led to the setting up of a Rival Dynasty, intended to supplant the House of Go-daigo,

For a period of sixty years, there were two rival Emperors in Japan—the Southern Line, that of Go-daigo, which was clearly the legitimate one, holding its own in Kyushu and the South; while the Northern Line, which was the usurping one, was recognized throughout the North. The strife ended in a compromise, which was, however, clearly to the advantage of the usurping North, for it was Go-Komatsu, of the Northern Line, who reunited the two dynasties upon the abdication of Go-Kameyama of the South; and after the death of his son Shōkō, the inheritance passed, with Go-Hanazono, Go-Tsuchimikado, etc., to the descendants of Sukō, the third Emperor of the Northern Line. Go-Komatsu reigned from 1392–1412; but his power was only what the Shōgun Yoshimōchi permitted him to have.

Let us follow the history of the country closely for a few years longer.

The Emperor Shōkō (1413–1428) was raised to the throne by Yoshimochi upon the abdication of his father Go-Komatsu. By this act, Yoshimochi deliberately broke his word; for the understanding between the two dynasties had been that the Emperors should be chosen alternately from the North and the South, and it was now the turn of the South. The appointment was not made without opposition, and many of the supporters of the Southern Dynasty rose in rebellion at the breach of faith; but the South had allowed the Sacred Treasures¹ to pass into the keeping of the North, and so long as the North held them, they felt themselves to be safe. Among the supporters

<page-num>344</page-num>

In the North there were also dissensions, for the Ashikaga Shoguns had offices of power and profit to bestow upon their followers, and there were many rivalries and jealousies among the great families who desired to increase their territories and wealth. Yoshimochi was not as great a man as his father Yoshimitsu, who had subdued the country in favor of Go-Komatsu, had built the beautiful *Kinkakuji* at Kyoto, and dealt with the Ming—the Chinese successors of the Mongols; but he had inherited a large amount of authority and influence, which he used without scruple. In 1418, he killed his own brother, whom he suspected of aiming for the Shogunate. In 1423, he became a monk, but continued to be the power behind the throne until his death five years later.

Shōkō’s successor, Go-Hanazono (1429–1465), had a long reign of thirty-six years entirely filled with civil wars. The great families of Hosokawa, Hatakeyama, Yamana, Shiba, etc., were engaged in a constant scramble for territories, power, and wealth. The Shogun Yoshimasa, who lived in luxury in his palace at Muromachi, added fuel to the fire by a high-handed act which produced a schism in his own family. He had been childless for a long time, and, an heir being imperatively necessary, had adopted his own younger brother Gijin, whom he took from a monastery for that purpose. The next year, however, a son was born to him, and he then proposed to disinherit Gijin and send him back to the monastery. But Gijin, having tasted the pleasures of secular life, refused to go, and the chaotic state of the country made an appeal to arms seem like an obvious remedy. The Civil War which followed is known in Japanese history as the *Ōnin no tairan*. It lasted for over ten years (1467–1477); then, after a short interval, it broke out afresh at the death of Yoshimasa, after which it raged for an unbroken century. When the

### BUDDHISM OF THE MUROMACHI AGE 345

Emperor Go-Hanazono’s son, Go-Tsuchimikado, died in A.D. 1500; his corpse remained unburied for forty days because the Imperial Palace lacked the money to bury him. Such was the poverty to which the Imperial House was reduced.

Go-Kashiwabara reigned from 1501 to 1527. The fighting was still going on, but a few of the more enterprising daimyos—the Mori, the Shimazu, the Otomo, the Hōjō of Odawara, and others—were organizing their territories into semi-independent states, and a few well-administered daimyates here and there stood out like oases in the wilderness of confusion and distress. In the succeeding reign, that of Go-Nara (1527—1558), the same kind of thing continued. Some of the great families, the Ouchi and the Hosokawa, etc., disappeared; while others, such as the Mōri and the Hōjō, increased in power and wealth. When the Emperor Go-Nara died, neither he nor the Ashikaga Shōgun had any actual power. But Nobunaga was twenty-four years of age, Hideyoshi twenty-one, and Ieyasu fifteen, and there was the first dawn of the hope for peace and order. St. Francis Xavier and his band of Jesuits were in the country, and Christianity was being openly preached.

And what, we may ask, did Japanese Buddhism do during this period of terrible misery to alleviate the sufferings of the people and to bring about a better state of affairs?

It would seem as though its record throughout the thousand years of its existence in Japan had been nothing but a dismal chronicle of broken promises. How often have we not read in the pages of this history of distinguished and saint-like men—Shōtoku, Kōbō, Dengyō, Hōnen, Shinran, Nichiren, and the fathers of the Zen sects—who, moved by the afflictions of their times, set their hands

Alas, in every case these hopes were shattered, and in every case, the disciples of the reformers exhibited in their lives those very vices which the reformers had sought to eradicate. When the saddest hour of Japan arrived, the Buddhist sects were not only powerless to help their countrymen, but they had actually become active aiders and abettors of the very evils of those distressful times.

The Tendai monks of Hieizan and Mi-idera had been old offenders in the practice of turning their monasteries into barracks and making religion the servant of political intrigue and oppression. The other sects followed suit. The disciples of Kōbō had turned the monastery of Kōya San into a military encampment. They had become divided into two sects; the leader of the schism (called the Shingi-ha of Shingon) had founded a rival temple at Negoro, in the province of Kii. This daughter temple, which could raise an army of 3,000 fighting monks, waged wars on its own account and ended by being besieged, taken by assault, and razed to the ground by Hideyoshi in 1585. The Jōdo-Shinshū were the ruling power in Echigo, Kaga, and other provinces, where they lived just like the Prince-Bishops of Germany, ruling their states as temporal barons or lords. These Hongwanji armies had more than one pitched battle with their brethren of Hieizan, and the Monto power counted for a great deal in the civil quarrels of the time. The older Jōdo, the followers of Hōnen, were quieter in their demeanor, but there were times when even they took up the sword to maintain their opinions;<note>A story which reflects well on their honor is told of this sect. The Nichirenists quickly became the greatest offenders of all. They quarreled among themselves, as the sectarian differences between the various sub-sects or schisms of Nichirenism were clearly and antagonistically marked. They quarreled with the Monto and Jodo; with the Tendai, they had a formal private war of their own, which history calls *Tembun Horan* (1532), the "Religious War of the Tembun period."¹ They quarreled with the authorities. They expressed a principle known as *Fuju fuze*, "not giving and not receiving," which may be translated as "uncompromising." The term was adopted as a denominational name by one of the many Nichirenist sub-sects, and the extremist *Fuju-fuze* sub-sect of Nichirenism was banned by the Tokugawa Shoguns at the same time as Christianity. All kinds of disreputable characters joined the ranks of the Buddhist clergy to escape from offended Justice (as little as existed in those sad times);² wandering *Ko-muso* spread the doctrines of the Nichirenists, and both sides appealed to Nobunaga, who appointed a day to hear their debates. The night before the debate, he sent for the Jodoist leaders. "If the decision should be given in your favor, what punishment do you think should be given to your adversaries?" "None at all," they replied; "we only want to have a clear statement of the Truth." Nobunaga then turned to the Nichirenists. "We," they said, not knowing what the Jodoists had answered, "should demand the death of our obstinate opponents." The verdict was given in favor of the Jodoists; the full penalty was extracted from the defeated Nichirenists.

A few bright names, to be sure, adorned the period. Such was, for instance, that of Rennyo Shōnin (1415–1499), the poet, preacher, and religious writer, and eighth Patriarch of the Shinshu, who was driven from the capital by the Hieizan monks, who were jealously enraged by the influence he had gained through his sanctity. Shortly afterward, he was able to return to Kyōto as Patriarch of his sect, but again, and despite Imperial protection, the Hieizan monks attacked him, burned the Hongwanji, and drove him into exile. He then went into the provinces of Echizen, Kaga, and Noto, preaching, building temples, and exhorting people to a better life with such vigor and success that his own Shinshu clergy rebelled and set fire to the monastery in which he was living. In spite of all his efforts, a civil war among his own people followed. It is known as *Ikkōtō no ran*, "the civil war in the Ikkō sect," and filled all the earlier years of the sixteenth century, until Nobunaga arose to put it down with a strong hand. It is from Rennyo Shōnin's time, and from the schism that these family squabbles produced, that we get the division of the disciples of Shinran into the two Hongwanji of the East and of the West, which still remains.

# CHAPTER XXVIII

## THE PERIOD OF THE CATHOLIC MISSIONS

If <term>St. Francis Xavier</term> and his associates had been acquainted with <term>Nichiren’s</term> apocalyptic interpretation of the <term>Hokekyō</term>, it is possible that they might have been tempted to apply the fulfillment of the prophecy to themselves. They might have claimed that they and theirs constituted the multitude headed by the four great <term>Bodhisattvas</term> who were supposed to appear in the middle of the last Buddhist Millennium for the purpose of preaching salvation to a world that was forgetting the Law.

The Buddhism of Japan, in the course of its long development since the time when the Chinese Emperor <term>Ming-ti</term> had his epoch-making dream, had on more than one occasion rubbed shoulders with Christianity. But it had either been the Christianity of the Near East—the vague syncretism of <term>Gnostics</term> and <term>Manichæans</term>—or the dull apathy of the <term>Nestorians</term>, who were deprived of vigor as a consequence of their estrangement from the main body of their fellow believers. When the <term>Franciscans</term> reached Beijing in 1300 A.D., and when the <term>Jesuits</term> landed at Kagoshima in 1549, the <term>Mahāyāna</term> of the Far East found itself confronted for the first time with the militant Christianity of Europe, which had gone halfway around the globe to challenge it to mortal combat.

It is not my intention to write even a sketch of the history of the Catholic missions of the sixteenth century.

Others <sup>1</sup> have done this at considerable length and with carefully weighed judgment. My task is somewhat different. It is to trace the movements, if any, that were going on in <term>Buddhism</term> during this period, and the effects, if any, that the <term>Jesuit Missions</term> had on the native faiths of <term>Japan</term>. In doing this, I shall be obliged frequently to mention the Christian propaganda, though without intending to make it the main purpose of this chapter.

Here let me say, by way of introduction, that none of the histories—not even that of <term>Murdoch</term>, who is no great friend of the <term>Jesuits</term>—can establish anything against the personal integrity or honesty of the <term>Jesuits</term>, who had the lion’s share of the Christian evangelization of that time, and who have had to bear more than their fair share of the hatred and ill will which has, ever since the seventeenth century, clung to the <term>Catholic</term> name in <term>Japan</term>. That they made mistakes is quite evident; but the best of men may do that. They came to the <term>Far East</term> without having shaken off the traditions and atmosphere of the <term>Far West</term>. They brought with them what I may call the “Walls-of-Jericho” theory of <term>Christian Missions</term>—the theory that they only had to blow the Gospel Trumpet long and loud, and behold! the walls erected by long-standing error and falsehood would fall down in a moment, and leave the way open for the armies of Light to make a triumphant entrance into the besieged city. The Jesuits first landed in Kyūshū; their labors on that island formed the first chapter of their activities in Japan. At the time, Kyūshū was divided into several small principalities—practically independent kingdoms—which hardly recognized the authority of Kyōto at all and were busily engaged in contests for supremacy on the island. Here, at first, the newcomers were eagerly welcomed, for wherever the priests went, the merchants followed with the guns and implements of war so dear to a warlike people. Consequently, the missionaries had their choice of many <term>daimyates</term> for their evangelization. Even the Buddhist <term>bonzes</term> spoke well of them and received them kindly, for Christianity seemed to them to be merely one more sect of the Buddhist faith. Indeed, it was described this way by Ōuchi Yoshitaka, lord of Suwo, when Xavier crossed the Straits of Shimonoseki into the territories of Yamaguchi. But it was soon found that the new religion was not at all disposed to accept such a humiliating classification. The Jesuits were as intolerant of other creeds as the Nichirenists themselves, and the kind sentiments of the Buddhist monks soon changed to feelings of suspicious hostility.

But before these feelings turned into acts of serious opposition, the Jesuit leaders concluded that if the friendship of local <term>daimyos</term>, such as Ōtomo and Ōuchi, was so advantageous to their cause, much more might be expected from the favor of the Emperor and Shōgun. They accordingly made their way to Kyōto to win the favor of those rulers, little knowing that the Emperor and Shōgun counted for so little in those days that the reigning Emperor Go-Nara could not have been crowned—just as one of his predecessors could not have been buried—had one of his generous subjects not paid the expenses of the coronation. The subject in this case was Ōuchi, the <term>Daimyo</term> of Suwō and the friend of Xavier.

The Jesuits did not succeed so easily in gaining a footing in the Imperial City, though it ultimately became one of the chief seats of their activity. However, their stays in Kyōto brought them into contact with Nobunaga, and thus ultimately with Hideyoshi, Iyeyasu, and Iyemitsu. It is around these names that the religious as well as the political history of Japan centers during the eventful century of the Catholic Missions.

Oda Nobunaga (1534–1582) was fifteen years of age when he succeeded his father as the head of a small <term>daimyate</term> in Owari. At first, he did not realize the importance of his position during this critical period of his country's history; the supreme power in Japan lay waiting for the first bold man to seize it, and his youthful escapades earned him the nickname of *Bakadono*, “the Fool-Lord.” He was recalled to a sense of duty by one of his retainers, who wrote and presented to his master a dignified protest against his follies, and then underscored his point by committing suicide. Nobunaga mended his ways and, fortunately for himself, found among his retainers another faithful adviser—an older man, Tokichirō, who is considered to have been an excellent judge of human character.

Acting on Tokichirō’s advice, in 1557 he suppressed a revolt among his own subjects which his foolish conduct had caused, and in which his own brother had participated. Three years later, his neighbor Imagawa—the lord of Suruga, Tōtōmi, and Mikawa, and one of the most powerful of the great princes—set out for Kyōto with an army. He intended to seize the persons of the Emperor and <term>Shōgun</term>, and thus to legalize his own designs of making

A second envoy reached Nobunaga, urging him to make his way to the capital, and this message was supported by an appeal from Ashikaga Yoshiaki. Yoshiaki was the brother of the last Shōgun, Yoshiteru, who had been assassinated by his ministers, Miyoshi and Matsunaga. Nobunaga's successes brought a great deal of ill will from rivals and competitors, and especially from those enemies whom he had been fortunate enough to defeat. Nobunaga returned and wiped out the families of Asakura, Asai, Miyoshi, and Sasaki, who now disappear from history. The suppression of this rebellion brought him into conflict with Buddhist monks. Around the same time, he came into personal contact with the Jesuits.

His heart remained absolutely untouched by Christian truths; his head saw the advantages to be gained from an alliance with the Christian organization.

Nobunaga next turned against the Monto priests. Under Kennio Kosa, they had established themselves in what is now Osaka, in a strategic position of prime importance which they had fortified extensively. It took him several years to subdue this priestly fortress, and it was not until 1580 that he became its master. "The slaughter," says Murdoch, "had been immense, and the stench of burning flesh poisoned the air for miles around." A small number of survivors surrendered and were spared, but the fortress itself was burned to the ground. Hideyoshi remarked in his later years that Kennio "had given Nobunaga more trouble than all his other enemies combined."

In the meantime, a dispute had broken out between the Jodo priests and their bitter enemies in the Nichiren sect. Nobunaga was invited to act as a judge, a role he accepted on the condition that the losers of the debate would agree to be beheaded. During the debate, the Nichiren champions were forced to admit they were defeated. Nobunaga not only enforced the agreed-upon penalty but also imposed a fine on the entire sect so heavy that the Nichiren priests could not pay it. They subsequently withdrew to remote provinces where Nobunaga’s influence had not yet been felt.<sup>1</sup>

Thus, Nobunaga became the "scourge of God" to the worldly and materialistic priests of the various Buddhist sects, and the Jesuit Fathers felt that the Dictator’s drastic measures were clearing the way for them. It was reserved for Iemitsu, his grandson and the third Shōgun of the Tokugawa line, to become a persecutor, and Iemitsu was a very different person from his grandfather.

With regard to Buddhism, Ieyasu was in a position to make use of it for his own purposes, and he did so with great success. Nobunaga and Hideyoshi had forever broken the military power of the Buddhist monasteries. There was no fear of a new Hieizan or Negoro rising from the ruins of the temples, and Hideyoshi had managed to effectively impoverish the sects that the sword had spared through his heavy taxes. Ieyasu was able to use the broken forces of the clergy for his own purposes. He encouraged the monks and turned them into a kind of religious police. For himself, he claimed to have been converted to the Tendai faith, and his great mausoleum at Nikko was entrusted to Tendai hands, as was also the great temple he built at Uyeno Park. But the women of his household seem to have divided their attention between the Nichiren and Jōdo sects, and the Jōdo Temple of Zōjōji was likewise founded by him.

In 1654, a little while after the death of Iemitsu (1651), a celebrated priest was summoned from China to become the founder of a new and enlightened sect of the Zen. His name was Ingen, and the sect he founded is known as the Ōbaku, a small body, but always influential. It shows the practical character of the Buddhism which the Tokugawas tried to propagate that Ingen's sect adopted modern Chinese as the language in which the Buddhist Scriptures and services should be read. The great mass of the Buddhist worship is in a dead language, the Chinese of fifteen centuries ago; in the Ōbaku worship, the ordinary Sinico-Japanese of the modern literary style has been, as it were, consecrated to the purposes of religion.

One part of Nichiren's contention had been now fulfilled. He had said that but one Sun ruled in the Heavens, but one Lord in the religious world, but one Ruler in the Empire. The Empire had been unified, and there was but one Ruler. It is true that it was not yet the legitimate ruler, but the reign of the usurper seems to have been necessary for the welding together of the whole.

## CHAPTER XXIX

### THE BUDDHISM OF THE TOKUGAWA PERIOD

After Ieyasu's victory at Sekigahara (October 21, 1600) over Ishida Kazushige and the *daimyos* who supported the claims of Hideyoshi's family, Japan became, for the first time in many centuries, practically united under one leader and was finally in a position to feel itself a national unit. It is true that the Imperial House still continued to sit on the throne in Kyōto as before; however, its position was a shadowy one, and the new Dictator made provisions for it to remain so. In readjusting the country's finances, an annual income of 150,000 *koku* of rice was deemed sufficient to meet all the expenses of the Imperial establishments, and even that modest sum came, not from any special appropriation, but out of the generous income of four million *koku*,¹ which the Shogunate appropriated for itself. The Imperial House thus became the pensioner of the Tokugawas, and it is a matter for wonder and admiration how, under most adverse circumstances, the Court at Kyōto managed to retain even the modicum of power and influence that remained in its hands. Those who believe in a Divine Providence which shapes the destinies of nations will readily see in

<summary>Following the Battle of Sekigahara, Ieyasu Tokugawa unified Japan and established a political system that marginalized the Imperial House, providing them only a modest stipend while the Shogunate controlled the nation's vast resources.</summary>
<keywords>Ieyasu, Tokugawa period, Sekigahara, Shogunate, Imperial House, koku, Japanese unification</keywords>

it was a gracious design watching over the line of the lawful sovereigns until the right moment should arrive for the Imperial House to resume its rightful place as the active head of the nation.

The *Pax Tokugawica*, which Ieyasu inaugurated, rested on very solid foundations, for it was supported by all the best elements of the Japanese social system.

It rested, of course, mainly on the power of the sword. The Hōjō Regents had demonstrated the potential importance of a comparatively small principality carefully administered on strictly military lines. Nobunaga, Hideyoshi, and Ieyasu walked in the footsteps of the Kamakura Regents, and, during the early days of the Shogunate, the samurai of the Tokugawa clans maintained the superiority of their military traditions. "After a victory," said Ieyasu on the bloody day of Sekigahara, "tighten the strings of your helmet"; and the maxim was acted upon by his descendants. The new capital at Yedo was the symbol of the new power, which could here expand itself, without a rival, as freely as the Hōjō had done at Kamakura. It was the rallying point for the Tokugawa clansmen and partisans, who were constantly brought together and taught to appreciate the strength that lay in their unity of obedience and discipline: it was the ruin of the distant daimyos from Kyushu and the South, whose attendance was required for half the year at the Court of the new Dictator. It reduced the Imperial Power to a shadow and a sentiment, for there was no use in raising the standard of loyalist revolt, or in occupying the city of Kyoto, so long as the military forces of the country were centered in and directed from the recently strengthened Castle of Yedo.<note>The ancient Castle of Yedo, on the site of the present Imperial Palace in Tokyo, was built in 1456 by Ōta Dōkwan.</note>

<summary>Following his victory at Sekigahara, Ieyasu Tokugawa established a stable military government centered in Yedo, effectively centralizing power and marginalizing the Imperial Court. This "Pax Tokugawica" relied on strict military discipline and the strategic oversight of regional lords to ensure lasting peace and Tokugawa dominance.</summary>

### BUDDHISM OF THE TOKUGAWA PERIOD

Again, it is certain that Ieyasu had the support of the merchant classes in the administrative reforms he established. Even the closing of the country to foreign trade by the government of his grandson Iemitsu was carried out without much protest. The truth is that closing Japanese ports to foreign commerce affected no established Japanese interests. The volume of trade was very small: the millions in Japan had no use for the items Europe brought them, and after those long years of anarchy and trouble, the country's products were not much greater than what the nation needed for its own private consumption. The Southern Daimyos, crushed and crippled, no longer had any need for the guns and military ammunition that the Portuguese had brought a century earlier; whatever was needed in this regard was made by the Japanese themselves. Closing the ports to foreign ships injured no one at the time; it only prevented the creation of new and artificial needs among the people, and the merchants were quite content with that. In the development of internal commerce, which has always been a major feature of the country's mercantile life, they could see their profits ahead of them. They wanted peace and a steady market, and Ieyasu's administration guaranteed them both.

And the Buddhists were content; for Buddhism has always been a merchants' religion, and in the prosperity of the commercial classes, there would always be something to spare for the alms bowl of the mendicant monk. They had good reason to be quite satisfied. Ieyasu did not treat them as Nobunaga or Hideyoshi had. He summoned them to his councils; he invited them to instruct him in the tenets of their religion; he declared himself a convert to the Tendai sect; he decorated his

Allied with the Buddhists were the Confucianists and the Shintoists. The former had, as we have already had more than one occasion to mention, always cultivated good relationships with the Zen priests. Only two factors were excluded from the new national life—the Catholics, and the extreme left wing of the intolerant Nichirenists. Everyone knows (who has read anything of Japanese history) that the persecutions of Christians were of a most severe and cruel character, and that the Buddhist clergy became the willing instruments of the Shogunate in the execution of a cruel legislation. No noblemen or persons of any position survived that ordeal, except through apostasy: a few of them were martyred, the rest saved their lives through a timely return to the religion of their fathers. It was reserved for the farmers of Kyūshū to set an example of heroism under persecution worthy of the earliest ages of the Christian Church. To him, both were anti-social forces because they preached celibacy and withdrawal from the world. Kaibara Ekiken (1630–1714) renounced Buddhism at an early age; Tani Jichū (1598–1680) was a lifelong enemy of the monastic system and of the religion of Shakyamuni <note>The historical Buddha</note>. These men were not anti-religious. "What does it mean," asked one of Kinoshita Junnan's (1621–1698) students, "when we are told that 'Heaven is Intelligent, Upright, and One'?" "It means," Kinoshita answered, "that Heaven knows what we have in our minds at the very moment our thoughts arise, that It judges with impartiality, and that It is always the same." Yamazaki Anzai (1618–1682), who was scolded as a boy by his monastic superiors for laughing in "chapel," excused himself by saying that "that fellow Shaka <note>Shakyamuni</note> talks such nonsense!" And yet that same man, whose doctrines contributed greatly to the eventual restoration of the Imperial House, possessed many qualities worthy of a Christian. The same may be said of Kaibara Ekiken. In the non-Christian world, it would be difficult to find a judge more fair and impartial than Arai Hakuseki, or a philosophical guide more trustworthy than Kaibara.

It must be admitted that when the Buddhist clergy had everything their own way—as they did once for a few unfortunate years during the eighteenth century—they gave their allies plenty of reason for grief. But the fifth Shogun, Tsunayoshi (1680–1709), was a literary pedant with a superstitious mind. He built schools, reformed the calendar, and spent large sums of money on the encouragement of art. On these projects he wasted his wealth, and by neglecting the sound political advice of his Confucianist advisers, <note>For example, Dazai Junsui. See articles by R. J. This did not make him popular with the common people, and even the submissive Court of Kyoto began to be restless when the state of the Shogunal treasury would not permit the payment of the annual allowance of 150,000 *koku* of rice. Then, as though this were not enough, Tsunayoshi gave himself up to monkish advisers and embarked on a series of most extraordinary decrees.

The taking of animal life was absolutely forbidden; kittens and puppies were saved from the water barrel, and the Yedo police had to keep track of all the litters that were born and make accurate lists of their sex, markings, and so on. A samurai of Akita, who had the misfortune of killing a swallow, was put to death for the crime, and his entire family was sent into exile (1686). The entire body of legislation was based on the theory that life is sacred—unless it was human life, which in the Japan of the Middle Ages was far from being treated with respect. The good citizens of Yedo were powerless against their master, but they took their revenge in lampoons about the *Inu-Kubō*, or Dog-Shogun, as they nicknamed him. Tsunayoshi was murdered by his wife in 1709, and it took the great Arai Hakuseki all his energy and skill during the next two reigns to restore the Shogunate to popular favor. The Tokugawas were almost always fortunate in the loyalty of their ablest followers. <note>Among these must be counted the celebrated O-oka Tadasuke, the judge under Tokugawa Yoshimune (1716–1745), whose wise though eccentric judgments did much to reconcile the people to the Shogunate.
