Another group, not to be neglected, was the small band of Dutch scholars. The policy of the <term>Shōgunate</term> had left one little loophole, the Dutch factory at <term>Deshima</term>, for the entrance of Western thought. The books and scientific instruments which came into the country in this way were enough to keep alive in many hearts the eager desire for a wider and less restricted interaction with the wonderful, because unknown, nations of the West.

All these elements combined against the <term>Shōgunate</term> and its allies, the Buddhist congregations. In the course of the two centuries between the accession of <term>Iemitsu</term> and the arrival of <term>Commodore Perry</term>, the <term>Shōgunal</term> Government had lost its dominant military strength, and the Buddhists had lost that chastened meekness which had characterized them after <term>Nobunaga</term>, <term>Hideyoshi</term>, and <term>Ieyasu</term> had brought them under control. It would have happened in any case, for the simple reason that intelligent Japan agreed on wanting it.

In the course of time, the prohibitions against Christianity were allowed to drop; the promulgation of the Constitution formally guaranteed to every subject of the Empire the free exercise of his religion.

Nichiren, who may be looked upon as the prophet of Buddhism, called the attention of his hearers to the condition of Japan as he saw it, distracted by many lords and many faiths. The subsequent religious development of the country has been, as it were, a commentary on that prophecy. The terrible troubles of the sixteenth century—the wars and the bloodshed—were the necessary instruments in the hands of Providence for the working out of the first step in the elevation of the country. Nobunaga and Hideyoshi hammered on the hot iron, and Ieyasu welded it into a consistent whole, able to stand the test of time.

Japan was united into one body, under one ruler—but the ruler was a usurper, and the legitimate House of Sovereigns did not seem to be in a position, at the time, to do what the powerful Tokugawa was able to accomplish. In this chapter I have tried to show the attainment of the second step. The Meiji Era has seen Japan still united, and united under its lawful sovereign. No one can read the moving history of the Imperial House of this country, with its strange vicissitudes and its long-continued afflictions, without feeling that it has had some divine mission to perform. Nothing but the special protection of God could have preserved that House through all the troubles of so many centuries, and these special gifts of divine protection generally imply some very special motive in the Giver.

<header>THE CREED OF HALF JAPAN</header>

Japan seems to have one more step ahead of her. She is now one nation, united under one ruler, who has the legitimate right to rule. When she has taken her next step and has reached the acknowledgment of the one God, who also has the legitimate right to rule, she will have reached the true peak of her moral greatness. In that fulfillment, the Mahāyāna, which has for so long occupied our thoughts, will find its proper place and its deserved honor and reward; for it also, like Nobunaga and the Jesuits, has been but a piece on the chessboard played by the hand of God, and not one such piece

> ->"shall be destroyed,<-
> ->Or cast as rubbish to the Void,<-
> ->When God has made the pile complete."<-

What means shall be employed in future development, or what other pieces shall be moved in the course of this interesting game, is a matter of secondary importance. The real player in the game is God, and we men—the best of us—are but pawns and knights, and here and there a bishop. Only, when the last move takes place and the game is about to be finished, I will ask for myself "that I may be there to see."

## CHAPTER XXX.

### RECAPITULATION

It will be my pleasant task in this concluding chapter to summarize for my reader everything that I have presented in a long and rather lengthy narrative.

First, I would like to call attention to the remarkable parallels between the history of Christianity and that of Buddhist *Mahāyāna*.

Both faiths began in that marvelous sixth century before Christ, which saw the beginnings of so much that has benefited mankind. Philosophy began for humanity in Greece, in India, and in China. *Shakyamuni* was founding a religion which, if not perfect, is at any rate one that deserves our most respectful sympathy and affection; meanwhile, the later representatives of Judaism—the exilic and post-exilic prophets and psalmists, the teachers of the law, and the great Fathers of the later Faith of Jerusalem—were distinctly raising the faith of Israel to a higher level in preparation for a great event to come.

The great event came. It arrived at the right moment for both East and West. It was like a stone thrown into the middle of a large pool, falling with a mighty splash and creating ripples that move outward equally in all directions, never resting until they break against the distant shores. We have been accustomed to watching the ripples that have moved West and North from the splash made in the world's religious history by the Advent of Christ. We

I have tried in this book—tentatively and with the uncertain step of a pioneer going through untracked brushwood—to trace the ripples that flowed out eastward from the splash of the stone. Occasionally, I have seemed to see the traces of Christ distinct and clear, though they are few and far between, and not sufficient in number or quantity to allow for anything very elaborate in the way of deduction and inference. But during the whole of the first millennium of the Christian era—a period corresponding very nearly with the millennium of <term>Image Law</term> of which Buddhists speak—I find the same phenomena both in the East and the West: a chaos of heresies, each claiming to be heard as the sole exponent of the Truth, and amidst them all one fact: the proclamation that there is one Being who has given Himself for man, so that man through Him might have life. The proclamation in the West, in spite of heresies and the many superstitions of a dark age, is clear and distinct. In the East, it is not so distinct; it is like a lotus seed, sown deep down in the slime at the bottom of the pool. It is there, and it grows, but it takes some time to reach the surface.

With the end of the first millennium of Christendom comes the period which the Buddhist knows as <term>*Mappō*</term>, the "last days," the period of the "Destruction of the Law." As this period begins, the Christian, forgetting the spirit he is of, grasps the sword for the conquest of the Holy Land and for the extermination of the Albigenses and other heretics. In the middle of this period, the disciples of the inquisition-loving Nichiren—who was nevertheless a seer—find themselves brought face to face with the disciples of the inquisition-loving St. Dominic. The seventeenth and eighteenth centuries witness the establishment of a permanent Inquisition in Japan. Yet this same period also sees the loud proclamation, so comforting to the outcast and the sinner, of Salvation by Faith alone, through the mercies of One whose compassion has been known from the beginning—though under different names—to both the Mahāyānist and the Christian. St. Francis and Wycliffe (they will forgive me for pairing their names in this way) are the Christian counterparts of Hōnen and Shinran. The Schoolmen, too, whose work was to reconcile Aristotle and Christ, find their counterparts in the work of the great Japanese scholars of the Middle Ages, who sought to reconcile Shakyamuni and Confucius.

The first Christian millennium did not pass away without its warning of impending change. The Muslim threat profoundly moved Christendom, just as the same threat challenged China under the Tang dynasty. In both parts of the world, the meaning of the warning was largely misunderstood, just as the similar warning from the Mongols was likely misunderstood at the beginning of the second millennium.

This second millennium, which is the Buddhist period of the *Mappō*, is not yet over; but might we not say that we have received a warning of an impending change? # THE CREED OF HALF JAPAN

The year 1757 saw the declaration of the Seven Years' War, which brought in its wake the rise of Prussia, the unification of Germany, and all that Germany represents in world civilization. It saw William Pitt the Elder come to power in England and the beginning of those operations against France which led to the conquest of Canada and the eventual securing of Anglo-Saxon supremacy on the North American continent. It witnessed the Battle of Plassey, which secured British supremacy in India and, for the first time in world history, enabled Eastern and Western thought to meet and compare notes. Had it not been for Plassey, there would have been no Oriental studies, and possibly only a few Christian missions in India. It saw, in France, those attacks on Christianity led by Montesquieu, Rousseau, and the Encyclopedists, which led to the French Revolution. It found the Wesleys at the beginning of their work. Surely it was a year full of profound significance.

This significance becomes deeper for us, whose hearts are in Japan, when we remember that it also found Kamo Mabuchi preparing to retire from his active duties in order to devote himself to those historical studies which ultimately led to the restoration of the Imperial House and the entry of Japan into the community of civilized nations.

The mills of God grind slowly. There is no hurry or haste in the workings of Providence. A long time has passed since the Swedish seer made his announcement, but today it requires no prophetic gift to tell us that a new era is at hand, that the old is passing away, and that a new day is dawning.

One thing never passes away. Heaven and Earth may change, the entire political and social structure of the world may perish, but God's Word will not. Whatever form the new world may take, it will have a religion, and that religion will be based on the Eternal Truths.

<page-num>385</page-num>
# RECAPITULATION

The Christian—and I will claim no title for myself other than that—finds it to be his duty, his pleasure, and his pride to present those Eternal Verities quietly, soberly, and temperately to the people among whom he lives. He must do this with sympathy, for even the most eloquent sermon will inevitably fail to touch the people's hearts if it lacks empathy.

Buddhism is the religion of the vast majority of the Japanese people. The farmers are Buddhists, as are the shopkeepers and the general population. The women of the upper classes are Buddhists, and so are most of their husbands, if they are honest with themselves. Buddhism does not seem to fit well with the frock coats and top hats that are the pride of the Japanese gentleman; therefore, he pretends to set it aside as something obsolete. However, a time comes for everyone when the frock coat and top hat fail to protect the head and heart against the terrors of that inevitable and universal change, and then I find that the Japanese man turns, after all, to the faith he spent his life pretending to ignore. One only has to learn the Japanese language and study the literature of modern daily life to understand the deep hold Buddhism has on the thoughts and affections of the people.

If Christianity wishes to win Japanese Buddhism for Christ (and surely that is an inspiring goal), it must take these things into account. Buddhism requires its own special preachers—men of sympathy and patience who, while proud of being Christians, are yet willing for Christ’s sake to follow <term>S’akyamuni</term> in all things that are lawful and honest. These are men who can say to the Buddhist, "I will walk with you, and together we will go to Him to whom you say <term>S’akyamuni</term> himself bore witness." It is primarily for such readers that I have ventured to write this *outline of Mahāyāna History*.
